- A 48-year-old receives regular sustained-release oxycodone and PRN immediate-release opioid for persistent radicular pain, with OSA and duloxetine use.
- **Before surgery:** verify total actual dose and last administration
- Review MRI/neurological deficit and possible surgically reversible pathology
- Discuss baseline opioid continuation, safe alternatives if nil by mouth, OSA monitoring, postoperative function and a patient-specific taper.
- **Intraoperatively:** multimodal analgesia and appropriate local/regional adjuncts; cautious titration of additional opioid, avoiding combinations that increase sedation.
- **After:** maintain baseline coverage, add monitored short-acting rescue (PCA if appropriate), frequent sedation/respiratory evaluation, neuro exam and early rehabilitation.
- **Discharge:** provide one reconciled opioid chart, avoid unexplained duplicate long-acting medications, agree how the rescue opioid will be reduced and maintain named follow-up.
- If pain suddenly changes with weakness or urinary retention, investigate compressive pathology, not “opioid tolerance”.

## 7.7 Clinical example: acute fracture with severe chronic nociplastic pain

- Separate pain from the fracture (acute nociceptive, treat fracture, regional option, appropriate rescue) from chronic widespread pain (long-standing functional/sleep problem that cannot be cured by an escalating fracture opioid).
- Validate both, prevent withdrawal if already taking opioids, use protected mobility and patient-specific pacing, and adjust regional therapy based on neurovascular safety.
- A patient who already reports pain 8/10 at baseline will not reliably reach a target “below 3/10”; assess fracture-specific pain on movement and safe mobilisation.
- Plan an analgesic taper as fracture heals, while continuing rehabilitation of the chronic condition.

items.title: 8. Opioid use disorder and maintenance medicines: methadone, buprenorphine and naltrexone
items.body:
## 8.1 Understand each medicine before choosing anaesthesia

### FOUNDATIONS FIRST  |  Agonist, partial agonist and antagonist: affinity versus efficacy

- **Affinity** is how strongly a drug binds to its receptor; **intrinsic efficacy** is how much signalling it produces after binding.
- Methadone is a full μ agonist, with variable, long elimination and a shorter useful analgesic duration than its maintenance/withdrawal-suppression action.
- Buprenorphine is a **high-affinity partial μ agonist**.
- “Partial” does not mean clinically weak or ineffective; it means the maximal receptor response differs from a full agonist.
- Its high affinity can reduce the incremental effect of a new full agonist, yet supplemental fentanyl or hydromorphone can still provide analgesia under careful monitoring.
- Naltrexone is an **antagonist:** it occupies μ receptors without activating them, reducing the effect of opioid agonists.

- This pharmacology determines the perioperative plan: **usually continue** a verified methadone or buprenorphine maintenance programme and separately treat surgical pain; **naltrexone** requires anticipated blockade, specialist planning and monitored rescue if an operation needs opioids.
- A buprenorphine/naloxone combination is not equivalent to naltrexone: the naloxone has minimal systemic antagonist activity when the sublingual product is used correctly.
- The drug’s formulation, indication, last dose and programme contact matter as much as the name in the notes. [R11, R12, R18]

![Methadone, buprenorphine and naltrexone: same receptor, different effect](set16-fig9.png)

- **Methadone** is a full µ-agonist with long and variable elimination; it prevents withdrawal/craving for OUD but a once-daily maintenance dose does not reliably provide around-the-clock postoperative analgesia.
- Important issues are accumulation, respiratory depression with other sedatives, QT prolongation and interactions, especially in hepatic dysfunction or electrolyte disturbance.
- **Buprenorphine** is a high-affinity partial µ-agonist, often combined with naloxone in a sublingual preparation (naloxone has minimal effect when properly taken sublingually).
- It provides maintenance and some analgesia; receptor occupancy can reduce the apparent effect of additional full agonists, but **adequate acute analgesia remains achievable**.
- **Naltrexone** is a competitive µ-antagonist given orally or as long-acting injection for alcohol/OUD indications; it blocks ordinary opioid analgesia and has no intrinsic opioid analgesic activity.
- A previous opioid use disorder may now be in remission, and a person on naltrexone may have **reduced opioid tolerance**, especially after abstinence.
- The three drugs require different acute-pain strategies. [R10–R12]

| Treatment | Preoperative approach | Acute pain strategy | Key transition/overdose concern |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Methadone maintenance** | Verify dose and formulation with programme/prescriber; normally continue. Check QTc, K/Mg, sedatives, missed doses and other risk. | Continue maintenance for withdrawal prevention; add condition-specific regional/multimodal analgesia and separate short-acting opioid if needed, carefully monitored. | Avoid inadvertent double dosing or a large unverified substitution; ensure uninterrupted maintenance and specialist follow-up. |
| **Buprenorphine maintenance** | Do not routinely stop/taper for surgery; involve regular prescriber and acute pain team. Record dose, last dose and schedule. | Multimodal/regional; divided buprenorphine dosing for analgesia may be considered with prescriber; supplemental titratable high-affinity full agonist in monitored setting when needed. | Stopping can destabilise OUD and increase overdose/relapse risk; taper supplemental full agonist and coordinate the usual buprenorphine dose. |
| **Oral naltrexone** | Elective painful surgery may justify supervised interruption (often around 72 h, context dependent). Record exact last dose, liver function and relapse/withdrawal plan. | When antagonist active: nonopioid and regional modalities are especially important; resistant severe pain needs specialist-supervised, highly monitored opioid strategy. | Opioid sensitivity may rise as antagonism wanes. Restart only after opioids have been cleared and an agreed opioid-free interval under addiction advice. |
| **Long-acting injectable naltrexone** | Date of last injection is critical; elective surgery may sometimes be scheduled late in dosing interval after specialist advice; blockade can persist weeks. | Avoid assuming a standard full agonist dose works; regional/nonopioid strategies, high-dependency rescue for severe pain. | Delayed transition from blockade to high sensitivity; coordinate any future injection carefully and avoid precipitated withdrawal. |

- These are **principles**, not a universal national washout protocol.
- A person’s history of relapse, planned procedure, current clinical urgency and availability of monitored care may make the usual elective stopping interval inappropriate.
- The **2021 multisociety buprenorphine consensus**, and subsequent perioperative reviews, recommend against routine buprenorphine discontinuation.
- The ANZCA Blue Book chapter on naltrexone (2023) is a targeted companion resource. [R10, R11, R18]

## 8.2 Methadone: keep maintenance separate from analgesia

**Before surgery:**

- Contact the maintenance programme, verify the actual dose and last administration (including take-home doses), ask about missed days (tolerance may fall after interruption), and review ECG/QTc if risk warrants.
- Review other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte abnormalities, CNS depressants, liver disease and OSA.
- Arrange a plan for nil-by-mouth periods with the dispensing team; **do not assume a once-daily oral dose can be switched to an equal numeric IV dose**.

**During surgery:**

- Maintain normal safe general/regional anaesthesia; use multimodal analgesia and consider regional techniques.
- **After surgery:** continue verified maintenance and provide an additional appropriate acute-pain plan, sometimes involving short-acting opioid/PCA with specialist input.
- Respiratory risk remains because methadone accumulates and concurrent additional opioids/sedatives add effects.
- The benefit of splitting the daily dose for analgesia in some settings needs agreement with the maintenance team.
- **Discharge:** ensure no missed maintenance supply, communicate added short-term opioids and taper, and confirm the next dispensing arrangements.
- If several methadone doses were missed, seek expert re-initiation guidance rather than blindly resuming a former high dose.

### Methadone-specific clinical decisions beyond “continue the dose”

**Why analgesia and withdrawal prevention diverge:**

- Methadone has a long and individually variable elimination half-life, whereas a maintenance dose’s useful analgesic effect is shorter.
- Consequently, once-daily supervised dosing can prevent withdrawal/craving without treating a fresh laparotomy or fracture.
- In an exam, distinguish treatment of:
- **a.** Established OUD
- **b.** Acute nociception
- **c.** Coexisting chronic pain.
- Do not count the once-daily dose as if it were a titratable postoperative rescue opioid.
- A patient may require additional short-acting analgesia, but methadone accumulation and co-sedatives still make ventilatory depression possible.

**Verify and reconcile precisely:**

- Contact the dispensing programme or named prescriber; confirm whether the dose was administered that morning and whether the patient has take-home supply, which can lead to duplicate dosing.
- When several doses are missed, tolerance and safe restart dose may change—this is a pharmacy/addiction-team decision, not a reason to automatically prescribe the old full dose.
- If oral dosing is interrupted, discuss a verified route/dose plan before the expected dose is due.
- Conversion to parenteral methadone is **not** a 1:1 milligram substitution; local formulation and bioavailability differ.
- Check interactions with antibiotics, antifungals, antidepressants and other sedatives, and investigate QTc risk when clinically indicated; correct potassium/magnesium and assess syncope or arrhythmia history.
- QT effects do not imply that every patient requires daily ECGs or automatic suspension.

**Example:**

- A stable patient on supervised once-daily methadone presents with an infected fracture.
- Verify the maintenance dose and avoid withdrawal.
- Treat infection, operate when needed, provide regional analgesia if safe, scheduled non-opioids and carefully titrated additional opioid in a monitored setting.
- Reassess respiratory status and function, and communicate every added opioid to the community team.
- If multiple methadone doses were omitted during a complicated ICU stay, re-initiation needs specialist review rather than an unexamined return to the former dose.
- At discharge, any temporary divided methadone strategy or added opioid must be reconciled with the ordinary programme, preventing multiple prescribers or unsupervised escalation. [R10–R12, R23, R25]

## 8.3 Buprenorphine: high receptor affinity is not a reason for abandonment

- High affinity and partial agonism mean buprenorphine can occupy a substantial proportion of µ receptors while leaving some receptor availability; clinical effects of supplemental opioids depend on drug, dose, time, competing occupancy and tolerance.
- **Stopping routine maintenance** can cause withdrawal and destabilise treatment, while the expected opioid analgesic requirement may remain high.
- Consensus recommendations therefore favour **continuation** in many operative settings.
- Use a strong **multimodal** foundation: surgical infiltration and regional analgesia, appropriate acetaminophen/NSAID, selected ketamine or alpha-2 adjunct and clear patient communication.
- For severe pain, use carefully titrated supplemental full agonist (commonly fentanyl or hydromorphone in a monitored environment) or patient-specific adjustment of buprenorphine frequency in collaboration with an addiction/pain prescriber.
- Avoid telling the patient that “opioids won’t work”; repeated unsupervised high doses can become dangerous when receptor occupancy changes. [R11]

- A useful **PACU decision:** if severe pain persists, first exclude surgical harm/withdrawal, confirm maintenance administration and local block efficacy, then use a monitored supplemental strategy and reassess sedation/ventilation.
- **Discharge** must reconcile the original buprenorphine regimen with any temporary full agonist and clarify who tapers the latter, so that the patient does not leave with contradictory prescriber advice.

### Formulation, receptor occupancy and operational management

**First establish the indication and product:**

- Sublingual buprenorphine or buprenorphine–naloxone at an OUD maintenance dose is not the same as a low-dose transdermal preparation prescribed for pain, or a long-acting injection with sustained effect.
- The naloxone in a correctly taken sublingual combination has little systemic antagonist effect; it does not ordinarily cause opioid blockade in the way naltrexone does.
- Receptor occupancy increases with dose but is not an on/off lock: supplemental full µ-agonists can provide analgesia.
- Nevertheless, they may require cautious titration, and their effects can change as buprenorphine exposure and postoperative conditions change.

**Build a team-approved plan:**

- Consensus favours continuing usual buprenorphine perioperatively in most patients with OUD; routine preoperative cessation or tapering risks withdrawal and OUD recurrence.
- For an expected highly painful procedure, arrange regional/neuraxial analgesia where suitable, non-opioids and appropriate adjuncts in advance.
- With the maintenance prescriber, consider dividing the same total daily buprenorphine dose into more frequent doses during acute pain (analgesic duration is shorter than suppression of withdrawal), or supplemental carefully monitored high-affinity full agonists for breakthrough pain.
- Do not independently impose a ceiling on opioid treatment just because buprenorphine is present, but equally do not deliver unmonitored serial large opioid doses and hope for displacement.
- A temporary change of maintenance dose is an **exceptional shared decision**, not an automatic protocol.

**Failure and rescue:**

- Persistent severe PACU pain should trigger examination of the operation, haemorrhage/compartment problems, block adequacy, withdrawal, last buprenorphine dose and respiratory status.
- Contact the acute pain service before escalating combinations of opioid, gabapentinoid and sedative.
- For discharge, ensure the maintenance prescriber knows whether any extra full agonist was used and who will supervise its rapid but safe reduction; define the schedule for returning to the person’s usual maintenance frequency if it was temporarily divided.
- If buprenorphine was interrupted despite the usual recommendation, re-start requires a deliberate plan to avoid precipitated withdrawal in the presence of substantial full-agonist exposure. [R11, R23–R25]

### Plan for long acting injectable buprenorphine

- Use the 2025 New Zealand opioid substitution treatment guidance and product data to identify the preparation and next injection date.
- A depot continues releasing drug after a missed injection.
- Preserve treatment continuity with the prescriber and provide separate acute pain treatment.
- For knee arthroplasty consider operation-specific regional and non-opioid techniques, and assess movement, motor strength and ventilation when adding opioid rescue.
- A respiratory ceiling in isolated buprenorphine exposure does not remove the risk of combining medicines.

- [NZ opioid substitution treatment guidance 2025](https://www.health.govt.nz/publications/new-zealand-practice-guidelines-for-opioid-substitution-treatment-2025) · [Medsafe Buvidal Monthly product information](https://www.medsafe.govt.nz/DbSearch/ProductDetail?Product_id=21082) · [Multisociety perioperative buprenorphine recommendations](https://doi.org/10.1136/rapm-2021-103007) · [BJA Education total knee arthroplasty analgesia 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.004)

## 8.4 Naltrexone: the classic Final Examination trap

### FOUNDATIONS FIRST  |  Why escalating opioids during naltrexone blockade can become dangerous later

- When naltrexone is active, a normal amount of opioid may have a much smaller effect than expected.
- The unsafe reflex is to repeatedly give larger and longer-acting opioid doses until something happens.
- **As antagonist activity wanes**, those previously ineffective agonist doses may become active and produce serious sedation or ventilatory depression.
- In a patient who has remained opioid-free, baseline tolerance may also be reduced.
- This creates a dynamically changing hazard rather than a static “opioids will not work” rule.

- For elective surgery, coordinate any interruption and restart with the usual addiction prescriber; the oral formulation is very different from a depot injection.
- In emergencies, do not delay critical surgery solely for washout: use multimodal non-opioid measures and regional analgesia where safe, and reserve opioid rescue for a staffed setting able to manage ventilation.
- Record who will decide when opioid agonists have been stopped long enough for safe naltrexone restart.
- Exact intervals are formulation-, drug- and patient-dependent and cannot be inferred from the diagram. [R12, R18]

![Naltrexone: the danger changes as opioid blockade wears off](set16-fig10.png)

- Oral naltrexone is an antagonist, **not buprenorphine**; it can render standard opioid doses ineffective while blockade persists.
- A person maintained on it after opioid dependence may no longer be tolerant to opioids.
- The clinically dangerous periods are:
- **a.** **active blockade**, tempting the team to escalate opioid doses dramatically
- **b.** **waning blockade**, when those doses may abruptly produce profound respiratory depression.
- Up-regulated receptor sensitivity after antagonist therapy is a plausible additional consideration, but clinical unpredictability is more important than a fixed “receptor count”.

**Elective surgery:**

- Confirm exact product, dose, last dose and expected pain; discuss with addiction/pain prescriber.
- Holding oral naltrexone for about 72 hours before an opioid-requiring operation is a commonly cited approach, but there is interindividual variability and a relapse-risk trade-off.
- Intramuscular depot naltrexone may block for several weeks; elective timing needs specialist agreement.
- Maximise nonopioid and regional strategies before and after surgery.
- If opioids are needed after a sufficient antagonist-free interval, treat the patient as potentially opioid-sensitive, with monitored titration.

**Emergency surgery while blockade is active:**

- Do not delay needed surgery solely to wait for antagonist washout.
- Discuss a realistic **regional analgesia** plan where safe, surgical local infiltration, acetaminophen/NSAID where appropriate, carefully governed ketamine/alpha-2 agents and other nonopioid measures.
- If severe pain remains unmanageable and high-dose opioid rescue is unavoidable, this requires an expert decision in a setting with airway/ventilatory and haemodynamic monitoring.
- Do not prescribe large repeated ward doses because a first dose appears ineffective.
- Continue assessing for other causes of severe pain.

**When and how to restart:**

- Do not restart naltrexone while the patient still needs or has recently received opioid agonists, as antagonist administration can abolish analgesia or precipitate withdrawal.
- A suitable opioid-free interval depends on the agonist, formulation and exposure—commonly **5–7 days or longer after the final short-acting opioid** in some perioperative naltrexone pathways and often 7–10 days in standard OUD initiation guidance, with longer intervals for long-acting agonists—with supervised assessment and addiction prescriber instruction.
- Protect recovery from OUD throughout, arrange follow-up and provide overdose education because tolerance may be reduced.
- This restart plan belongs in the preoperative plan when possible, not as an afterthought on discharge.

**Evidence from exam reports:**

- The 2025.2 Final SAQ on **high-dose oral naltrexone and emergency spinal surgery** highlighted failure to identify competitive opioid antagonism, insufficient perioperative analgesic alternatives, and failure to plan safe resumption.
- The 2020.1 examiner report noted that some candidates confused naltrexone with buprenorphine.
- A passing answer should clearly state mechanism, elective versus urgent plan, rescue setting, washout uncertainty, and postoperative restart.
- These are historical examiner emphases; current local guidance governs actual patient care. [R19]

## 8.5 Untreated active OUD: treat pain and addiction together

- Assess intoxication, withdrawal, injection-related infection/endocarditis, bloodborne infections, pregnancy where relevant, trauma history, patient goals and capacity.
- Avoid stigmatising labels.
- **Acute analgesia remains necessary** regardless of illicit drug history.
- Clarify what was used and when, current tolerance and contamination risks of the drug supply.
- Treat respiratory depression urgently and monitor for recurrence after naloxone (its duration may be shorter than the opioid).
- For acute pain with OUD, combine appropriate analgesia with **early addiction-team assessment** for initiation/continuation of effective MOUD and overdose-prevention planning.
- In a person declining MOUD, still provide evidence-informed acute pain treatment, a safe discharge plan and access to nonjudgemental follow-up.

- A person with high opioid tolerance can experience both severe acute pain and withdrawal in hospital.
- **Do not confuse withdrawal management with analgesia**.
- A maintenance programme may stabilise withdrawal but additional acute analgesia is still required.
- Likewise, increasing short-acting opioid doses to treat withdrawal without an overall plan increases harm.
- For discharge, consider take-home naloxone, safe supply limits, infectious disease and mental-health care, and a clear named contact.
- Some patients need supervised medication administration rather than standard PRN ward ordering.

### Treating pain without perpetuating untreated OUD

- A patient presenting after injury with recent non-prescribed fentanyl or heroin use may have **acute nociceptive pain, opioid tolerance, withdrawal, intoxication and a substance-use disorder simultaneously**.
- Assess immediate airway/ventilation, mental status, last use, other sedatives, infection risk and the patient’s priorities.
- Investigate traumatic injury with the same diligence as in anyone else.
- Where possible, explain that analgesia and treatment for OUD are compatible objectives: do not force the patient to choose between treatment of a fracture and a discussion of addiction care.
- Offer a non-stigmatising assessment and specialist addiction consultation, and arrange naloxone, overdose education, appropriate infection screening and community follow-up.

**Avoid confusing withdrawal management with sufficient analgesia:**

- A medication for opioid use disorder can stabilise cravings/withdrawal yet leave significant fracture or postoperative pain requiring separate nonopioid, regional and sometimes short-acting opioid treatment.
- Conversely, repeated doses of short-acting opioid alone do not constitute evidence-based long-term addiction treatment.
- Starting buprenorphine requires assessment of recent full-agonist exposure and withdrawal state, since inappropriate timing can trigger severe precipitated withdrawal; low-dose initiation pathways exist in some specialist services but should not be improvised as an exam “universal regimen”.
- Acute respiratory compromise from intoxication takes priority over maintenance planning; support ventilation and use naloxone as indicated.
- Discharge requires a genuinely arranged link to ongoing treatment, not just advice to “see GP.” [R10, R11, R23–R25]

### Why methadone, buprenorphine and naltrexone are not interchangeable

- Maintenance treatment is separate from acute analgesia.
- General formulary safety checks help, but a formulary is not a comprehensive reference on addiction-treatment medicines.
- Methadone is a long-acting full µ-agonist; once-daily maintenance suppresses withdrawal/craving longer than it provides useful analgesia.
- Buprenorphine has strong receptor affinity but partial agonist efficacy: a full agonist may still provide analgesia after careful, monitored titration, despite receptor competition.
- Naltrexone is a pure opioid antagonist and creates the opposite immediate problem: full agonists may initially have little effect, while sensitivity can increase as blockade wanes. [R35, pp.
- 1176–1179]

• Methadone: verify with the supplying programme, maintain or safely substitute if unable to take orally, and treat surgical pain separately. Consider QT, electrolytes, co-sedatives and the danger of dose duplication or an unverified restart after several missed doses.

• Buprenorphine: current expert consensus usually supports continuation rather than routine preoperative cessation. Explain that high affinity does not mean that additional opioid analgesia is impossible. A regional/multimodal plan and coordinated postoperative prescriber are essential.

• Naltrexone: distinguish oral from depot formulation, document the last dose and obtain a specialist plan for elective interruption, opioid rescue and restart. The 72-hour oral hold quoted in some older sources is a common elective approximation, not a universal washout or an excuse to delay urgent surgery.

A common exam error is to use a single “opioid dependence” plan for all three drugs. In an answer, first state agonist/partial agonist/antagonist, then explain the implications for withdrawal prevention, acute pain, toxicity as drug exposure changes and follow-up.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book 2023, Whately and Stead on naltrexone](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/bitstream/11055/1178/1/Blue_Book_COMBINED_v10.pdf) · [BJA Education opioid-tolerant patients](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw049)

items.body:
- The relevant Final exam verb is to **describe anaesthetic implications and perioperative risk**, not to produce a general psychiatric textbook.

## 9.1 Alcohol misuse: intoxication, dependence and withdrawal are different problems

### FOUNDATIONS FIRST  |  Why a dependent patient withdraws even when they initially look well

- Chronic heavy alcohol exposure enhances inhibitory **GABA** signalling and reduces excitatory **NMDA-glutamate** effects acutely; the nervous system adapts by weakening inhibition and increasing excitatory drive.
- When alcohol is suddenly removed, excitation becomes relatively unopposed.
- The clinical result may be tremor, anxiety, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, agitation, hallucinations, seizures or delirium tremens.
- A patient admitted after surgery may therefore develop withdrawal many hours later despite not appearing intoxicated on arrival.

- Separate **acute intoxication** (airway protection, aspiration risk, hypoglycaemia, consent and trauma), **withdrawal** (autonomic and neurological toxicity treated through an alcohol-withdrawal protocol) and **chronic organ disease** (cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, malnutrition, coagulopathy).
- Screen previous complicated withdrawal and last drinking; monitor appropriately; use locally approved benzodiazepine-based regimens and thiamine for patients at risk.
- Check sodium, potassium, magnesium, phosphate and glucose.
- In an unstable, delirious or intubated patient, a symptom score dependent on patient responses may be unreliable; assess alternative causes of agitation and use an ICU-appropriate protocol. [R26]

- Preoperative assessment covers amount/pattern/last drink, previous severe withdrawal or seizures, liver and cardiac disease, malnutrition/thiamine deficiency, GI bleeding, infection, anaemia/thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy, aspiration risk, other substance use and capacity/consent.
- **Acute intoxication** impairs judgement, airway protection and haemodynamic stability; it can increase aspiration/trauma risk, mask head injury and affect drug responses.
- Consider postponing elective surgery where safe.
- **Urgent surgery** still requires safe airway management and identification of reversible metabolic/traumatic problems.
- Chronic heavy use can increase anaesthetic requirements in some circumstances while cirrhosis, acute intoxication and malnutrition may reduce tolerance of standard doses; avoid a universal “alcohol increases MAC” rule.

- **Withdrawal** typically follows a fall in heavy sustained exposure and may progress from autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, insomnia and agitation to hallucinations, seizures or delirium tremens.
- Assess previous history and use a validated local monitoring pathway (e.g. symptom-triggered protocols where reliable), with appropriate benzodiazepine treatment and specialist escalation when severe.
- Give **thiamine** promptly in malnourished/high-risk patients (before or alongside carbohydrate replacement rather than allowing care to be delayed).
- Check K/Mg/phosphate, glucose, dehydration, liver function and sepsis.
- Consider that delirium may also reflect intracranial injury, hypoxia, sepsis, medication toxicity or Wernicke encephalopathy—do not attribute every confused patient to alcohol withdrawal.

**Intraoperative:**

- Secure airway according to aspiration and urgency, consider altered circulation/coagulation and liver disease, anticipate withdrawal after admission, treat pain appropriately, and avoid under- or over-sedation.
- **Postoperative:** monitor for withdrawal, respiratory suppression, delirium, infection and poor nutrition; use addiction referral, medication reconciliation and a compassionate discharge plan.
- High-dose opioid plus alcohol/benzodiazepine exposure substantially increases ventilatory risk.
- For eye/trauma presentations, also consider patient cooperation, ocular pressure/foreign body precautions and aspiration; detailed ophthalmic management remains in its designated set.

### Perioperative alcohol risk stratification and a withdrawal plan

- **Ask quantitatively** about usual intake, last drink, previous morning drinking, recent attempts to stop, seizures/delirium tremens, previous detoxification, prior withdrawal under anaesthesia, other sedatives and malnutrition.
- Assess intoxication separately from chronic dependence.
- A patient who appears sober on admission may still develop withdrawal over the next several days.
- Examine vitals, hydration, confusion, tremor, liver disease and cardiomyopathy; order indicated FBC, liver tests, electrolytes (especially Mg/K/PO₄), glucose and coagulation studies, with targeted ECG/echo.
- Do not use normal liver enzymes or absence of a smell of alcohol to exclude dependence.
- In elective surgery, plan supported cessation and withdrawal risk mitigation early; active intoxication, infection, haemodynamic instability and uncontrolled withdrawal may justify deferral if surgery can safely wait.

**Three syndromes need different treatments:**

- Acute intoxication raises aspiration, airway, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, trauma and drug-interaction risks; assess capacity and protect the airway.
- Withdrawal reflects neuroadaptation (reduced GABAergic inhibition with compensatory excitatory activity) and produces tremor, autonomic hyperactivity, agitation, hallucinosis, seizures and sometimes delirium tremens.
- Chronic organ damage includes hepatic dysfunction, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy, peripheral neuropathy, cytopenias and nutritional deficiency, each modifying drug effects and perioperative risk.
- Withdrawal can coexist with a positive blood alcohol level in a heavily dependent patient.

**Risk-based management:**

- Use a hospital alcohol-withdrawal pathway, with a validated risk assessment for severe withdrawal (e.g. PAWSS where used) and an ongoing symptom assessment.
- CIWA-Ar is **not a diagnostic test** and may be unreliable in delirious, non-communicative, intubated or medically unstable patients: use an appropriate observable/ICU scale and specialist judgement instead.
- Benzodiazepines are usual first-line therapy for moderate/severe alcohol withdrawal or prophylaxis in high-risk patients; choose agent, symptom-triggered versus fixed approach and monitored setting using local policy and liver function.
- Phenobarbital is an alternative/adjunct for experienced teams, with additive respiratory toxicity risk.
- Provide thiamine, nutrition, fluid/electrolyte correction and monitoring for seizures, arrhythmias, aspiration, over-sedation and delirium.
- Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy promptly with the local **treatment-dose parenteral thiamine pathway**, rather than assuming a prophylaxis dose is adequate.
- Definitive alcohol-use treatment and supported follow-up are required; a successful withdrawal course is not treatment of the underlying disorder. [R26]

**A useful exam case:**

- A daily heavy drinker is agitated, tachycardic and hypertensive 36 hours after laparotomy.
- Examine for haemorrhage, sepsis, hypoxia, opioid withdrawal, pain, urinary retention and delirium as well as alcohol withdrawal.
- An isolated high CIWA score in a patient with sepsis does not establish alcohol withdrawal.
- Begin a protocolised withdrawal response and thiamine if indicated while treating other causes; review whether the ward can safely provide the required monitoring and sedative doses.
- Avoid assigning increasing benzodiazepines to “pain” without reassessing mechanism.

## 9.2 Illicit substances: mechanism and timing determine risk

### FOUNDATIONS FIRST  |  One core concept: stimulant intoxication is not the same as a past positive urine test

- Methamphetamine and cocaine increase catecholaminergic activity through different mechanisms and may cause acute hypertension, tachycardia, myocardial ischaemia, arrhythmia, hyperthermia, agitation and seizures.
- Some patients with prolonged heavy use may then have impaired endogenous catecholamine responses and develop hypotension during anaesthesia.
- Thus the same drug history can predict very different haemodynamics depending on **when it was taken and the current physiology**.

- Ask which substance, route, amount, last exposure, co-ingestants and current symptoms.
- A urine test may remain positive after important acute effects have resolved and can fail to detect some synthetic substances.
- For elective surgery, make decisions from clinical toxicity and urgency; for emergency surgery, manage actual hyperthermia, coronary risk, airway, blood pressure and organ injury, with direct-acting vasopressors often preferable if catecholamine depletion is plausible.
- Do not assume every person who uses drugs is intoxicated or that reported pain is unreliable.

| Exposure | Anaesthetic implications | Reasoned response |
|---|---|---|
| **Stimulants (methamphetamine/cocaine)** | Acute sympathomimetic state: tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmia, coronary ischaemia, hyperthermia, agitation; later catecholamine depletion can cause profound hypotension. | Evaluate current clinical toxicity rather than urine-screen result alone; postpone elective surgery in overt intoxication, stabilise emergencies, monitor ECG/temp, treat agitation and avoid uncontrolled sympathetic stimulation. For hypotension consider direct-acting vasopressors rather than relying on indirect catecholamine release. |
| **Opioids/heroin/fentanyl-contaminated products** | Variable tolerance, intoxication or withdrawal, respiratory depression, infection, OUD, adulterants. | Assess ventilation and last exposure; secure adequate acute analgesia, prevent withdrawal, engage addiction team, plan naloxone/harm reduction. |
| **Cannabis** | Possible tachycardia, altered anxiety/cognition, airway irritation with smoking, possible delayed gastric emptying and drug interactions; chronic and acute effects differ. | Ask formulation, dose, last use, route, intoxication, and cardiopulmonary implications; avoid categorical claims that all users need a fixed anaesthetic dose change. |
| **Sedatives (benzodiazepines, GHB, other CNS depressants)** | Additive depression with opioids/anaesthetics, withdrawal risks after chronic use; GHB withdrawal can be severe. | Verify exposure, prevent abrupt inappropriate cessation, anticipate airway/ventilation and withdrawal monitoring. |
| **Injected substances** | Endocarditis, skin/soft-tissue infection, hepatitis/HIV and difficult access may coexist. | Examine for systemic illness, obtain targeted investigations, use safe asepsis/vascular access, coordinate infection and substance-use care. |

- An **asymptomatic positive screening test** does not establish acute intoxication, and a negative routine screen does not exclude all synthetic agents.
- Explain elective decisions using clinical status, urgency and expected benefit; emergency surgery requires stabilisation and monitoring, not automatic refusal to provide anaesthesia.
- Use respectful language and local security only for genuine risk, not as a substitute for care.

### Substance-specific perioperative phenotype and first response

| Exposure | Important perioperative hazards | Practical anaesthetic and postoperative implications |
|---|---|---|
| **Methamphetamine/amphetamines** | Acute tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, agitation, arrhythmia, myocardial ischaemia, rhabdomyolysis; after prolonged use possible catecholamine depletion and hypotension. | Decide if acute intoxication makes elective surgery unsafe. In emergencies, control agitation/hyperthermia and assess ECG, electrolytes, CK and organ injury as indicated; induction may reveal hypotension. Choose haemodynamic support based on observed physiology and local toxicology guidance. |
| **Cocaine** | Sympathomimetic vasoconstriction, ischaemia, arrhythmia, seizures, hyperthermia and aortic pathology; a positive urine screen can outlast intoxication. | Assess current symptoms and vital signs rather than declaring every historical exposure an automatic cancellation. For acute toxicity, manage ischaemia/arrhythmia, benzodiazepine-responsive agitation and temperature with expert advice; avoid an unnecessary stimulant–vasopressor cascade. |
| **Non-prescribed opioids, including fentanyl** | Tolerance and withdrawal may coexist with overdose, respiratory depression, other sedatives or adulterants; infection and blood-borne exposure may matter. | Airway/ventilation take priority in intoxication; naloxone as indicated. Verify recent use before initiating an OUD agonist; plan baseline withdrawal prevention, separate acute analgesia and overdose prevention at discharge. |
| **Cannabis** | Variable tachycardia, anxiety, airway irritability with smoking, potentially altered anaesthetic requirements; chronic frequent use may be associated with postoperative nausea and vomiting or hyperemesis. | Ask product, route, frequency and time last used. Assess acute intoxication and capacity; avoid assuming cannabis is an opioid-sparing strategy or applying a universal anaesthetic dose change. |
| **Benzodiazepines/non-prescribed sedatives** | Additive opioid/anaesthetic respiratory depression; withdrawal after abrupt discontinuation may cause agitation, autonomic changes and seizures. | Check actual daily use and last dose, avoid sudden unexplained withdrawal, and plan monitored continuation/substitution or specialist withdrawal management as indicated. |

**Exam decision rule:**

- First establish whether the patient is acutely intoxicated, in withdrawal, or has remote use without current physiological effects.
- Then assess airway/respiratory, cardiovascular, neurological and renal consequences; review interactions with anaesthetic drugs; decide whether surgery can wait; and provide a recovery/withdrawal plan.
- A urine drug screen may support context but cannot precisely determine current intoxication, timing, tolerance, or whether reported pain is genuine.
- For an emergency operation, treat the physiology and protect staff/patient while avoiding stigma; for elective work, a careful reassessment and shared decision is preferable to an unqualified positive-screen rule. [R23, R27]

### Act on the observed intoxication and withdrawal phenotype

- For alcohol-related delirium use an objective monitored approach when the patient cannot participate in CIWA-Ar.
- Give prompt parenteral thiamine when indicated and treat hypoglycaemia immediately.
- In acute stimulant toxicity give suitable sedation and supportive care, and use direct vasopressors for hypotension when needed.
- The 2025 AHA recommendations support vasodilators in severe cocaine-related vasospasm or hypertension and sodium bicarbonate for wide-complex tachycardia due to sodium channel effects.
- For cannabis, distinguish route, intoxication and capacity.
- ASRA’s minimum two-hour elective delay applies after smoking and does not establish fitness if symptoms remain.

- [Association of Anaesthetists alcohol consensus 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39780754/) · [AHA 2025 resuscitation guidance, special circumstances](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation) · [Perioperative psychostimulant review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10437106/) · [ASRA perioperative cannabis guidance](https://doi.org/10.1136/rapm-2022-104013)

## 9.3 Anxiety, depression and psychosis/schizophrenia

- Anxiety/depression may increase perioperative distress and pain interference and are associated with worse functional recovery in some populations.
- Establish active symptoms, suicidal risk, previous post-operative complications, ability to understand/consent, support, and medication adherence.
- **SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs/MAOIs**, lithium and antipsychotics have distinct implications: serotonergic toxicity with some drug combinations, QT prolongation, hypotension, anticholinergic effects, sedation, seizure threshold and interactions with anaesthetic/analgesic agents.
- Avoid blanket instructions to stop all antidepressants—withdrawal, relapse and psychiatric destabilisation can be serious.
- Most decisions are individualised with the treating team, perioperative pharmacist and product guidance.

- For psychosis/schizophrenia assess baseline cognition and mental state, capacity, support, smoking effects on drug metabolism, metabolic syndrome, cardiac risk (e.g. QT), clozapine-related adverse effects where prescribed, and the possibility of delirium due to other causes.
- **Clozapine** deserves particular attention for hypotension, sedation, tachycardia, severe constipation/ileus and infection/neutropenia; abrupt interruption and restarting after missed doses require specialist protocol.
- Continue essential psychiatric therapy where feasible, and reconcile medicines rather than improvising.
- Treat acute pain normally but choose monitored analgesia mindful of sedative interactions.
- Explain planned procedures clearly and provide additional consent support rather than assuming incapacity from diagnosis alone.

### Assess each psychiatric condition, its treatment and the acute pain implications

**Depression and anxiety:**

- Identify symptoms and severity, sleep disruption, prior perioperative panic or pain experiences, adherence, support and self-harm risk where clinically indicated.
- Depression/anxiety may amplify suffering and reduce rehabilitation participation, but are not evidence that pain lacks a physical cause.
- Continue most established antidepressants unless a clear interaction or other specialist reason exists; abrupt stopping may cause discontinuation symptoms and destabilisation.
- SSRIs/SNRIs can be associated with platelet effects, hyponatraemia and interactions with serotonergic drugs; consider serotonergic toxicity if altered mental state, autonomic disturbance and neuromuscular hyperactivity develop after a new interacting agent.
- TCAs have anticholinergic, conduction and orthostatic effects; review dose and ECG when indicated.
- Tailor postoperative follow-up and ensure the patient knows whom to contact if mood deteriorates.

**Psychosis/schizophrenia:**

- Assess baseline symptoms, cognition, consent/capacity for the specific decision, insight and medication adherence without assuming incapacity solely from diagnosis.
- Consider smoking, obesity/metabolic disease, sleep apnoea, cardiovascular risk and antipsychotic adverse effects.
- Many antipsychotics cause sedation, orthostasis and QT effects, potentially compounded by anaesthetic agents or electrolyte abnormalities; some lower seizure threshold or cause extrapyramidal effects.
- Continue necessary psychiatric treatment in most circumstances after an individual medication review; abrupt cessation may precipitate relapse and complicate surgical recovery.
- Coordinate with psychiatry if severe psychosis, acute behavioural disturbance or uncertain depot-drug timing.
- Distinguish postoperative delirium, malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome if fever, rigidity and autonomic dysfunction occur—the treatment and triggers differ.

**Bipolar disorder and other psychotropic medicines (adjacent safety issues):**

- Lithium has a narrow therapeutic margin, renal handling and interactions with dehydration/NSAIDs/diuretics/ACE inhibitors; perioperative continuation or temporary withholding should be planned with psychiatry according to operation, renal function and toxicity risk rather than a blanket rule.
- MAO inhibitors and some other psychoactive medicines present major interaction concerns with particular opioids and sympathomimetics; seek expert medication-specific advice rather than stopping established psychiatric therapy automatically.
- Avoid unnecessarily adding benzodiazepines or gabapentinoids to opioid-heavy regimens in OSA or frailty.
- Document an escalation plan if the patient cannot take usual oral drugs after surgery.

**Integrated oral answer:**

- For a patient with schizophrenia on an antipsychotic and severe acute abdominal pain, (1) diagnose the abdomen and treat genuine nociceptive pain
- (2) establish baseline cognition, capacity and medication timing
- (3) examine QT, orthostasis, sedation, smoking/respiratory and metabolic risks
- (4) use a coherent anaesthetic and monitored postoperative regimen
- (5) restart/continue psychiatric treatment safely and arrange liaison if oral intake or behaviour limits care.
- No single psychiatric diagnosis is an indication to withhold opioids, to assume deliberate drug misuse, or to ignore postoperative pathology. [R1, R23, R28]

### Psychotropic mechanisms before perioperative management

Translate each diagnosis into drug mechanisms and anaesthetic hazards. The key is not the psychiatric label alone; it is whether the disorder affects consent and cooperation, whether the drug changes haemodynamics/ventilation, and whether withdrawal or an interaction may be more dangerous than continuation. [R36, pp. 327–339]

- • SSRIs/SNRIs: inhibit monoamine reuptake, so review serotonin-toxicity interactions (notably tramadol, pethidine, linezolid and methylene blue), bleeding tendency with other antithrombotic drugs, hyponatraemia and possible discontinuation symptoms.
- Most established therapy is ordinarily continued; individual agents have different CYP/QT profiles.
- A single SSRI prescription is not a reason to cancel anaesthesia.

- • TCAs (e.g. amitriptyline): serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake inhibition plus antimuscarinic, α-adrenergic and cardiac sodium-channel effects explain dry mouth, constipation, orthostatic hypotension and ECG conduction abnormalities.
- In overdose, a wide QRS, hypotension and seizures can require emergency toxicology treatment.
- Consider additive sedation, but do not abruptly stop stable treatment without a reason.

- • MAO inhibitors: reduced monoamine metabolism explains interactions with serotonergic opioids and sympathomimetic agents.
- An elective plan must be agreed with the prescriber/psychiatrist; indiscriminate cessation risks relapse, whereas certain combinations can cause severe toxicity.
- Treat an unexpected need for vasopressors with cautious, closely observed use of appropriate agents under local guidance.

- • Antipsychotics (including clozapine): D2 antagonism and off-target α1/H1/muscarinic effects explain orthostasis, sedation, QT prolongation, ileus, temperature disturbances and altered seizure threshold.
- Clozapine requires special monitoring for neutropenia, ileus and potentially dangerous dose restart after interruption.
- Coordinate with psychiatry and pharmacy rather than using a generic “stop all antipsychotics” rule.

• Lithium: narrow therapeutic window and renal handling make dehydration, AKI, sodium changes, diuretics and NSAIDs important; it may prolong neuromuscular blockade. Review renal function, drug levels if indicated and a specific perioperative continuation/withholding plan with the treating team.

- Serotonin toxicity versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): serotonin toxicity often develops rapidly after serotonergic exposure and prominently causes clonus/hyperreflexia (sometimes diarrhoea).
- NMS is commonly associated with dopamine blockade or interruption of dopaminergic therapy and typically features severe generalised rigidity with autonomic instability.
- Both require immediate identification, stopping implicated agents, supportive care and specialist escalation.
- This is an exam differential, not permission to rely on one sign alone. [R36, comparison table 13.1]

### Make a named medication interruption and restart plan

- Recent clozapine can increase aspiration, sedation and hypotension risk, and stopping tobacco smoking can increase exposure.
- UKCPA suggests a 12-hour elective hold, with the local plan agreed with psychiatry and pharmacy.
- More than 48 hours without treatment calls for specialist re-titration advice before returning to the usual dose.
- In clozapine-related hypotension avoid adrenaline as a routine vasopressor because of possible paradoxical hypotension.
- Standard cardiac arrest protocols still apply.
- For lithium distinguish minor surgery from major surgery or substantial renal or fluid risk.
- Check the local hold interval and agree restart after stable renal function and hydration.

- For serotonin toxicity, recognise clonus and hyperreflexia after a plausible drug combination, and prioritise stopping triggers, benzodiazepines, cooling and ventilation or non-depolarising paralysis if severe.
- Enteral cyproheptadine is an adjunct of uncertain benefit.
- Medsafe distinguishes high-risk combinations with tramadol or pethidine from context-dependent risk with fentanyl or methadone.

- [UKCPA clozapine perioperative handbook](https://periop-handbook.ukclinicalpharmacy.org/drug/clozapine/) · [UKCPA lithium perioperative handbook](https://periop-handbook.ukclinicalpharmacy.org/drug/lithium/) · [Medsafe opioid and serotonergic medicines](https://www.medsafe.govt.nz/profs/PUArticles/September2022/Opioids-and-serotonergic%20medicines-risk-of-serotonin-syndrome.html) · [BJA Education perioperative serotonin syndrome](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.10.003) · [Chiew and Isbister, management of serotonin toxicity](https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16152)

## 9.4 Integrated urgent-care example

- A 47-year-old with chronic alcohol dependence, depression and past heroin use presents with an acute abdomen requiring laparotomy.
- Assess sepsis/shock, aspiration, last alcohol/opioid intake, withdrawal risk, liver disease/coagulation and current MOUD/psychiatric medicines in parallel with surgery.
- Prepare haemodynamic and airway support, controlled analgesia, appropriate antimicrobials/source control and a postoperative ICU/ward plan.
- Do not omit analgesia because of OUD history; do not mistake emerging alcohol withdrawal for uncontrolled surgical pain.
- Continue essential verified maintenance, provide thiamine and electrolyte care as indicated, and plan addiction/psych follow-up.

### Alcohol and stimulants: recognise the physiology, not just the screening result

- Distinguish immediate intoxication, physiological dependence/withdrawal and organ damage from longer exposure.
- An acutely intoxicated patient may have impaired capacity, vomiting and aspiration risk, while a chronically dependent but apparently sober patient can develop withdrawal during admission.
- The most useful history is amount, pattern, last use, previous withdrawal seizures/delirium tremens and concurrent sedatives. [R36, pp.
- 336–338]

- Alcohol withdrawal is an adaptive excitatory response when sustained alcohol exposure decreases.
- Look for tremor, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis and later hallucinations, seizures or delirium.
- But in a postoperative patient these signs may also reflect sepsis, bleeding, hypoxia, pain or opioid withdrawal.
- Manage through current local withdrawal pathways, with thiamine where indicated and monitoring appropriate to the severity; historical drug doses in older texts must not replace current local protocols.

- For stimulants, the timing of actual intoxication is crucial.
- Sympathomimetic toxicity can produce agitation, hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, myocardial ischaemia and hyperthermia.
- Later hypotension may reflect depleted stores, hypovolaemia or other illness, and often requires directly acting vasopressors titrated to physiology.
- A urine test identifies exposure over a variable period; it does not establish present toxicity or mandate postponement of all surgery.

items.title: 10. Acute back and musculoskeletal pain: identify danger, keep people moving
items.priority: P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 10.1 A framework that changes with the pain phenotype

### FOUNDATIONS FIRST  |  The first 30 seconds of a back-pain consultation

- The major initial distinction is between **non-specific mechanical back pain**, **radicular pain** (leg pain from nerve-root irritation, sometimes with dermatomal symptoms), **lumbar canal stenosis** (classically walking-provoked leg symptoms relieved by sitting or flexion), and **dangerous structural/vascular pathology**.
- Check new urinary difficulty or altered sensation, saddle symptoms, progressive weakness, systemic fever/infection risk, malignancy, fracture/trauma and sudden vascular pain.
- A new cauda-equina syndrome requires urgent senior assessment and MRI pathway, regardless of analgesic response.

- If serious pathology has been reasonably excluded, give an explanation, activity plan and proportionate symptom relief.
- If the patient has true radiculopathy, follow the neurological examination over time and consider imaging when it will alter intervention.
- **Gabapentinoids are not recommended for routine sciatica in NICE NG59**, whereas they can be useful in other established peripheral neuropathic syndromes.
- This is why “shooting” does not automatically mean “start pregabalin”.
- Strong opioid treatment is not the default for uncomplicated acute axial low-back pain. [R7–R9]

![Acute back pain: the first decision is urgency, not the analgesic](set16-fig11.png)

- Back pain is a **symptom**, not one diagnosis.
- Separate: **non-specific mechanical low-back pain** without concerning systemic features
- **radicular pain/sciatica** from irritated or compressed nerve root, often dermatomal leg radiation
- **spinal stenosis** with posture-related neurogenic claudication
- **inflammatory back pain**, fracture or malignancy
- **cauda-equina / spinal cord compression**
- And acute-on-chronic nociplastic pain.
- Serious pathology is uncommon in general back-pain presentations, but the consequence of missing it is high.
- Do not order MRI solely because someone reports severe pain or has an old abnormal scan; do not withhold emergency MRI when progressive neurological or sphincter signs appear. [R7]

**Focused history:**

- Onset and trauma, mechanical versus nocturnal/inflammatory features, radicular distribution, bilateral symptoms, gait and functional change, fever/IVDU/immunosuppression, cancer history, steroid exposure/osteoporosis, bladder/bowel/saddle function and progressive weakness.
- Ask about analgesic and substance exposure, psychosocial stress and job demands.
- **Examination:** gait, posture, active range, neurologic power/reflexes/sensation (including appropriate dermatomal mapping), straight-leg-raise or femoral stretch where relevant; abdominal, vascular and hip examination when indicated.
- Red flags guide urgent investigation, while absence of red flags supports an active conservative plan.

**Cauda equina:**

- New bladder disturbance, altered perineal sensation, bilateral sciatica, progressive leg weakness or bowel/sexual dysfunction warrants urgent senior assessment and MRI/spinal team pathways.
- Classic urinary retention is a late feature; normal anal tone alone does not exclude early disease.
- **Spinal infection:** fever may be absent, especially with immunosuppression/IVDU; focal pain plus bacteremia, systemic upset or new deficit warrants urgent assessment/imaging.
- **Fracture:** consider trauma, osteoporosis or steroid exposure.
- **Vascular mimic:** sudden severe back/abdominal pain with shock/pulse differences may indicate aortic catastrophe rather than “muscular strain”.

## 10.2 Non-specific acute low-back pain: a justified initial plan

- Explain expected course and red-flag return instructions, encourage continued ordinary activity as tolerated, avoid prolonged bedrest, and offer simple symptom measures such as heat and adapted movement.
- Select a short trial of an **NSAID** if safe, at the lowest effective dose and shortest necessary course, with explicit renal, GI, cardiovascular and anticoagulation assessment.
- Paracetamol alone has limited supporting evidence for non-specific low-back pain; avoid promising it will speed recovery.
- Opioids are not first-line: if severe pain temporarily blocks essential function after other options and safety review, a very short course might occasionally be justified with an exit plan, not a default modified-release regimen.
- Avoid routine benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids and systemic steroids for non-specific back pain. [R7]

- Risk-stratify early for persistent disability (e.g. STarT Back, work constraints, fear-avoidance, prior prolonged pain).
- A low-risk patient needs reassurance, an activity plan and review if symptoms persist/change; higher-risk patients may benefit from a coordinated exercise and psychologically informed functional approach.
- **2026 nuance:** NICE’s withdrawal of two earlier NG59 psychological-therapy recommendations reflects problems with evidence informing those recommendations, **not** a categorical “do not offer”.
- FPM/ANZCA wider multidisciplinary principles and NG193 for chronic primary pain remain relevant; don’t transplant one disease-specific statement to all persistent pain. [R7, R8]

- **Follow-up:** check expected functional recovery and new signs after an agreed interval. Persistent severe limitation, progressive deficit or failure to improve after an adequate course justifies reassessment of diagnosis and individualised referral, rather than indefinite repeat emergency presentations or repeat opioid prescriptions.

## 10.3 Radicular sciatica and stenosis: not the same as non-specific back pain

- A true **radiculopathy** includes pain in a neuroanatomically plausible leg distribution, often with altered reflex, sensory change or motor deficit; **radicular pain** can occur without objective loss.
- Lumbar canal stenosis commonly produces walking-provoked leg pain relieved by sitting/flexion, with relatively better cycling tolerance.
- Ask about how far the patient can walk, progressive foot drop and saddle/sphincter symptoms.
- MRI is appropriate if red flags exist or findings would affect a specialist/surgical decision, not reflexively at presentation for every painful leg.

- Management includes informed activity, adapted physiotherapy and addressing sleep/function; neuropathic drugs have inconsistent or poor evidence in sciatica and should not be prescribed purely because symptoms “sound nerve-like”.
- In NICE NG59, gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids and benzodiazepines are **not recommended** for routine sciatica, and opioids are not recommended for chronic sciatica.
- This is different from NICE CG173’s first-line drug options for other neuropathic syndromes such as diabetic neuropathy.
- Severe unresponsive acute sciatica may justify selected epidural injection under specialist pathways after imaging/diagnostic review; progressive motor deficit or cauda-equina symptoms warrant urgent spinal assessment.
- Discectomy/decompression requires appropriate compressive pathology, symptom concordance and shared decision-making. [R7, R9]

### Acute back pain: triage by mechanism and urgency

**A practical differential matters more than the pain score:**

- Mechanical non-specific pain has no progressive deficit or major systemic red flags; axial pain usually predominates and many patients recover with explanation, maintained activity and appropriate short-lived symptom relief.
- Sciatica suggests irritation/impairment of a nerve root with dermatomal radiating leg pain, possible sensory loss, weakness or altered reflexes.
- **Cauda equina** requires urgent evaluation of new urinary retention or altered urinary sensation, saddle sensory change, progressive bilateral weakness and bowel or sexual dysfunction; do not reassure merely because pain temporarily improves after morphine.
- Vertebral fracture may follow trauma or occur with osteoporosis/steroid exposure; spinal infection or malignancy may present with fever, risk factors, persistent severe pain or neurological change.
- Visceral/vascular causes (AAA, renal colic, pelvic/abdominal disease) sometimes masquerade as back pain.
- Trauma, anticoagulation, immunosuppression and recent spinal procedures change urgency.

**Imaging is selective:**

- In routine non-specific acute back pain without red flags, early routine imaging can identify incidental degeneration that does not explain symptoms and may worsen unhelpful treatment escalation.
- Imaging is required or urgently considered where serious pathology, progressive deficits, invasive intervention or surgical planning would change management; MRI is generally the key test for suspected neural compression/infection, while the chosen pathway depends on local availability and clinical urgency.
- Analgesia proceeds concurrently with investigation and must not delay decompression of a threatened cauda equina or correction of vascular pathology.

**Treatment choices are distinct:**

- For non-specific acute low back pain, encourage tolerable movement and usual activities, avoid prolonged bed rest, use short-course NSAID when suitable and consider additional nonpharmacological assistance.
- For sciatica, counsel on the usual course and assess motor progression; NICE NG59 specifically does **not** recommend gabapentinoids, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for sciatica because their evidence of benefit does not justify harm.
- Epidural local anaesthetic/steroid injection can be considered for **acute severe sciatica** in a selected patient after specialist assessment, while decompressive surgery may be considered for persistent symptoms when imaging and symptoms are concordant.
- This is not an instruction that every MRI-confirmed disc bulge needs an injection.
- Reassess function, neurological signs, adverse drug effects and need for follow-up. [R7, R8]

## 10.4 Other acute musculoskeletal presentations

**Acute fracture/sprain:**

- Confirm mechanism and neurovascular status; assess compartment syndrome if disproportionate pain with escalating opioid need, painful passive stretch or tense compartments.
- Treat injury (reduction, splint/immobilisation where indicated, surgery or early protected mobilisation), use multimodal analgesia and an appropriate regional block only after a plan for serial motor/sensory and compartment surveillance.
- For elderly hip fracture, early analgesia (e.g. fascia iliaca block by competent team), delirium prevention, prompt surgery optimisation and mobility are central.
- NSAID suitability depends on renal, bleeding and bone-healing context; absolute long-term healing claims vary by injury/exposure.

**Acute joint inflammation:**

- Fever, warmth, inability to weight-bear and significant systemic risk require exclusion of septic arthritis, not simply escalation of oral analgesia.
- **Acute gout:** anti-inflammatory treatment selection depends on kidney function, interactions and contraindications; confirm diagnosis when atypical and avoid overlooking infection.
- **Muscle strain/tendinopathy:** rehabilitate progressively, modify load temporarily, support return to work and avoid unnecessary repeated imaging.
- **Rhabdomyolysis:** after prolonged pressure/trauma/exertion, severe muscle pain/swelling and high CK require renal/electrolyte monitoring; treat hyperkalaemia and compartment syndrome promptly.
- **Inflammatory rheumatological disease:** control the disease through the appropriate specialty while preserving function, not merely adding chronic opioid.

## 10.5 Musculoskeletal pain prescribing and patient communication

- Match drug to mechanism and risk: NSAID for demonstrable inflammatory nociception if suitable, limited simple analgesia for short-lived pain, and targeted neuropathic medicine for a diagnosed neuropathic syndrome with careful titration.
- Review existing opioids and sedation burden.
- Consider chronic analgesic overuse, especially with recurring headaches and repeated acute prescriptions.
- Communicate a return-to-activity plan, work restrictions if clinically indicated, warning signs, duration of each medicine and reassessment point.
- **Avoid “painkillers until pain is zero”:** the key endpoint is functional progression and safe recovery.

items.title: 11. Acute neuropathic pain: diagnose the nerve problem and treat it
items.body:
## 11.1 Establish neuropathic pain rather than labelling every shooting pain

### FOUNDATIONS FIRST  |  Positive symptoms, negative signs and a plausible neural map

**Positive sensory findings mean extra sensations:**

- Burning, electric shocks, spontaneous pain, allodynia or exaggerated pin pain.
- **Negative findings** mean lost function: reduced pinprick, temperature, light touch, vibration or reflexes and, when relevant, weakness.
- Both often coexist in the same nerve territory.
- Draw the distribution: a single named peripheral nerve, a dermatome for a nerve root, a stocking–glove pattern for distal polyneuropathy, or a central distribution after stroke/spinal injury.

- A neuropathic pain diagnosis needs a plausible lesion/disease affecting that neural pathway, not just a descriptive adjective.
- For example, sudden postoperative foot drop with altered dorsum-of-foot sensation needs urgent assessment for nerve compression, positioning injury or haematoma.
- Pregabalin does not address a compressive lesion.
- Once the cause is assessed, select a neuropathic treatment whose pharmacology and harms fit the patient; target sleep, functional movement and intolerable allodynia rather than promising complete abolition of pain. [R9]

- Neuropathic pain requires a **lesion or disease of the somatosensory system**.
- Diagnosis combines:
- **1.** A suggestive history
- **2.** Neuroanatomically plausible distribution
- **3.** Sensory signs in the same territory
- **4.** Objective confirmation of nerve lesion/disease when available.
- Clinical grading often progresses from **possible** (history/distribution) to **probable** (supportive sensory signs) and **definite** (confirmatory lesion/disease test), recognising that a test may be unavailable and absence of one does not invalidate genuine pain.
- Descriptors—burning, electric shocks, shooting pain, painful cold, allodynia—support but do not prove the diagnosis.
- DN4 and painDETECT are useful screening tools but are not independent diagnostic gold standards. [R9]

- Examine both positive (mechanical allodynia, pin hyperalgesia, spontaneous dysaesthesia) and negative (reduced pinprick/cold/light touch, numbness, weakness) findings.
- Map the pattern: **single nerve** (e.g. superficial peroneal nerve), **dermatome** (nerve root), **length-dependent symmetrical** (polyneuropathy), **hemibody** (central lesion), or **patchy multifocal** (multiple neuropathies).
- Evaluate time course: acute progressive deficit requires evaluation for compression, ischaemia, inflammation or infection even when pain responds to an adjuvant.
- Sudden postoperative foot drop is not safely managed with pregabalin alone.

## 11.2 Useful clinical phenotypes and differentials

| Syndrome | Mechanism / features | What to exclude or address promptly |
|---|---|---|
| **Acute nerve injury after surgery or trauma** | Pain in named nerve territory, paraesthesia/allodynia, sensory or motor change, possible entrapment or traction injury. | Haematoma/compartment syndrome, direct nerve compression, block-related effect, positioning injury or new vascular compromise; document baseline and arrange urgent team review if deficit progresses. |
| **Herpes zoster-associated neuropathic pain** | Dermatomal unilateral vesicular eruption with burning/allodynia, or prodromal neuropathic pain; immunosuppression can complicate. | Ophthalmic/disseminated disease, immunosuppression, bacterial superinfection. Early antivirals where indicated; analgesia may need targeted neuropathic treatment. Antivirals do not reliably eliminate later PHN risk. |
| **Painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy** | Symmetrical distal length-dependent burning, nocturnal pain, sensory loss and fall/ulcer risk. | Non-diabetic causes, foot injury, B12 deficiency where relevant; glycaemic and foot management plus symptom therapy. |
| **Trigeminal neuralgia** | Brief, unilateral, electric facial attacks, often triggered by light touch/chewing, in trigeminal distribution. | Dental/intracranial causes, atypical sensory loss, MS; MRI and condition-specific carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine pathway. More detail belongs to Head & Neck/Neuro sets. |
| **Central post-stroke/spinal lesion pain** | Contralateral or below-lesion burning/temperature abnormalities and sensory deficits; delayed onset possible. | Recurrent stroke/new neurological deficit, spasticity or musculoskeletal pain; specialist neurological assessment. |
| **Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)** | Regional disproportionate pain with autonomic, sensory, sudomotor/oedema and motor/trophic changes; not restricted to one nerve territory. | DVT, infection, new fracture, arterial/venous ischaemia, peripheral neuropathy and other causes better explaining symptoms. |

### Additional acute syndromes that change the investigation or referral

**Compression neuropathy around an operation:**

- New median, ulnar, common peroneal or femoral nerve symptoms should be mapped anatomically, with strength/reflexes and sensory modality documented immediately.
- Evaluate position, tight dressings, haematoma, regional catheter or vascular compromise.
- A painful expanding haematoma with progressive weakness is a different emergency from stable paraesthesia after an expected block.
- Contact the surgical/anaesthetic teams and arrange urgent imaging or decompression when indicated; do not hide a progressive deficit beneath escalating pregabalin.

**Postherpetic and trigeminal phenotypes:**

- Acute zoster has an evolving skin disorder where early antiviral treatment may address the underlying infection, with separate control of neuropathic pain.
- Ophthalmic involvement, immunosuppression and disseminated disease require prompt specific review.
- In trigeminal neuralgia, the paroxysmal stereotyped shock-like pain and triggers suggest a different treatment pathway—carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine under appropriate monitoring, MRI to assess secondary causes and specialist referral for refractory disease.
- Persistent facial numbness, bilateral symptoms or abnormal cranial nerves require closer evaluation than a routine dental pain diagnosis.

**Painful mononeuritis or inflammatory neuropathy:**

- Acute focal nerve deficits with severe pain and evolving weakness require consideration of vasculitic neuropathy, immune neuropathy, herpes zoster, metabolic injury and structural compression, with directed neurology investigation.
- Central neuropathic pain after stroke/spinal cord lesion may coexist with spasticity, pressure injury, autonomic symptoms or depression; treating only the burning sensation misses the functional problem.
- CRPS remains a **regional**, rather than a single named-nerve, syndrome. [R9, R20]

## 11.3 Stepwise management with explicit goals

- A.
- Treat the cause or emergency.
- Surgical nerve compression, evolving haematoma, spinal cord compression, acute ischaemia, infection and major deficit require urgent intervention, not a months-long oral drug trial.
- For zoster, antiviral treatment is considered early according to age, timing and risk.
- For diabetic neuropathy, address metabolic disease, feet and falls, though glycaemic improvement may not promptly reverse established pain.
- B.
- Explain the mechanism and protect function.
- Sensory loss increases burns/ulcer/falls; set a sleep, mobility or return-to-work target and arrange physiotherapy/occupational therapy where useful.
- C.
- Initiate a mechanism-appropriate pharmacological trial if pain warrants it.
- NICE CG173 offers **amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin** as initial choices for neuropathic pain other than trigeminal neuralgia; choose by comorbidity, contraindications, interactions, patient preference and prior response. [R9]

- D.
- Titrate and review: start low when frail, renal-impaired or receiving CNS depressants; escalate only after sufficient tolerability and meaningful functional benefit, with a defined review in days/weeks.
- Gabapentinoids require renal adjustment and monitoring for sedation, falls and respiratory depression, especially with opioids.
- TCAs require attention to anticholinergic, cardiac and cognitive adverse effects.
- Duloxetine may help coexistent mood and neuropathic pain but can worsen nausea/BP and requires interaction/withdrawal care.
- E.
- Consider localised treatment such as topical lidocaine or capsaicin when suitable; high-concentration capsaicin belongs to trained specialist services.
- F.
- Escalate early for rapid deficit, severe disability, uncertain diagnosis, CRPS, failed sequential adequate trials, complex psychiatric/addiction factors or procedural consideration.

**Do not generalise:**

- A drug recommended for painful diabetic neuropathy is not automatically supported for sciatica, widespread nociplastic pain or an undiagnosed postoperative surgical complication.
- Short-term rescue opioid can occasionally be necessary for severe acute neural injury, but it is not a reliable long-term primary strategy for chronic neuropathic pain; ongoing functional and respiratory risk must be reviewed.
- Avoid abrupt withdrawal of chronic gabapentinoids/antidepressants when discontinuing after sustained use.

### Choose and review a neuropathic medicine using clinical pharmacology

- An **SNRI such as duloxetine** may be attractive when there is coexisting depression or generalised anxiety, but consider BP, nausea, interactions and hepatic/renal cautions.
- A **TCA such as amitriptyline** may help sleep and neural pain in selected younger patients, but anticholinergic burden, orthostasis, conduction effects and overdose toxicity make it less suitable for many frail older patients or those at high self-harm risk.
- **Gabapentin/pregabalin** require dose adjustment for renal impairment and can cause dizziness, gait instability and significant respiratory sedation when combined with opioids or other depressants.
- They are not interchangeable as mg-for-mg drugs, do not have an immediate reliable rescue effect, and should not be continued indefinitely without evidence of functionally meaningful benefit.
- **Topical lidocaine** is useful for some focal allodynic areas without systemic sedation; **capsaicin**, particularly high concentration, requires correct diagnosis, skin safety and trained application.
- Carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine belong primarily to trigeminal-neuralgia pathways, with attention to sodium, blood counts and interactions.

- **What constitutes an adequate trial?** Confirm appropriate indication
- Explain delayed onset and likely partial—not necessarily complete—pain reduction
- Begin with a patient-specific low starting dose, adjust in steps as tolerated and review after enough time at a therapeutically reasonable dose to judge response.
- Measure an individual goal (e.g. tolerating shoes, less nocturnal awakening, walking further), sleep, falls, cognitive effects and adherence.
- If there is no useful improvement or harms outweigh gains, taper the relevant treatment according to its withdrawal risk and try an alternative rather than simply adding a fourth sedating medicine.
- Reassess diagnosis if treatment consistently fails or the neurological examination evolves.
- Mixed nociceptive pain still requires injury/pathology management and appropriate simple analgesia.

- **When function is threatened**, multidisciplinary rehabilitation and timely referral matter as much as choosing between neuropathic medicines.
- In CRPS, provide desensitisation, oedema control and graded hand/limb use with patient agreement, while avoiding immobilisation driven solely by fear.
- Evidence for bisphosphonates, corticosteroids in selected early inflammatory presentations, sympathetic blocks and neuromodulation is heterogeneous or specialist-dependent; do not present any as a guaranteed cure or automatic first-line intervention. [R9, R20]

## 11.4 Complex regional pain syndrome: Budapest criteria and early rehabilitation

### FOUNDATIONS FIRST  |  How to remember the Budapest criteria without a memorised paragraph

- Think **S–V–S–M:** Sensory (hyperalgesia or allodynia); Vasomotor (temperature or skin-colour asymmetry); Sudomotor/oedema (sweating change or swelling); and Motor/trophic (range of motion, motor dysfunction, skin/hair/nail change).
- The clinical criteria require continuing disproportionate regional pain, **patient-reported symptoms in at least three of the four categories**, **observed signs in at least two categories at assessment**, and no better explanatory diagnosis.
- The signs and symptoms are not limited to one named nerve distribution.

- The first tasks are to exclude infection, vascular compromise, DVT, new fracture or nerve injury, then arrange early skilled rehabilitation.
- Sensory desensitisation, oedema management, graded motor imagery or mirror therapy and supported use may be appropriate.
- Medication and selected sympathetic procedures can facilitate participation but are not universally curative.
- An early change in hand colour or swelling after a fracture does not alone prove CRPS; examine and reassess systematically. [R20]

![CRPS Budapest criteria: four symptom and sign domains](set16-fig12.png)

- CRPS can follow fracture, surgery, immobilisation or seemingly minor injury.
