- It is characterised by continuing regional pain disproportionate to the usual inciting event and a characteristic constellation of **sensory**, **vasomotor**, **sudomotor/oedema**, and **motor/trophic** abnormalities.
- **Budapest clinical criteria:** disproportionate continuing pain; symptoms in **at least three of four** categories; observed signs in **at least two of four** categories at assessment; and **no better alternative diagnosis**.
- Categories: sensory (hyperalgesia/allodynia), vasomotor (temperature/skin-colour asymmetry), sudomotor/oedema (swelling/sweating asymmetry), motor/trophic (reduced range, weakness, tremor/dystonia, nail/hair/skin changes).
- Type I has no confirmed major nerve injury; type II follows a defined nerve injury. [R20]

- CRPS is primarily a **clinical diagnosis**.
- Imaging/tests help exclude fracture, infection, neuropathy or ischaemia but are not a single required diagnostic test.
- Early recognition matters: reduce prolonged unnecessary immobilisation and arrange skilled **graded active rehabilitation**, desensitisation, graded motor imagery/mirror therapy where appropriate, oedema management, education and psychological support.
- Analgesia should enable tolerable movement: targeted neuropathic medicine, selected anti-inflammatory or short-course therapies in specialist circumstances, and sometimes specialist sympathetic block or other intervention.
- No one drug or injection consistently cures CRPS, and evidence for many modalities is limited; progression should reflect phenotype and tolerance, not forceful manipulation or months of inactivity.

**Case:**

- Four weeks after distal radius fracture, a patient has severe allodynia, swollen shiny hand, colour and temperature asymmetry and limited finger movement.
- Examine pulses, infection/fracture position and nerve function; apply Budapest categories; refer early for hand therapy/pain assessment; provide analgesia sufficient for safe participation and coordinated follow-up.
- Do **not** tell them to “work through anything no matter how severe”, nor diagnose CRPS solely from pain intensity after a fracture.

### Apply CRPS findings to a newly fractured limb

- Use the Budapest clinical criteria, with disproportionate pain, symptoms in at least three of four categories, signs in at least two and no better diagnosis.
- Warn that fracture, infection, pressure from dressings and acute neurovascular compromise can mimic or coexist with CRPS.
- For fixation, document baseline findings and coordinate anaesthesia, monitoring and hand therapy.
- Regional analgesia can facilitate recovery, but a dense catheter or routine ketamine is not established flare prevention.
- No routine perioperative prophylaxis with steroids, bisphosphonates or vitamin C is justified for established CRPS.

[CRPS diagnosis and treatment guidelines, fifth edition](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9186375/) · [Cochrane overview of CRPS interventions](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37306570/) · [NEJM clinical review of CRPS](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMcp2415752)

## 11.5 When to refer to specialist pain medicine

- Refer early for **rapidly progressive neuropathy or new neurological deficit** (often urgent neurological/surgical referral first), **CRPS**, severe refractory pain with major loss of function, multiple failed evidence-based medications, uncertainty about mechanism, significant opioid harms/OUD, consideration of neuromodulation or invasive procedures, or high psychosocial complexity.
- A specialist pain clinic is not a substitute for urgent decompression of a compressed nerve.
- Clearly state the question to be answered: diagnosis, functional rehabilitation plan, drug rotation, procedural eligibility or coordinated weaning.
- Provide prior imaging, medication-trial details and patient goals, not only the pain score.

### An injured nerve after surgery is a diagnosis of exclusion, not automatically a block complication

- Postoperative nerve dysfunction has several competing causes: pre-existing disease, surgical traction or transection, positioning pressure, tourniquets, vascular ischaemia, haematoma, immobilisation and less commonly block-related needle or injectate injury.
- The practical lesson is to document the neurological territory and the time course rather than decide that a nerve block caused the deficit without assessment. [R37, section “Regional anaesthesia and nerve injury”]

• New weakness after a block: first establish expected block distribution, last local anaesthetic dose and anticipated resolution time; examine motor, sensory and perfusion findings against the preoperative baseline.

• Escalate immediately for progressive deficit, severe focal pain, vascular compromise, compartment syndrome, suspected spinal/plexus haematoma or a deficit inconsistent with the block. Haematoma causing neural compression is time-critical and needs urgent specialist imaging/decompression.

• For stable non-progressive sensory symptoms, provide documentation, review and clear follow-up; persistent or motor symptoms often warrant neurologic consultation and appropriate investigations (e.g. EMG/NCS at a suitable interval).

• Regional analgesia may still be valuable in opioid-tolerant patients, but consider anticoagulants, infection and nerve assessment needs. Older anticoagulation timing tables are based on superseded guidance: use the current ANZCA/institutional neuraxial and deep-block anticoagulant recommendations, not the historical numbers. [R37]

items.title: 12. Transition from acute to chronic pain, and chronic postsurgical pain
items.body:
## 12.1 Define chronic postsurgical pain and understand why it develops

### FOUNDATIONS FIRST  |  Place chronic postsurgical pain on a timeline

- **CPSP** is not simply “the incision still hurts one week later”.
- The pain must develop or increase after surgery, persist for at least three months, involve the surgical or referred territory, and not be better explained by another cause such as infection, recurrence or a new neurological problem.
- Relevant mechanisms include surgical nerve injury, persistent inflammation, peripheral and central sensitisation, pre-existing pain vulnerability, impaired sleep, distress and prolonged high opioid exposure.
- Several mechanisms may coexist; severe acute pain is a risk marker, not proof of one deterministic cause.

- Visualise the entire patient journey.
- **Before:** document pre-existing pain, opioid therapy, anxiety, sleep and realistic expectations.
- **During:** minimise avoidable nerve trauma and provide operation-appropriate analgesia.
- **After:** identify unusually persistent pain or allodynia, promote function and supervise temporary opioid cessation with early follow-up.
- A regional technique may improve acute recovery and may help in particular operations, but a routine universal ketamine, gabapentin or block protocol has not been demonstrated to prevent all CPSP. [R14, R21]

![Chronic postsurgical pain: risk recognition spans the entire pathway](set16-fig13.png)

- **Chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP)** is pain that develops or increases after an operation, persists beyond the normal healing period for at least three months, is located in the surgical field or a referred territory, and is not better explained by infection, cancer recurrence, new disease or an unrelated pre-existing pain disorder.
- Pain can be mainly neuropathic, nociceptive or nociplastic, and multiple mechanisms can coexist.
- A patient who had severe pain before surgery can develop **increased** pain with new features rather than pain entirely new in onset.
- A case definition requires explicit comparison with the preoperative baseline. [R14]

- Mechanisms include direct peripheral nerve injury, prolonged nociceptor/inflammatory activation, peripheral and central sensitisation, altered descending modulation, and neuroimmune processes.
- Repeated severe acute pain can contribute, but **a causal “acute pain becomes chronic because analgesia was poor” story is oversimplified:** surgical nerve damage, pre-existing pain, patient factors and recovery context also matter.
- The observed association between severe early postoperative pain and later CPSP does not demonstrate that any single analgesic intervention can entirely prevent CPSP.
- Some types of surgery—thoracotomy, mastectomy, amputation, hernia repair and major joint procedures—have differing risks and characteristic nerve-injury pathways.
- Rates vary considerably by definition, procedure and follow-up; do not memorise one universal incidence percentage. [R14, R21]

## 12.2 Predictors grouped by time of exposure

| Before surgery | During surgery | After surgery |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-existing pain at operative or remote sites, high pain intensity, prior persistent pain, long-term opioid exposure, anxiety/depression, catastrophising or distress, sleep disturbance, major functional limitation and relevant demographic/disease factors. | Extent and type of tissue/nerve injury, traumatic nerve handling or unavoidable nerve sacrifice, duration/complexity of surgery and acute inflammatory burden; some procedures present higher risk. | Severe persistent early postoperative pain, neuropathic signs/allodynia, infection or complications, prolonged immobility, poor sleep and distress, repeated high opioid exposure, inadequate follow-up and persistent loss of function. |

- A **risk factor is not destiny:** multiple prediction models have limited transportability across operations, and some associations are confounded.
- Still, these features identify patients who merit a more deliberate pain plan and follow-up.
- A patient with severe preoperative pain and daily opioids undergoing thoracotomy should not be given the same education and discharge planning as an opioid-naïve patient having a minor procedure.

## 12.3 Prevention: a phase-specific strategy with appropriate humility

**Preoperative:**

- Identify existing pain, neuropathic phenotype, opioid exposure, depression/anxiety, expectations and sleep problems.
- Optimise pre-existing conditions and function where possible; document a baseline sensory exam if nerve injury risk is prominent.
- Discuss the probability of prolonged pain and a realistic analgesic/rehabilitation plan.
- Do not promise that surgery will necessarily eliminate all pre-existing pain.
- In high-risk patients consider early specialist/transitional pain service review and a coordinated approach to existing opioid therapy.

**Intraoperative:**

- Minimise avoidable nerve trauma through surgical technique where possible.
- Use effective **multimodal analgesia** suited to the procedure and patient, with regional techniques when they improve acute recovery and can be performed safely.
- Regional anaesthesia can reduce acute input and may reduce CPSP incidence in certain operations, but trial populations and certainty vary; do **not** describe a single block, ketamine dose, pregabalin schedule or opioid-free general anaesthetic as a guaranteed prevention strategy.
- Excessive remifentanil or escalating opioids without functional need may have disadvantages, but quantitative claims about causal CPSP reduction require operation-specific evidence.
- Avoid masking an important neurological examination.

**Postoperative:**

- Treat acute pain and complications promptly; restore movement and function; screen for new neuropathic features, excessive opioid needs, anxiety, insomnia and inability to resume activities.
- Ensure planned taper of new postoperative opioids, review chronic maintenance separately, and provide appropriate rehabilitation.
- At early follow-up, a patient with continuing allodynia or severe pain in a nerve territory needs reassessment and potential pain referral rather than automatic repeat opioid prescribing.
- Contact points, handover and patient empowerment matter as much as which drug was used on day one. [R14, R21]

**Evidence nuance:**

- The 2022 BJA Education review of CPSP summarises associations and promising interventions; it does not establish that all regional techniques, ketamine infusions or prehabilitation reliably prevent all CPSP.
- A 2026 risk-mitigation review highlights potentially modifiable psychological distress, baseline pain and perioperative opioid exposure, but high-quality prevention trials remain heterogeneous.
- Evaluate population, surgical procedure, outcome definition and follow-up before translating an apparent benefit to another operation. [R14, R21]

### Applying the prevention outcome to operations with different risks

- A prevention strategy must specify **what it is trying to prevent:** poorly controlled acute nociception, persistent nerve injury pain, prolonged immobility, or unhelpful long-term opioid exposure.
- Before high-risk surgery, identify the existing pain site/quality, opioid exposure, previous neuropathic features, anxiety/catastrophising, depression, sleep, prior surgical pain and the risk of major nerve disruption.
- Explain realistic postoperative pain, planned mobilisation and the expected period for reducing acute opioid prescriptions; arrange acute or transitional pain input for patients with substantial preoperative opioid use, severe persistent pain or previous CPSP.

- During surgery, minimise avoidable nerve injury through surgical technique and positioning; provide reliable, procedure-appropriate multimodal analgesia and regional techniques when indicated, but recognise that an excellent early block is **not proven to prevent all chronic postsurgical pain**.
- Avoid unnecessary prolonged high-dose opioid exposure and monitor for opioid-related harm.
- After surgery, reassess high-intensity pain that persists beyond the expected trajectory, new dysaesthesia or allodynia, opioid escalation and inability to mobilise.
- Investigate infection, prosthesis problems, recurrence, instability or nerve injury rather than prematurely labelling CPSP.
- For a patient with probable evolving neuropathic pain, introduce mechanism-specific treatment, protect function and refer when needed.
- Transitional pain services coordinate the surgical, acute-pain and community teams, using follow-up and taper planning rather than an unsupported routine prophylactic gabapentinoid regimen. [R14, R21–R23]

## 12.4 The transitional-pain-service concept

- High-risk patients benefit from bridging acute and chronic teams: preoperative plan → inpatient acute pain review → early outpatient review of functional recovery and analgesic use → timely referral if severe pain or neuropathic signs persist.
- The team can monitor opioid taper, sleep, mood, wound recovery, rehabilitation and patient expectations.
- This prevents the “discharge cliff” in which a patient leaves hospital with many opioids but no prescriber willing to adjust them, and it avoids preventable transition to persistent high-dose use.
- Services and resources vary, so describe an achievable local pathway and clear responsibility rather than assuming a formal transitional clinic exists everywhere.

### Established CRPS and fibromyalgia: special perioperative planning

For established complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) and fibromyalgia the common principle is that another operation or minor procedural stimulus can be particularly distressing in a sensitised system; the patient needs an individual plan, not an assumption that high pain equals ongoing tissue destruction. [R35, pp. 1178–1179]

- For established CRPS, document the baseline sensory/motor and autonomic changes, discuss positioning/immobilisation and anticipated postoperative rehabilitation, give proportionate multimodal/regional analgesia when appropriate, and facilitate early graded return of limb use.
- Vitamin C and ketamine/regional approaches are sometimes suggested but the evidence is limited or empirical; do not portray these as guaranteed prevention of recurrent CRPS.

- For fibromyalgia or predominantly nociplastic widespread pain, distinguish expected local postoperative nociception from baseline widespread sensitivity.
- Explain the operation-specific recovery trajectory, avoid reflexively increasing long-acting opioid prescriptions to treat diffuse distress, and coordinate sleep, graded activity and psychological support.
- New focal neurological or surgical red flags still require investigation.

### Assess chronic pain and ongoing opioid use separately

- Chronic postsurgical pain is new or increased pain related to surgery and present at least three months after exclusion of other causes.
- Persistent postoperative opioid use describes exposure beyond early recovery, with thresholds that vary by study.
- A patient may have either or both.
- The 2025 Blue Book Hong Kong chapter describes an association with discharge opioids even in a relatively low-use setting.
- Study definitions and local policy matter, and an observational association does not prove causation.
- A 2026 regional network meta-analysis supports a possible preventive role for selected regional approaches.
- Procedure, technique and follow-up affect interpretation.
- Transitional pain services can coordinate rehabilitation and de-escalation, with prevention evidence still developing.

- [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, Ho and Cheung on Hong Kong opioid harms](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [BJA Education chronic postsurgical pain](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.11.008) · [BJA 2026 regional anaesthesia and chronic postsurgical pain](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42425794/) · [Anesthesiology 2025 transitional pain service scoping review](https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000005606) · [Chronic postsurgical pain risk and mitigation review 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42479827/)

items.title: 13. Neurolytic blocks in chronic pain: indication, mechanism, risk and limits
items.body:
## 13.1 What neurolysis actually means

### FOUNDATIONS FIRST  |  Know what is intentionally being done to the nerve

- A standard local-anaesthetic block reversibly inhibits sodium channels for hours.
- **Chemical neurolysis**, by contrast, deliberately injures neural structures—usually using alcohol or phenol—to interrupt pain signalling for a potentially longer time.
- **Radiofrequency ablation** uses thermal energy to lesion a selected target, though different RF methods have different biological effects.
- **Neuromodulation**, such as spinal cord stimulation, aims to alter signal processing using a device without deliberate chemical destruction.
- The procedures are not interchangeable and do not form an automatic ladder.

- For selected refractory pancreatic or upper abdominal malignant visceral pain, a **coeliac plexus** target may be anatomically relevant because visceral sympathetic afferents travel through that region.
- The same procedure cannot reliably treat an abdominal-wall somatic nerve injury.
- Explain why the target matches the pain, the possibility of only partial benefit and what may be lost through intentional neural injury, including hypotension, diarrhoea, neuritis or rare serious vascular/neurological complications.
- This is a specialist consent, imaging, anticoagulation and follow-up decision, not routine “stronger regional anaesthesia”. [R15]

![Interventional pain treatments: how reversible is the intervention?](set16-fig14.png)

- **Neurolytic block** means intentional destruction or substantial interruption of neural transmission to reduce pain, often using chemicals such as alcohol or phenol.
- Destructive radiofrequency or other ablative procedures may be discussed alongside chemical neurolysis, but are not identical in mechanism or selectivity.
- **Local-anaesthetic diagnostic/prognostic blocks** temporarily interrupt nerves without intention to destroy them; their response may support but does not conclusively prove a pain generator.
- **Sympathetic blocks** may be diagnostic/therapeutic without chemical neurolysis.
- **Neuromodulation** (e.g. spinal cord stimulation) seeks adjustable modulation and should not be called neurolysis.
- This vocabulary prevents a common exam error: suggesting a “neurolytic epidural” as though it were a routine reversible neuraxial technique.

- Chemical neurolysis causes protein denaturation/axonal injury, interrupting nociceptive and sometimes autonomic or motor fibres.
- Its effect may last weeks to months or longer but is **unpredictable** because nerves regenerate, the underlying disease progresses or nearby structures are injured.
- The technique must have a plausible, defined pain target and a favourable balance between expected relief and permanent sensory/motor/autonomic injury. [R15]

## 13.2 Where it may be appropriate

- The most established role is **selected refractory cancer-related pain**, especially when systemic medication produces unacceptable adverse effects or insufficient analgesia and life expectancy/symptom burden favour a potentially longer-lasting intervention.
- Common examples include **coeliac plexus or splanchnic neurolysis** for appropriately selected pancreatic/upper abdominal visceral cancer pain, **superior hypogastric plexus** for pelvic visceral pain, and **ganglion impar** for selected perineal cancer pain.
- Somatic intercostal or other neurolysis may be considered for highly selected focal malignancy pain but carries risk of painful neuritis or irreversible deficit.
- Some sympathetically mediated non-malignant pain conditions may receive reversible sympathetic blocks; chemical destructive neurolysis is generally a much more cautious choice in benign, long-life-expectancy disease.

- Before a procedure ask: Is the pain predominantly **visceral sympathetic**, somatic or neuropathic?
- Is the intended nerve/plexus anatomically related?
- Has the underlying malignancy been assessed for other treatable causes (obstruction, fracture, infection)?
- What is the patient’s prognosis, anticoagulation, infection risk and neurological baseline?
- Are less destructive options adequate?
- How will benefit be assessed?
- Palliative care, interventional pain, oncology and the patient should agree on expectations.
- Pain relief is often partial and does not replace all other analgesia or psychosocial support.

### Selection of neurolytic target: what tissue is interrupted and what is lost?

**Upper abdominal visceral cancer pain:**

- Coeliac plexus neurolysis may be considered for selected severe pancreatic or upper abdominal malignant visceral pain after appropriate assessment; it targets sympathetic visceral afferent traffic and will not reliably abolish abdominal-wall somatic pain.
- A response to a diagnostic block may help but does not guarantee a durable neurolytic benefit.
- Anticipate hypotension and diarrhoea from sympathetic interruption, plus procedural bleeding, organ/nerve injury and rarely severe neurological complications.
- **Pelvic visceral cancer pain:** superior hypogastric plexus or ganglion impar approaches may have a role for appropriate pelvic/perineal pain, each with different organ targets and visceral/somatic limitations.
- **Selected peripheral/facet/sympathetic targets:** radiofrequency lesioning or other neuroablative techniques belong to a clearly diagnosed generator and specialist service; “neurolytic” is not a generic label for any analgesic injection or a treatment for widespread primary pain.

**Informed comparison:**

- Discuss realistic duration, probability and uncertainty of relief, potential sensory or motor deficit, neuritis/deafferentation pain, bleeding/infection, hypotension and effects on bowel, bladder or sexual function, alongside alternatives (treat tumour, systemic analgesia, radiation, reversible local blocks, rehabilitation, neuromodulation in selected conditions).
- The stronger indication often exists when prognosis, goals and limited time make rapid relief important despite irreversible risk.
- Neurolysis requires documented informed consent, specialist image-guided technical skill, antithrombotic review, recovery monitoring and ongoing analgesia even after a technically successful block.
- A case that is not clearly a defined peripheral/visceral target usually needs a different diagnosis or therapy, not stronger neurolytic chemicals. [R15]

## 13.3 Risks, contraindications and safe practice

- **Possible complications** include bleeding/retroperitoneal haematoma, infection, inadvertent vascular injection, toxicity/systemic effects of injectate, unintended motor/sensory deficit, neuropathic neuritis/deafferentation pain, spinal cord ischaemia from vascular injury, pneumothorax/visceral puncture depending on site, and autonomic effects such as hypotension or diarrhoea after coeliac plexus neurolysis.
- Technique and imaging guidance reduce but do not eliminate risk.
- For coeliac neurolysis, profound sympathetic block can cause orthostatic hypotension and diarrhoea; anticipate fluids/vasopressors if clinically appropriate and counsel the patient.
- For pelvic sympathetic targets, bladder, bowel and sexual effects are relevant.

- Check anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy, infection, coagulation, imaging/pathway anatomy, drug allergy and inability to give informed consent.
- **Do not attempt deep plexus neurolysis simply because a ward patient has a high pain score.** It requires a specialist with image-guided expertise, sterile technique, appropriate monitoring, consent that acknowledges potential irreversibility, emergency rescue availability and follow-up.
- ANZCA FPM **PS11(PM)** provides a procedures-in-pain clinical care standard; local procedural and antithrombotic guidance must be applied. [R15]

## 13.4 Compare with other procedures rather than overpromising

| Procedure | Goal | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Diagnostic local-anaesthetic block | Short interruption to help map a pain generator or predict potential benefit. | False positive/negative, placebo/context effects, technical spread; response not conclusive proof. |
| Therapeutic local-anaesthetic/steroid procedure | Temporary suppression of defined pain source where evidence supports; may enable rehabilitation. | Often time-limited; steroid/systemic and procedural risks. |
| Chemical neurolysis | Intentional longer-lasting interruption, most relevant to selected refractory visceral cancer pain. | Destructive, less reversible; neuritis, autonomic/motor, bleeding and organ injury risk. |
| Radiofrequency ablation | Targeted thermal/pulsed modulation or ablation depending on method; condition-specific indications. | Requires validated diagnostic pathway; not all radiofrequency variants cause neurolysis or have durable benefit. |
| Spinal cord/peripheral neuromodulation | Adjustable electrical modulation in selected refractory neuropathic syndromes. | Selection, trial process, device infection/migration, cost and ongoing follow-up. |

**Worked example:**

- A patient with advanced pancreatic cancer reports severe upper abdominal/back visceral pain, limited opioid escalation because of drowsiness/constipation, and imaging confirms appropriate anatomy.
- Discuss oncology/palliative management and consider coeliac plexus neurolysis as one component of a multidisciplinary plan.
- Explain potential partial benefit, short- and long-term adverse effects including hypotension/diarrhoea and rare neurological injury, antithrombotic safety and continued analgesia review.
- In contrast, an otherwise well 35-year-old with non-specific chronic low-back pain and no identifiable target is **not** an appropriate candidate for destructive chemical neural ablation simply because tablets have been unsuccessful.

### Separate an implanted stimulator from a drug delivery pump

- Identify the manufacturer and model, lead position and planned surgery mode before theatre.
- Seek implant-team advice on device deactivation, electrosurgery, neuraxial access and MRI conditionality.
- Prefer bipolar electrosurgery and plan return-pad placement and the current path if monopolar use is unavoidable.
- Reactivate and check function after surgery.
- An intrathecal baclofen pump is different.
- Unexpected interruption can cause severe withdrawal and needs urgent specialist involvement.

[BJA Education spinal cord stimulators and anaesthesia](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.02.005) · [Practical perioperative spinal cord stimulation guide 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12605233/) · [2026 perioperative spinal cord stimulator case discussion](https://doi.org/10.1213/XAA.0000000000002303)

items.body:
- This chapter **applies** the teaching rather than reproducing the separate historical SAQ bank.
- The answers are written in the form expected of a near-independent anaesthetist: assess risks, state a safe plan, justify alternatives and define monitoring/handovers.

## 14.1 Major abdominal surgery in a patient receiving high-dose opioids

**Scenario.** A patient with chronic post-traumatic lower-back pain takes regular modified-release morphine, short-acting oxycodone, a sedating evening medicine and reports poor sleep. Urgent laparotomy is needed for perforated diverticulitis. On arrival the patient is tachycardic, has worsening abdominal pain and has missed their morning morphine.

**Preoperative – differentiate problems and identify risks:**

- The immediate surgical problem is suspected abdominal sepsis with an acute nociceptive inflammatory insult.
- Assess shock/organ injury and resuscitate with the surgical team.
- Obtain accurate current opioid/other sedative exposure and timing, baseline pain/function, renal/hepatic status, OSA risk, prior withdrawal/overdose and whether the long-term drugs actually help.
- **Do not attribute the tachycardia solely to withdrawal**—it may reflect sepsis or pain.
- Nonetheless, missing baseline therapy can precipitate withdrawal in parallel with the surgical problem.
- Check aspiration/full-stomach risk and anticipated postoperative ventilatory support.
- Involve acute pain and pharmacy early if available; explain increased need for acute analgesia while acknowledging opioid toxicity remains possible.

**Intraoperative – treat physiology and nociception:**

- Undertake urgent safe GA and haemodynamic resuscitation, with source control and appropriate antibiotics.
- Ensure analgesic treatment of the laparotomy while preventing abrupt withdrawal; where possible, choose a multimodal adjunct and consider a regional technique only if infection/coagulation/haemodynamic status permits.
- Epidural may be inappropriate during septic shock or coagulopathy; intraperitoneal/local wound techniques and systemic agents may be more feasible.
- Titrate short-acting opioid to observed response with monitored ventilation and postoperative plan; ketamine may be considered in selected tolerant patients but not as a universal rule.
- Avoid automatically adding gabapentinoids to an already sedated high-risk patient.

**Postoperative – separate baseline, new pain and complication:**

- Reconcile baseline opioid when safe, use a monitored rescue strategy such as specialist-directed PCA when suitable, treat nausea/constipation and facilitate coughing, mobilisation and sleep.
- Watch sedation, RR/ventilation, renal deterioration, delirium, ongoing sepsis and possible surgical complication.
- Pain that worsens with a rigid abdomen or rising lactate is not simply “opioid tolerance”.
- Plan transition to oral short-acting rescue, quantify actual use and taper the additional postoperative opioid as inflammation resolves.
- A clear discharge prescriber and follow-up protect against indefinite escalation.

- **Examiner-level rationale:** continuation/substitution of baseline prevents withdrawal; new surgery demands separate analgesia; acute illness changes opioid distribution and metabolite clearance; opioid tolerance does not protect against respiratory depression. The chosen intervention and monitoring must match this individual and the procedure.

## 14.2 Emergency spinal decompression in a patient taking oral naltrexone

**Scenario.** A person in stable recovery from OUD takes oral naltrexone daily and presents with cauda-equina syndrome requiring urgent decompression. The last tablet was taken this morning.

**Preoperative:**

- Recognise **competitive antagonist blockade** and likely loss of former opioid tolerance; document last dose, exact product (consider combination products), renal/hepatic factors and relapse risk.
- Discuss emergency surgical need and realistic analgesic options with the patient and addiction/acute pain teams.
- Do not delay urgent decompression to permit washout.
- Ensure neurological documentation and urgent surgical coordination.
- Agree how and by whom naltrexone will be withheld/restarted safely.

**Intraoperative:**

- Use a robust nonopioid/multimodal strategy and appropriate local/regional adjuncts when consistent with neurological examination and procedure.
- Full agonist analgesia can be attenuated or unpredictable; if severe noxious stimulus requires additional opioid, choose a short-acting, titratable agent and a setting equipped for high-level airway/ventilation support as blockade wanes.
- Avoid uncontrolled escalation of a long-acting opioid because the first dose appeared ineffective.
- Specific ketamine/alpha-2 approaches require haemodynamic and psychiatric assessment; no one adjunct reliably replaces analgesia after major spine surgery.

**Postoperative:**

- Continue close pain and respiratory monitoring, document when opioid antagonism is likely decreasing and reassess whether full agonist dose should be reduced.
- Early mobilising neurological assessment remains crucial.
- If postoperative opioids are required, do **not** restart naltrexone until an appropriate drug-specific opioid-free interval and specialist review; include OUD support and overdose counselling.
- Arrange one responsible maintenance prescriber and a written analgesic plan.
- For comparison, if the patient had been taking **buprenorphine**, maintenance would usually be continued and supplemental full agonist/regional analgesia would be planned rather than treating it as antagonist blockade.

- **Examiner-level rationale:** state naltrexone’s mechanism, plan for elective vs emergency context, nonopioid/regional strategies, monitored opioid rescue, increased risk as blockade wanes and explicit restart/discharge. The 2025.2 and 2020.1 reports identify these as meaningful differentiators.

## 14.3 Persistent back pain with high-dose morphine and escalating disability

**Scenario.** A person takes modified-release morphine 60 mg twice daily for years, remains unable to work full-time, has poorly controlled sleep and asks for a stronger opioid because a repeat MRI again shows “degenerative disc disease”. No new neurological deficit or surgical target is evident.

**Reassess and formulate:**

- Confirm no red flags or new diagnosis, compare prior imaging and current clinical signs, identify predominant mechanical/nociplastic/neuropathic components, screen mood, sleep, inactivity, work and family stress, opioid adverse effects and dependence/OUD.
- Distinguish the presence of age-related degenerative changes from a proven pain generator.
- Clarify what improved after opioids initially and what current functional benefit remains.
- OMEDD is high and risk warrants overdose prevention, but do not rely on one dose threshold as the only reason for intervention.

**Integrated plan:**

- Validate pain and explain central amplification without trivialising symptoms.
- Agree specific functional goals, a supported exercise/physio plan, sleep and mood intervention, practical work/occupational help, and perhaps pain-programme referral.
- Review the effectiveness and harms of current opioid treatment under FPM PS01(PM) 2025; absent sustained benefit and with harms, propose **collaborative gradual taper** with a safety plan, not immediate withdrawal.
- Consider selected nonopioid drugs only where the phenotype supports them and contraindications permit.
- Avoid repeated injection/surgery without a meaningful anatomically concordant target and evidence of benefit.
- Agree scheduled review of walking, sleep, attendance and withdrawal symptoms; offer naloxone education and a single prescribing coordinator.

- **Why this is exam level:** the treatment is justified by mechanism, function and safety rather than a simplistic “opioids bad—stop”; it incorporates the psychological/social formulation, shared decision-making and a measurable review. A patient with red flags or concordant progressive deficit would need a different path.

## 14.4 Severe neuropathic limb pain after fracture: CRPS or missed surgical injury?

**Scenario.** Six weeks after wrist fixation, a patient has burning pain, allodynia, swelling and altered skin colour and temperature. Finger movement is limited and the patient fears therapy.

**Immediate differential:**

- Failed fixation/new fracture, infection, vascular compromise, venous thrombosis, nerve injury/entrapment, compartment problem if acute, and CRPS.
- Review operative course, immobilisation and any new deficit.
- Examine perfusion, wounds, motor and sensory function and trophic/autonomic changes; apply Budapest categories, looking for symptoms in three domains and **signs in two**, with no better alternative diagnosis.
- X-ray/ultrasound or other investigations are selected to exclude competing conditions, not to “confirm CRPS” with a nonspecific scan.

**Management:**

- Explain what is known and uncertain, provide analgesia allowing gentle hand use, begin early skilled hand therapy with graded movement/desensitisation and active occupational goals, address oedema and sleep/fear, and involve a pain specialist early if severe/complex.
- A neuropathic medicine can be trialled with side-effect review; do not insist that a nerve block or sympathetic neurolysis will cure the syndrome.
- Follow finger function and colour/temp changes as well as pain.
- Reassess the diagnosis if new focal weakness, fever or vascular deficit emerges.

- **Why this is exam level:** recognises alternative emergencies, applies formal criteria, balances active rehabilitation with proportionate analgesia and describes when to refer.

## 14.5 Advanced pancreatic cancer with severe visceral pain and opioid harm

**Scenario.** A person with unresectable pancreatic cancer has severe upper-abdominal and back pain despite carefully titrated opioid; escalating doses cause sedation and constipation. They value alertness and being at home.

**Assessment:**

- Confirm whether this is visceral cancer pain, obstruction, bowel pathology, vertebral metastasis, neuropathy or new infection; review current analgesic efficacy and adverse effects, performance status, life expectancy, coagulopathy/antithrombotics and patient values.
- Discuss ongoing cancer/palliative disease treatment, bowel regimen, adjuvant treatment for neuropathic component, and safe opioid rotation if appropriate (with specialist involvement).
- Coeliac plexus neurolysis may be an option for carefully selected visceral pain because it can reduce sympathetic transmission and potentially opioid burden.

**Justification and consent:**

- Explain expected partial/variable duration of relief, need for continued overall analgesia/psychosocial support, procedural bleeding/infection, transient hypotension/diarrhoea and rare serious neurological injury; assess anatomy and anticoagulation and ensure trained image-guided service.
- If pain predominantly arises from a somatic vertebral fracture, coeliac neurolysis may not address it: direct treatment and possibly radiotherapy/orthopaedic management may be more relevant.
- Coordinate palliative care and outpatient safety.
- **Neurolysis is not automatically a terminal-only or universal cancer intervention**, but its invasiveness is weighed carefully against prognosis, mechanism and goals.

items.body:
## 15.1 What contemporary guidance says and what it does not say

- **ANZCA PS45 (2025)** is a rights and clinical responsibility framework. It supports validation, equity, safe and fair evidence-informed pain care and transitions; it does not require one drug/procedure or override clinical judgement. [R1]
- **FPM PS01(PM) (2025)** makes self-management central in chronic non-cancer pain and opioid initiation exceptional, with ongoing trials, harm surveillance, dose minimisation and naloxone consideration. It does not mean abrupt unsupported discontinuation of a long-established opioid. [R2]
- **FPM PS17(PM) (October 2026, pilot)** supports multidisciplinary/interdisciplinary specialist services; it is not a guarantee every hospital has an inpatient pain-rehabilitation team. [R4]
- **ANZCA PS41(G) (2023)** governs acute pain across surgical and non-surgical presentations, especially individual assessment, analgesic stewardship, safety, monitoring and coordinated transitions. Apply it in opioid-tolerant surgical cases; never claim PS45 replaces acute-pain governance. [R22]
- **NICE NG193** concerns chronic primary pain medication recommendations; do not generalise its “do not initiate opioids” guidance to acute fracture/cancer pain, or its gabapentinoid position to diagnosed peripheral neuropathy. [R3]
- **NICE NG59, updated July 2026**, is specific to low-back pain/sciatica; removal of two psychology recommendations because underlying evidence was problematic is not a universal recommendation against psychological treatment, as explained by the UK FPM. [R7, R8]
- **NICE CG173** supports specific neuropathic drug choices outside sciatica; for trigeminal neuralgia it has separate carbamazepine-based recommendations. [R9]
- **Multisociety buprenorphine consensus (2021)** advises not routinely discontinuing buprenorphine for OUD. Opioid agonists, partial agonists and antagonists are pharmacologically different; naltrexone needs a specific plan. [R11, R18]

## 15.2 High-yield BJA Education reading with a purpose

| Article | Why read it alongside the notes | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| **Rosenberger & Pogatzki-Zahn, “Chronic post-surgical pain—update on incidence, risk factors and preventive treatment options” (2022)** [R14] | Best focused review for CPSP definitions, transition mechanisms, risk factors, trial limitations and what regional/analgesic prevention can plausibly achieve. | Much of the intervention evidence is heterogeneous; no block or drug guarantees prevention. |
| **Gauntlett-Gilbert & Brook, “Living well with chronic pain: the role of pain-management programmes” (2018 issue; online 2017)** [R5] | Explains active self-management, interdisciplinary rehabilitation, acceptance/functional goals and how to avoid repeated rescue-only medicalisation. | Older review; pair with 2025 PS45 and 2026 PS17 and with the condition-specific 2026 NICE changes. |
| **Gallagher & Galvin, “Opioids for chronic non-cancer pain” (2018)** [R13] | Clinical pharmacology, limited long-term benefits, tolerance/dependence/OIH and risk appraisal; helps build a critical opioid SAQ answer. | Apply the **newer PS01(PM) 2025** position for prescribing/THN, rather than treating a 2018 review as current policy. |
| **Royds & McCrory, “Neuroimmunity and chronic pain” (2018)** [R16] | Helps understand glia, neuroinflammation and central sensitisation without reducing persistent pain to a single peripheral lesion. | Mechanistic evidence is not a patient-level diagnostic test or justification for unproven neuroimmune drugs. |
| **Cox & Srivastava, “The genetics of pain” (2024)** [R17] | Optional higher-level explanation of susceptibility and pharmacogenomics; useful for why patients with similar surgery have heterogeneous pain. | Genetic effects are probabilistic; not a routine stand-alone prescribing algorithm. |

**Additional targeted resources:**

- The ANZCA **2023 Blue Book chapter “Perioperative management of patients on naltrexone”** is particularly high yield for the two recent Final SAQs (R18); the 2025 ANZCA opioid and rights statements are more current for general clinical practice.
- NICE CG173 and NG59, Budapest criteria, and the CRPS clinical review are practical cross-checks for the moderate-priority disease chapters.

### Reading order

- For **P1 complex chronic pain and rehabilitation**, prioritise Gauntlett-Gilbert and Brook, Living well with chronic pain: the role of pain-management programmes (BJA Education, 2018), alongside ANZCA/FPM PS45 (2025) and the October 2026 pilot PS17(PM).
- The BJA article explains programme design and active self-management; the official positions update the professional and equity framework.
- For **P1 opioid harm and tolerance**, read Gallagher and Galvin, Opioids for chronic non-cancer pain (BJA Education, 2018) as a physiology/evidence foundation, then interpret prescribing decisions through 2025 PS01(PM), the multisociety buprenorphine consensus and the dedicated naltrexone Blue Book chapter.
- For the **P5 mechanisms and CPSP** material, Rosenberger and Pogatzki-Zahn, Chronic post-surgical pain—update on incidence, risk factors and preventive treatment options (BJA Education, 2022), provides a useful risk framework and cautions about intervention evidence.
- Royds and McCrory, Neuroimmunity and chronic pain (BJA Education, 2018), helps explain biological mechanisms but should not be memorised as a diagnostic test or guaranteed treatment target; Cox and Srivastava, The genetics of pain (BJA Education, 2024), is supplementary biology rather than a perioperative drug algorithm.
- For **P3 back/neuropathic pain**, use NICE NG59 and CG173 for current choices and their differing indications, then apply the bedside assessment in Chapters 10–11. [R3, R5–R9, R14, R16–R18]

### Targeted BJA Education and Blue Book reading

- Use the BJA Education reviews on pain programmes and chronic non-cancer opioids to compare rehabilitation with escalation of medication.
- Pair the opioid-tolerant perioperative review with the opioid stewardship review and the New Zealand opioid substitution guidance.
- The 2025 BJA Education pregnancy review helps compare drug mechanisms and medication continuity.
- Use pregnancy-specific recommendations for obstetric patients.
- The serotonin toxicity and implanted-stimulator articles help answer the corresponding clinical cases.
- The postsurgical pain review covers mechanisms and risk, and the recent regional meta-analysis and transitional pain service review address prevention uncertainty.

Use the 2019 Blue Book chapters on CRPS, medicinal cannabis and opioid harm for background and check updated recommendations in the current guidance. Use the 2023 naltrexone chapter alongside the dedicated Set 15 cases, and the 2025 Hong Kong chapter to distinguish population prescribing, individual care and the limitations of observational data.

- [BJA Education living well with chronic pain](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2017.09.001) · [BJA Education opioids for chronic non-cancer pain](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2018.06.006) · [BJA Education opioid-tolerant patients](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw049) · [BJA Education opioid stewardship](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.007) · [BJA Education substance use disorder in pregnancy 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.07.006) · [BJA Education perioperative serotonin syndrome](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.10.003) · [BJA Education spinal cord stimulators and anaesthesia](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.02.005) · [BJA Education chronic postsurgical pain](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.11.008) · [ANZCA Blue Book editions](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) · [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, Ho and Cheung on Hong Kong opioid harms](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [FPM PS17(PM) specialist pain services pilot](https://www.anzca.edu.au/news-and-safety-alerts/ps17%28pm%29-multidisciplinary-and-interdisciplinary-care-in-specialist-pain-services-and-pain-units)

## 15.3 Common errors that cost marks

- 1. Conflate dependence, tolerance, OIH and OUD: , or call a stable prescribed opioid patient “addicted” without diagnostic assessment.
- 2. Confuse naltrexone with buprenorphine: and fail to explain competitive antagonism, response as it wears off, supervised opioid rescue and restart timing.
- 3. Continue methadone or buprenorphine but forget to treat new surgical pain: , or conversely withhold baseline therapy and precipitate withdrawal.
- 4. Give only a drug list: in the complex chronic-pain plan instead of biopsychosocial formulation, explicit functional goals, physical/psychological treatment, review and discharge roles.
- 5. Use imaging findings alone: to diagnose the cause of chronic low-back pain, or miss the red flags in new back pain or postoperative neuropathy.
- 6. Apply gabapentinoid recommendations indiscriminately: to sciatica, chronic primary pain and any pain described as “burning”, without neuropathic diagnosis or safety assessment.
- 7. Claim regional techniques or ketamine reliably prevent CPSP: from every operation; they may be valuable but evidence depends on procedure, population, endpoint and timeframe.
- 8. Offer destructive neurolysis for benign undifferentiated pain: , ignoring prognosis, anatomical target, irreversibility and procedural risks.
- 9. Ignore coexisting alcohol/stimulant intoxication or withdrawal: during urgent anaesthesia, or treat a positive drug screen as equivalent to active intoxication.
- 10. Discharge with several conflicting opioid prescriptions: and no single clinician responsible for monitoring or tapering postoperative additions.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
Selected trials that materially change clinical decisions in Set 16. The links open original trial reports, not secondary summaries. These trials do not establish a single treatment rule for every pain syndrome, and perioperative methadone/buprenorphine/naltrexone recommendations rely substantially on pharmacology, observational evidence and expert consensus rather than a definitive head-to-head RCT.

| **Trial — original paper** | **Primary finding** | **Final Exam interpretation / limitation** |
|---|---|---|
| [SPACE (Krebs et al., JAMA 2018)](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2673971) | 240 adults with chronic back or hip/knee osteoarthritis pain: an opioid strategy was not superior to nonopioid medication for pain-related function over 12 months. | Supports function-centred, nonopioid-first chronic non-cancer pain care. Excluded already opioid-dependent patients; do not generalise to acute major surgery, cancer or palliative care. |
| [I-WOTCH (Sandhu et al., JAMA 2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10208139/) | 608 adults taking long-term strong opioids: structured group education plus individual support increased opioid cessation at 12 months (29% vs 7%); pain interference did not differ significantly. | Supports voluntary, supported tapering with functional monitoring—not abrupt withdrawal. Discontinuation was self-reported, and applicability to unwilling or very high-dose patients is limited. |
| [RESTORE (Kent et al., Lancet 2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37146623/) | 492 people with chronic disabling low-back pain: individualised cognitive functional therapy, with or without sensor feedback, improved activity limitation versus usual care at 13 weeks; benefits persisted to 52 weeks. | Supports psychologically informed movement rehabilitation. Specific trained therapy and low-back population; 3-year follow-up had attrition and does not prove efficacy for every persistent-pain syndrome. |
| [STarT Back (Hill et al., Lancet 2011)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21963002/) | 851 primary-care patients with low-back pain: risk-stratified care matched to a screening tool improved disability modestly at 4 and 12 months compared with best current care. | Demonstrates value of prognostic/psychosocial assessment and matched treatment intensity; specific primary-care pathway, not a universal hospital pain score or drug algorithm. |
| [PRECISE (Mathieson et al., NEJM 2017)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28328324/) | In acute or chronic sciatica, pregabalin did not significantly reduce leg-pain intensity versus placebo at 8 weeks and caused more adverse events. | Avoid equating radicular sciatica with every peripheral neuropathic pain syndrome. Does not disprove all gabapentinoid benefit for other indicated neuropathic conditions. |
| [OPAL (Jones et al., Lancet 2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37392748/) | 347 adults with acute nonspecific low-back or neck pain: adding short-course oxycodone–naloxone to guideline care did not improve pain at 6 weeks versus placebo. | Avoid routine opioids for uncomplicated nonspecific spinal pain. Does not apply directly to fracture, ischaemia, major operative injury or severe cancer pain. |

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Linked references and source register

- **[R1] ANZCA/FPM, PS45 — Position statement on patients’ rights to pain management and associated responsibilities (2025).** Primary position statement: [ANZCA professional documents](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents). Use: person-centred assessment, validation, equity, evidence–harm balance and transitions; position rather than prescriptive drug choice.
- **[R2] FPM ANZCA, PS01(PM) — Statement regarding opioid analgesics in chronic non-cancer pain (2025).** [Official document](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/7d7d2619-6736-4d8e-876e-6f9b2b45c435/PS01%28PM%29-Statement-regarding-the-use-of-opioid-analgesics-in-patients-with-chronic-non-cancer-pain). Use: exceptional opioid role, self-management, functional evidence of benefit, harm surveillance and take-home naloxone thresholds.
- **[R3] NICE NG193 — Chronic pain (primary and secondary): assessment and chronic primary pain management.** [Recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng193/chapter/recommendations). Use: chronic primary versus secondary, person-centred assessment, supervised exercise, ACT/CBT and condition-specific pharmacology.
- **[R4] FPM ANZCA, PS17(PM) — Multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary care in specialist pain services (pilot launched 22 October 2026).** [Launch and scope](https://prod-anzca-094930.xperience-sites.com/news-and-safety-alerts/ps17%28pm%29-multidisciplinary-and-interdisciplinary-care-in-specialist-pain-services-and-pain-units). Use: coordinated specialist team practice; status is **pilot**, not final binding regulation.
- [R5] Gauntlett-Gilbert J, Brook P. “Living well with chronic pain: the role of pain-management programmes.” BJA Education 2018;18:3–7 (online 2017). [Full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807918/). Use: self-management, rehabilitation, team integration and risks of repeated rescue medicalisation.
- [R6] Gallagher H, Galvin D. “Opioids for chronic non-cancer pain.” BJA Education 2018;18:337–341. [Full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808073/). Use: opioid benefits/harms and chronic-prescribing limitations; modern policy from PS01(PM).
- **[R7] NICE NG59 — Low back pain and sciatica in over-16s, recommendations, updated 29 July 2026.** [Recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59/chapter/Recommendations) and [update statement](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59/chapter/Update-information). Use: triage, activity, drug treatment, radicular versus non-specific pain and **psychology recommendation withdrawal nuance**.
- **[R8] UK Faculty of Pain Medicine — Statement on July 2026 NICE NG59 update.** [Faculty statement](https://www.fpm.ac.uk/fpm-position-statement-july-2026-update-nice-ng59). Use: deletion ≠ a recommendation against psychological/MDT care; consider NG193 and wider chronic-pain evidence.
- **[R9] NICE CG173 — Neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management.** [Recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg173/chapter/Recommendations). Use: neuropathic medicine selection/review, early referral and trigeminal-neuralgia exception; **exclude sciatica** from uncritical application.
- **[R10] Murnion B et al. “Opioid use disorder in anaesthesia and intensive care: prevention, diagnosis and management.” Anaesthesia and Intensive Care (2022).** [Publisher review](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0310057X211066929). Use: diagnosis, perioperative OUD, opioid agonist treatment and clinician harm reduction.

items.title: What is the difference between allodynia and hyperalgesia?
items.los: BT_PM 1.33; BT_PM 1.34; AT_PM 1.8; AT_PM 1.11; IT_PM 1.1; IT_PM 1.16; BT_PM 1.30
items.q: What is the difference between allodynia and hyperalgesia?
items.a:
- Allodynia: pain from a normally non-painful stimulus.
- Hyperalgesia: increased pain from a painful stimulus.
- Both occur with sensitisation.
- Hyperpathia is a prolonged explosive response.

items.title: How do nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic pain differ?
items.los: BT_PM 1.33; BT_PM 1.34; AT_PM 1.8; AT_PM 1.11; IT_PM 1.1; IT_PM 1.16; BT_PM 1.30
items.q: How do nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic pain differ?
items.a:
- Nociceptive: tissue damage or inflammation.
- Neuropathic: lesion of the somatosensory system.
- Nociplastic: altered nociception without clear damage.
- Treatment differs for each.

items.title: What is the biopsychosocial model of chronic pain?
items.q: What is the biopsychosocial model of chronic pain?
items.a:
- Pain is shaped by biological, psychological and social factors.
- Central sensitisation maintains pain.
- Aim is function and quality of life.
- Treatment is multidisciplinary.

items.title: How do you assess a patient with chronic pain?
items.q: How do you assess a patient with chronic pain?
items.a:
- History, pain mechanism and red flags.
- Function, sleep and mood.
- Psychosocial yellow flags and medication use.
- Set patient-defined goals.

items.title: How do you assess and manage chronic daily headache?
items.q: How do you assess and manage chronic daily headache?
items.a:
- History and red flags; exclude intracranial pathology.
- Explain medication helps but does not cure.
- Withdraw overused analgesics; prophylaxis.
- Avoid full mu agonists; multidisciplinary care.

Past exam: 2022.1 Q2

items.title: What is medication overuse headache?
items.q: What is medication overuse headache?
items.a:
- Headache on 15 or more days a month from analgesic overuse.
- Simple analgesics over 15 days or opioids and triptans over 10 days.
- Withdraw the drug with support.
- Start prophylaxis.

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient with fibromyalgia?
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient with fibromyalgia?
items.a:
## Preop

Ask about baseline function, symptoms, medicines and recovery goals.

## Intraop

Use procedure-specific multimodal analgesia and careful positioning.

## Postop

Assess new pain, avoid excessive sedation and support graded activity.

items.title: Which psychosocial factors predict chronic pain?
items.los: BT_PM 1.33; BT_PM 1.34; AT_PM 1.8; AT_PM 1.11; IT_PM 1.1; IT_PM 1.16; BT_PM 1.30
items.q: Which psychosocial factors predict chronic pain?
items.a:
- Anxiety, depression and catastrophising.
- Fear-avoidance and poor coping.
- Compensation issues.
- Previous trauma and poor support.

items.title: What are the risks of long-term opioid therapy for chronic non-cancer pain?
items.q: What are the risks of long-term opioid therapy for chronic non-cancer pain?
items.a:
- Tolerance, dependence, addiction and hyperalgesia.
- Overdose and respiratory depression, especially above 50 mg morphine equivalent.
- Endocrine effects, constipation, cognitive impairment and falls.
- Little proven long-term benefit.

Past exam: 2021.1 Q8

items.title: How do you taper long-term opioids?
items.q: How do you taper long-term opioids?
items.a:
- Slowly: 5 to 10% every 2 to 4 weeks.
- Pause for distress or withdrawal.
- Single prescriber; support with non-drug therapy.
- Continue baseline if taper incomplete at surgery.

items.title: How do you convert between opioids?
items.q: How do you convert between opioids?
items.a:
- Convert to oral morphine equivalents using the college table.
- Reduce the new dose by 25 to 50% for incomplete cross-tolerance.
- Methadone conversion needs specialist input.
- Monitor for withdrawal and sedation.

items.title: How do you distinguish opioid tolerance from opioid-induced hyperalgesia?
items.q: How do you distinguish opioid tolerance from opioid-induced hyperalgesia?
items.a:
- Tolerance: more opioid helps.
- Hyperalgesia: more opioid worsens pain with diffuse allodynia.
- Reduce or rotate the opioid.
- Add ketamine or an alpha-2 agonist.

items.title: Why is rotation from high-dose oxycodone to methadone a specialist decision?
items.q: Why is rotation from high-dose oxycodone to methadone a specialist decision?
items.a: The conversion is nonlinear and depends on previous dose. Methadone can accumulate for days despite shorter analgesia, causing delayed respiratory depression. Consider QT and interactions, use an approved monitored protocol and specify rescue and follow-up.

items.title: How do you assess severe pain in an opioid-dependent patient labelled drug-seeking?
items.q: How do you assess severe pain in an opioid-dependent patient labelled drug-seeking?
items.a:
- Take her account and pain scores.
- Full opioid and drug history; look for withdrawal or intoxication.
- Review the anaesthetic and medication charts and the nurses’ view.
- Exclude a surgical complication.

Past exam: 2010.1 Q11

items.title: What is the pain management plan for an opioid-dependent patient after foot surgery?
items.q: What is the pain management plan for an opioid-dependent patient after foot surgery?
items.a:
- Negotiate a plan with patient and nurses.
- Continue background opioid and titrate extra, such as PCA.
- Regular paracetamol and NSAID, regional block, ketamine or clonidine.
- Contact the opioid prescriber for discharge.

Past exam: 2010.1 Q11

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient using high-dose fentanyl patches before knee replacement?
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient using high-dose fentanyl patches before knee replacement?
items.a:
## Preop

Check tolerance, sedation risk, dose and patch site. Agree baseline cover.

## Intraop

Avoid direct warming and choose motor-sparing regional analgesia.

## Postop

Titrate rescue, monitor ventilation and mobilise with assistance.

Past exam: 2017.1 Q8

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for an older patient taking oxycodone 80 mg daily before hip replacement?
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for an older patient taking oxycodone 80 mg daily before hip replacement?
items.a:
## Preop

Verify the baseline dose and risks, and arrange pain-team input if needed.

## Intraop

Preserve baseline opioid cover and use procedure-specific analgesia.

## Postop

Monitor sedation, ventilation and mobility. Taper additional rescue.

Past exam: 2015.1 Q7

items.title: How do you manage an acute flare of chronic pain in hospital?
items.los: BT_PM 1.33; BT_PM 1.34; AT_PM 1.8; AT_PM 1.11; IT_PM 1.1; IT_PM 1.16; BT_PM 1.30
items.q: How do you manage an acute flare of chronic pain in hospital?
items.a:
- Exclude red flags and compare with baseline.
- Continue baseline medication.
- Multimodal analgesia and a short opioid course above baseline.
- Early rehabilitation and a discharge plan.

items.title: What is the first principle of perioperative opioid management in an opioid-dependent patient?
items.q: What is the first principle of perioperative opioid management in an opioid-dependent patient?
items.a:
- Continue the baseline opioid to prevent withdrawal.
- Verify the dose with the prescriber or program.
- Treat acute pain on top of the baseline.
- Do not label requests as drug-seeking without assessment.

Past exam: 2010.1 Q11

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient on methadone maintenance having surgery?
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient on methadone maintenance having surgery?
items.a:
## Preop

Verify last and usual dose, QT risk and co-sedatives. Agree the maintenance plan.

## Intraop

Continue verified maintenance where safe and add surgical analgesia.

## Postop

Monitor ventilation, taper rescue and coordinate the return to the programme.

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient using a low-dose analgesic buprenorphine patch?
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient using a low-dose analgesic buprenorphine patch?
items.a:
## Preop

Confirm indication, site and timing. Usually continue.

## Intraop

Avoid warming the patch and use titrated multimodal rescue.

## Postop

Check ventilation and continue the usual replacement schedule.

Past exam: 2011.2 Q10

items.title: What is the pharmacology of buprenorphine?
items.q: What is the pharmacology of buprenorphine?
items.a:
- Partial mu agonist with high affinity and slow dissociation.
- Kappa antagonist; ceiling on respiratory depression.
- Patch gives slow onset and offset (24 to 30 hours after removal).
- Absorption increases with heat or fever.

Past exam: 2011.2 Q10

items.title: How does naltrexone affect perioperative analgesia?
items.q: How does naltrexone affect perioperative analgesia?
items.a:
- Competitive mu-opioid antagonist, effect lasts 24 to 72 hours.
- Opioids may be ineffective or need very high doses.
- Risk of respiratory depression when it wears off.
- Use non-opioid and regional analgesia; monitor.

Past exam: 2020.1 Q5

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient on oral naltrexone having elective surgery?
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient on oral naltrexone having elective surgery?
items.a:
## Preop

Check formulation and indication, and agree whether to hold treatment with the prescriber.

## Intraop

Use multimodal and regional analgesia. Titrate rescue if needed.

## Postop

Plan monitoring and prescriber-led restart after an adequate opioid-free interval.

Past exam: 2020.1 Q5

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient on high-dose naltrexone needing emergency surgery?
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient on high-dose naltrexone needing emergency surgery?
items.a:
## Preop

Check the last dose and organise monitored recovery. Avoid delay for washout.

## Intraop

Prioritise non-opioid measures and titrate rescue only with monitoring.

## Postop

Watch for ventilatory depression as blockade wanes and plan a safe restart.

Past exam: 2025.2 Q14

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient on depot buprenorphine having surgery?
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient on depot buprenorphine having surgery?
items.a:
## Preop

Verify formulation and injection dates. Usually maintain the schedule.

## Intraop

Use procedure-specific analgesia and titrate additional opioids when needed.

## Postop

Monitor ventilation, taper rescue and coordinate the next injection.

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient with chronic unhealthy alcohol intake?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient with chronic unhealthy alcohol intake?
items.a:
## Preop

Distinguish intoxication, dependence and withdrawal risk. Assess organ disease.

## Intraop

Plan aspiration mitigation and titrate anaesthesia to physiology.

## Postop

Monitor for withdrawal, give thiamine as indicated and arrange follow-up.

Past exam: 2015.2 Q12

items.title: When does alcohol withdrawal present?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: When does alcohol withdrawal present?
items.a:
- Tremor and anxiety at 6 to 24 hours.
- Seizures at 12 to 48 hours.
- Delirium tremens at 48 to 96 hours.
- Treat with benzodiazepines and thiamine.

Past exam: 2015.2 Q12

items.title: How do you treat delirium tremens?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: How do you treat delirium tremens?
items.a:
- ABC, monitoring and ICU if severe.
- Thiamine, electrolytes and fluids.
- Benzodiazepines titrated (diazepam, or lorazepam in liver disease).
- Adjuncts: haloperidol, dexmedetomidine, phenobarbitone.

items.title: What are the acute effects of methamphetamine on anaesthesia?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What are the acute effects of methamphetamine on anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Hypertension, tachycardia, arrhythmia and coronary spasm.
- Agitation, psychosis and hyperthermia.
- Raised MAC when acutely intoxicated.
- Avoid ketamine and ephedrine; use direct vasopressors.

Past exam: 2020.2 Q11

items.title: How does chronic methamphetamine use differ from acute?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: How does chronic methamphetamine use differ from acute?
items.a:
- Catecholamine depletion with hypotension.
- Reduced MAC and poor response to indirect vasopressors.
- Cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension.
- Withdrawal: fatigue and depression.

Past exam: 2020.2 Q11

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a methamphetamine-intoxicated patient who needs urgent surgery?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a methamphetamine-intoxicated patient who needs urgent surgery?
items.a:
## Preop

Assess urgency, capacity and toxicity. Treat agitation and hyperthermia.

## Intraop

Titrate anaesthesia and use direct vasopressors for hypotension when indicated.

## Postop

Observe for recurrent instability, rhabdomyolysis and a stimulant crash.

Past exam: 2024.2 Q1

items.title: What are the cardiovascular dangers of cocaine?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What are the cardiovascular dangers of cocaine?
items.a:
- Coronary vasospasm and infarction.
- Arrhythmia with wide QRS.
- Hypertension, aortic dissection and stroke.
- Treat with benzodiazepines and vasodilators; avoid beta-blockers.

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient who regularly uses cannabis?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient who regularly uses cannabis?
items.a:
## Preop

Establish route, last use, symptoms and capacity. Defer elective surgery if acutely impaired.

## Intraop

Titrate to effect and manage airway or cardiovascular changes.

## Postop

Check pain, nausea, ventilation and possible withdrawal.

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient who injects opioids and needs urgent surgery?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient who injects opioids and needs urgent surgery?
items.a:
## Preop

Check source control, sepsis, access, last opioid and maintenance treatment.

## Intraop

Provide procedure-specific analgesia and titrate short-acting rescue.

## Postop

Prevent withdrawal, monitor ventilation and arrange continuity with addiction care.

items.title: What are the clinical features of serotonin syndrome?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What are the clinical features of serotonin syndrome?
items.a:
- Neuromuscular: clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, rigidity.
- Autonomic: tachycardia, hyperthermia, sweating, diarrhoea.
- Mental: agitation and confusion within hours.
- Hunter criteria: serotonergic drug plus clonus or tremor with hyperreflexia.

Past exam: 2021.2 Q15

items.title: What drugs commonly cause serotonin syndrome in the perioperative period?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What drugs commonly cause serotonin syndrome in the perioperative period?
items.a:
- Tramadol, pethidine, methadone, fentanyl.
- Ondansetron, metoclopramide, methylene blue, linezolid.
- SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, MAOIs.
- Combinations and dose increases are the risk.

Past exam: 2012.1 Q1

items.title: What is the differential diagnosis of serotonin syndrome?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What is the differential diagnosis of serotonin syndrome?
items.a:
- Neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
- Malignant hyperthermia.
- Anticholinergic toxicity.
- Emergence delirium and sepsis.

Past exam: 2021.2 Q15

items.title: How do you treat serotonin syndrome?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: How do you treat serotonin syndrome?
items.a:
- Stop serotonergic drugs and admit.
- Benzodiazepines, cooling and fluids.
- Discuss enteral cyproheptadine with toxicology in selected cases. Outcome benefit is uncertain.
- Severe: paralyse with a non-depolarising agent and ventilate; avoid suxamethonium.

Past exam: 2021.2 Q15

items.title: How does neuroleptic malignant syndrome differ from serotonin syndrome?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: How does neuroleptic malignant syndrome differ from serotonin syndrome?
items.a:
- Slow onset over days.
- Bradyreflexia and lead-pipe rigidity.
- Dopamine antagonists or withdrawal of dopamine agonists.
- Treat with cooling, dantrolene or bromocriptine.

items.title: How do you recognise opioid overdose on the ward?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: How do you recognise opioid overdose on the ward?
items.a:
- Reduced consciousness, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression.
- Use sedation score and capnography.
- Check other causes (sedatives, glucose, stroke).
- Stop the opioid source.

items.title: How do you give naloxone for opioid overdose?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: How do you give naloxone for opioid overdose?
items.a:
- Support ventilation first. Use the local naloxone protocol. In a monitored patient with a pulse, titrate to adequate breathing.
- Titrate to breathing, not to full reversal.
- Duration is 30 to 60 minutes: repeat or infuse and observe.
- Remove patches; look for the cause.

items.title: Who should receive take-home naloxone?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: Who should receive take-home naloxone?
items.a:
- Patients on opioid substitution or with OUD.
- High-dose opioid recipients and those with risk factors.
- Teach family or carers.
- Part of stewardship and harm reduction.

items.title: What are the features of the anticholinergic and cholinergic toxidromes?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What are the features of the anticholinergic and cholinergic toxidromes?
items.a:
- Anticholinergic: dry skin, dilated pupils, delirium, retention.
- Cholinergic: salivation, lacrimation, bradycardia, pinpoint pupils.
- Treat anticholinergic supportively with benzodiazepines.
- Treat cholinergic with atropine.

items.title: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient taking an antidepressant?
items.sub: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.eyebrow: Alcohol, other drugs and psychiatric disease
items.q: What are the perioperative considerations for a patient taking an antidepressant?
items.a:
## Preop

items.title: 1. Pain terms and the three pain mechanisms
items.q: Define allodynia, hyperalgesia, hyperpathia, paraesthesia and dysaesthesia, and explain how nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic pain differ.
items.a:
## Definitions (IASP)

- **Allodynia:** pain caused by a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain (for example light touch or clothing).
- **Hyperalgesia:** increased pain from a stimulus that normally provokes pain. Primary hyperalgesia is at the injury site (peripheral sensitisation); secondary hyperalgesia is in surrounding undamaged tissue (central sensitisation).
- **Hyperpathia:** an abnormally painful, explosive and prolonged reaction to a repetitive stimulus, with a raised threshold; often delayed onset and after-sensation.
- **Paraesthesia:** an abnormal sensation, spontaneous or evoked, that is **not unpleasant** (pins and needles).
- **Dysaesthesia:** an abnormal sensation that **is unpleasant**, spontaneous or evoked.
- (Also hypoalgesia, anaesthesia dolorosa and neuralgia may be asked.)

## Types of pain

| Feature | Nociceptive | Neuropathic | Nociplastic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Activation of nociceptors by tissue damage or inflammation | Lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system | Altered nociception without clear tissue damage or nerve lesion (central sensitisation) |
| Examples | Postoperative wound, fracture, arthritis | Diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, post-amputation, radiculopathy | Fibromyalgia, chronic widespread pain, irritable bowel, some low back pain, CRPS type I features |
| Quality | Aching, throbbing, well localised; mechanical and inflammatory | Burning, shooting, electric shock; allodynia, dysaesthesia; dermatomal | Diffuse, widespread, with fatigue, sleep and cognitive disturbance, hypersensitivity |
| Drug response | Paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids | Tricyclics, SNRIs, gabapentinoids, topical agents | Centrally acting agents (amitriptyline, duloxetine, pregabalin) plus non-drug therapies |
| Examination | Local tenderness | Sensory loss or hypersensitivity in a neuroanatomical distribution | Widespread tenderness; no clear lesion |

## Points to note

- **Central sensitisation** (wind-up, NMDA receptor activation, glial activation) underpins secondary hyperalgesia and nociplastic pain; the CRPS chapter describes spreading pain, sensory deficits and altered body perception in the chronic phase as central features.
- Many conditions are **mixed** (for example cancer pain, post-surgical pain, chronic back pain with radiculopathy).
- Identification influences treatment: neuropathic and nociplastic pain respond poorly to opioids and best to adjuvants and rehabilitation.
- Tools such as DN4 and PainDETECT help distinguish neuropathic features.

Mechanisms may coexist. A patient with rheumatoid joint injury may have nociceptive pain, nerve entrapment with a plausible sensory territory and widespread amplified pain. Examine each component and tailor treatment and functional goals accordingly. The label nociplastic requires a coherent clinical assessment rather than a normal scan alone.

Apply the mechanism to treatment selection and explain its uncertainty.
