**Sources:** [CRPS diagnosis and treatment guidelines, fifth edition](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9186375/) · [NeuPSIG neuropathic pain meta-analysis, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40252663/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines allodynia and hyperalgesia with primary and secondary types
- Defines hyperpathia, paraesthesia and dysaesthesia correctly (unpleasant versus not)
- Compares nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic pain mechanisms
- Gives examples, qualities and drug responses
- Mentions central sensitisation and mixed pain
- Tools for screening neuropathic pain

items.title: 2. Assessing persistent widespread pain and disability
items.q: A 45-year-old woman is referred with persistent widespread pain and disability. Describe your assessment and your approach to management.
items.a:
## Assessment

Persistent widespread pain with disability needs a **biopsychosocial** assessment, exclusion of serious disease, and clarity about what the patient wants.

**History**
- **Pain:** onset and trigger, distribution, quality (nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic features), severity, pattern, aggravating and relieving factors, and effect on sleep, mood, work, relationships and activity.
- **Previous treatments and opioid use:** every drug, dose, duration and response; ask about alcohol, cannabis and other substances.
- **Psychosocial factors and yellow flags:** depression, anxiety, trauma, catastrophising, fear-avoidance, beliefs ("hurt equals harm"), expectations, secondary gain, compensation, family and work.
- **Red flags:** weight loss, fever, night pain, neurological deficit, cancer, inflammatory disease, systemic features.

**Examination:** general and musculoskeletal examination, neurological examination, tender points and allodynia, signs of inflammatory arthritis, thyroid or neuropathic signs, and observe movement and behaviour.

**Tools:** pain intensity and interference scales (brief pain inventory), mood and anxiety screens (PHQ-9, GAD-7, DASS), the Pain Self-Efficacy Questionnaire, sleep questionnaires, catastrophising and fear-avoidance measures, screening for neuropathic pain (DN4), and opioid risk tools (Blue Book: SOAPP is more reliable than the Opioid Risk Tool).

**Investigations:** targeted: FBC, ESR/CRP, thyroid function, vitamin D, B12, glucose, and imaging only if indicated; avoid over-investigation.

## Management

- **1.** **Explain and validate:** a clear explanation of central sensitisation and the biopsychosocial model; emphasise that hurt does not equal harm; agree on realistic **functional goals** and a plan with the patient. Positive communication is part of treatment (Blue Book placebo chapter).
- **2.** **Active rehabilitation:** graded activity and exercise, physiotherapy, pacing, occupational therapy and work rehabilitation.
- **3.** **Psychological therapy:** CBT, acceptance and commitment therapy, mindfulness, and treatment of depression, anxiety and trauma.
- **4.** **Sleep and lifestyle:** sleep hygiene, weight, smoking and alcohol.
- **5.** **Drugs, used sparingly:** paracetamol and NSAIDs are of limited value; amitriptyline or duloxetine and gabapentinoids for neuropathic or widespread pain; avoid long-term opioids (stewardship); deprescribe ineffective drugs.
- **6.** **Interventions** only for defined pain generators (selected injections or neuromodulation).
- **7.** **Multidisciplinary pain program** and shared care with the GP, with regular review of function rather than pain scores.

Use a baseline functional measure and agree a patient-selected goal such as walking for ten minutes or returning to a weekly activity. Review progress, adverse effects and barriers at an agreed interval. Coordinate care across services to avoid contradictory messages.

**Sources:** [BJA Education living well with chronic pain](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2017.09.001) · [NICE chronic primary pain NG193](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng193/chapter/recommendations) · [ANZCA professional documents, including PS41 and PS45](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents) · [FPM PS17(PM) specialist pain services pilot](https://www.anzca.edu.au/news-and-safety-alerts/ps17%28pm%29-multidisciplinary-and-interdisciplinary-care-in-specialist-pain-services-and-pain-units)

## Self-marking checklist

- Takes a biopsychosocial history including function, drugs, psychosocial yellow flags
- Screens for red flags
- Examination and targeted investigations
- Uses validated tools for pain, mood, sleep and opioid risk
- Explains the model and agrees functional goals
- Active rehabilitation and psychological therapy
- Judicious drug therapy and deprescribing
- Multidisciplinary program and review

items.title: 3. Fibromyalgia: perioperative considerations for hysterectomy
items.q: A woman with fibromyalgia is booked for laparoscopic hysterectomy. Discuss the perioperative considerations, including analgesia.
items.a:
## Preop

Fibromyalgia commonly presents with widespread pain, fatigue, poor sleep and cognitive symptoms. Nociplastic mechanisms may coexist with nociception from the uterine condition or another diagnosis. Acknowledge symptoms and identify baseline movement, sleep and previous perioperative experiences. Ask about current pain therapies, functional goals, mood, sleep apnoea and flare triggers. Review medication-specific risks, including sedation with opioids and gabapentinoids, anticholinergic effects of tricyclics and serotonin risk with combinations such as tramadol plus an SNRI. Continue regular treatments when clinically appropriate, with a specific plan for high-risk drugs and withdrawal. Avoid routine preoperative escalation of sedatives. Agree on an analgesia plan with the patient and acute pain service when complexity warrants.

## Intraop

Provide a technique suited to laparoscopic hysterectomy, anticipated surgical pain and patient preferences. Pad sensitised areas and minimise prolonged pressure. Use paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor if renal, bleeding and cardiovascular risk allow. Consider surgical local infiltration or an appropriate abdominal wall block for somatic port pain. Explain that this cannot cover every visceral pain component. Dexamethasone or other antiemetic prophylaxis is reasonable according to risk. Titrate opioid rescue and avoid unnecessary high doses. In severe opioid tolerance or refractory pain, discuss ketamine with the acute pain team. Fibromyalgia alone provides insufficient evidence for a routine prolonged ketamine or lignocaine infusion or multiple systemic adjuncts.

## Postop

Anticipate pain fluctuation and assess the surgical site and symptoms before labelling new or disproportionate pain a flare. Assess ventilation and alertness during opioid treatment, especially if OSA or co-sedation is present. Optimise suitable non-opioids and use short-acting rescue only when necessary, with clear goals and reassessment. Plan gentle activity, pacing, early mobilisation and protection of sleep. Ask which strategies help the patient manage flares and agree on a threshold for contacting the team. At discharge record functional progress, baseline medicines and any limited short-acting opioid taper. Continue usual multidisciplinary fibromyalgia care through primary care, physiotherapy and psychological or sleep supports as appropriate. A recovery plan should address independence and return to activity as well as pain intensity. Arrange a named review if pain or function fails to improve.

Consider involvement of the existing clinician if the patient has had a particularly difficult recovery from an earlier operation.

**Sources:** [BJA Education living well with chronic pain](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2017.09.001) · [NICE chronic primary pain NG193](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng193/chapter/recommendations) · [BJA Education opioid-tolerant patients](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw049)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises nociplastic and other pain mechanisms
- Assesses baseline function and medication risks
- Selects an operation-specific multimodal regimen
- Qualifies systemic adjunct evidence
- Checks surgical red flags, sedation and ventilation
- Plans rehabilitation, discharge and follow-up

items.title: 4. Opioid conversion, rotation and pre-operative dose reduction
items.q: Explain the principles of opioid conversion and rotation, and how you would reduce the dose of a patient on long-term opioids before elective surgery.
items.a:
## Conversion principles

Use oral morphine equivalent daily dose to compare exposure across routes and formulations. Use the applicable local table and total the actual baseline and rescue dose. Equivalents provide a population estimate, and clinical effect depends on the patient, drug, metabolism and route.
- Equianalgesic tables derive from single-dose studies in opioid-naive volunteers, so they are **a guide only** (BJA).
- **Oral to IV morphine** is about 3:1 to 2:1 (BJA example: 400 mg oral is about 133 mg IV a day, 5.5 mg/h).
- Methadone conversion is nonlinear and dose-dependent. A pain or addiction specialist should use the appropriate protocol and account for accumulation, QT prolongation and interactions.

## Rotation

Rotation is used for intolerable side effects or inadequate analgesia despite escalation, exploiting **incomplete cross-tolerance** (BJA). The safe method is:
- **1.** Calculate the 24-hour OMEDD from all sources, including breakthrough.
- **2.** Convert to the new drug.
- **3.** Reduce the calculated dose conservatively for incomplete cross-tolerance, accounting for pain severity, patient sensitivity and clinical monitoring. This standard rotation step does not provide a methadone conversion rule.
- **4.** Give the new drug in divided doses with breakthrough access, reassess within 24 to 48 hours and titrate.

## Reducing the dose before elective surgery

A gradual, supported reduction may be appropriate when anticipated harms exceed benefits, while surgery timing, current function and patient preference guide the decision. Evidence does not establish universal preoperative taper targets.
- Start weeks to months before surgery with the GP and pain service, agree goals with the patient, and tell them that reducing opioids may reduce hyperalgesia.
- Agree a gradual reduction with regular reviews, pausing or slowing if withdrawal or function worsens. Consider behavioural support and rehabilitation. The I-WOTCH trial supports structured taper support, and does not establish a mandatory schedule for surgical patients.
- Add non-opioid options: paracetamol, NSAID, neuropathic agents, physiotherapy, CBT, and psychological support; treat withdrawal symptoms (clonidine, antiemetics, loperamide).
- If tapering is not feasible (cancer pain, substitution therapy), **do not stop**: continue the baseline and manage perioperatively as an opioid-tolerant patient.
- **Perioperatively:** continue the baseline opioid on the day of surgery, avoid unnecessary high opioid exposure, including high-dose remifentanil, use ketamine and regional analgesia.
- **After surgery:** plan to return to or below the preoperative dose, set an explicit end date for any new opioid, and arrange review.
- Provide naloxone and warn that restarting a previous dose after a taper risks overdose.

**Sources:** [FPM ANZCA PS01(PM) chronic non-cancer pain, 2025](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/7d7d2619-6736-4d8e-876e-6f9b2b45c435/PS01%28PM%29-Statement-regarding-the-use-of-opioid-analgesics-in-patients-with-chronic-non-cancer-pain) · [I-WOTCH trial](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2023.6454) · [BJA Education opioid-tolerant patients](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw049)

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains OMEDD and approximate equivalence for common opioids
- Oral to IV conversion ratio and limits of equianalgesic tables
- Methadone is non-linear and needs specialist conversion
- Explains conservative adjustment for incomplete cross-tolerance
- Personalises the taper and prevents withdrawal
- Does not stop abruptly in cancer pain or substitution therapy
- Perioperative and postoperative plan and naloxone

items.title: 5. Flare of chronic back pain in a patient on regular opioids
items.q: A 55-year-old man with chronic low back pain on regular opioids is admitted with a flare of severe pain. Outline your assessment and management.
items.a:
## Assessment

**Take the pain seriously and find out why it has changed.** A flare in a chronic back pain patient is not always a flare.
- **History:** onset, trigger (lifting, fall, stopping a drug), character, radiation, bladder/bowel and leg symptoms, fever, weight loss, new neurology; opioid and other drugs (dose, last dose, adherence, missed doses or lost supply); alcohol and substance use; mood and sleep.
- **Red flags** needing urgent action: cauda equina syndrome, epidural abscess or haematoma, vertebral fracture or collapse (osteoporosis, cancer), metastases, discitis, aortic aneurysm, renal colic or other visceral cause, and infection.
- **Examination:** vital signs, spine tenderness, neurological examination including saddle sensation and anal tone, abdomen and pulses.
- **Investigations** guided by findings: FBC, CRP, urgent MRI for red flags.
- **Opioid-related:** withdrawal (COWS), intoxication or oversedation, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, and tolerance (BJA).
- Measure function (can he sit, stand, walk) and use a validated pain scale; set a realistic goal.

## Management

- **1.** **Treat the cause** (urgent imaging and surgery for cord or cauda equina compression, antibiotics for infection).
- **2.** **Continue the baseline opioid** (including formulation and timing) to prevent withdrawal, and add acute analgesia.
- **3.** **Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia:** regular paracetamol, NSAID if safe, heat and positioning, neuropathic agent (gabapentinoid or tricyclic) for a separately established responsive neuropathic condition, not routine sciatica, **low-dose ketamine** for opioid-tolerant patients (BJA: 1 to 3 days), lidocaine infusion, and consider an epidural or targeted block.
- **4.** **Rescue opioid:** titrated immediate-release oxycodone or hydromorphone, or PCA with a larger bolus, with doses above the opioid-naive range; BJA suggests one-sixth of the 24-hour dose every 4 hours as a start.
- **5.** **Monitoring:** sedation score, respiratory rate and oximetry, no additional sedatives, naloxone available.
- **6.** **Communication:** involve the acute pain service early; give a plan and avoid labelling as drug-seeking.
- **7.** **Rehabilitation and discharge:** early mobilisation, a limited rescue supply, a single prescriber, a plan to return to baseline within days to weeks, and follow-up with the GP or pain clinic; avoid permanent dose escalation.

Check what changed compared with baseline rather than assuming a flare. If no red flags or new deficit are present, agree a time-limited rescue plan and continue movement as tolerated. Ask who will review the opioid prescription, return to baseline and functional recovery after discharge.

**Sources:** [FPM ANZCA PS01(PM) chronic non-cancer pain, 2025](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/7d7d2619-6736-4d8e-876e-6f9b2b45c435/PS01%28PM%29-Statement-regarding-the-use-of-opioid-analgesics-in-patients-with-chronic-non-cancer-pain) · [NICE low back pain and sciatica NG59](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59/chapter/recommendations) · [ANZCA professional documents, including PS41 and PS45](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

## Self-marking checklist

- Assesses cause of the flare and screens for red flags
- Examines neurology and sends targeted investigations
- Evaluates opioid-related factors: withdrawal, tolerance, hyperalgesia
- Treats the cause if identified
- Continues baseline opioid and adds multimodal analgesia
- Rescue opioid dosing and ketamine for opioid-tolerant patients
- Monitoring and communication
- Discharge plan avoiding dose escalation

items.title: 6. Methadone maintenance patient for elective cholecystectomy
items.q: A patient on methadone 80 mg daily from an opioid treatment programme presents for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Outline the perioperative considerations, including analgesia.
items.a:
## Principles

Methadone is a full μ agonist with variable, prolonged elimination. Once-daily maintenance suppresses withdrawal longer than it provides analgesia. Preserve verified treatment for opioid use disorder and make a separate plan for new surgical pain.

## Preop

If the patient reports missed doses, confirm the gap and ask the programme whether re-titration is needed. Avoid treating sedation or recent intoxication as though it were withdrawal.

- **Verify the dose** and last dose with the prescriber or dispensing pharmacy; do not rely on the patient alone. Tell the program about the admission.
- Assess for withdrawal, other substance use, hepatitis, HIV, liver disease and sleep apnoea.
- Review QT risk, other QT-prolonging drugs, renal function and electrolytes. Check ECG when risk warrants, and correct clinically important potassium or magnesium abnormalities.
- Involve the acute pain service and addiction medicine early, explain the plan, and give non-judgemental reassurance.

## Intraop

- Continue verified maintenance on the day of surgery if safe. If oral or enteral dosing is unavailable, ask the prescriber, pharmacy and acute pain service to arrange a monitored, formulation-specific substitute. Do not use a fixed methadone-to-morphine ratio or independently start a background infusion.
- Choose operation-specific multimodal analgesia such as paracetamol, an NSAID if appropriate and local infiltration or an abdominal wall technique. Consider specialist adjuncts only when indicated.
- Titrate an additional short-acting opioid if needed. Split maintenance may be considered in hospital with prescriber agreement, avoiding duplicate dosing and specifying how the usual schedule will resume.

## Postop

- Assess movement pain and provide independently titrated rescue. Consider demand-only PCA when appropriate and define who reviews dosing. Avoid mixed agonist-antagonists that can precipitate withdrawal. Any change from methadone to buprenorphine requires a separate specialist plan.
- Monitor sedation and respiratory rate, and avoid additional sedatives; naloxone available.
- **Discharge:** return to the program, a single prescriber, a limited supply of additional opioid only if needed, communication with the program, take-home naloxone and a plan to stop extra opioids.

## Pitfalls

Withholding opioids because of addiction, and unrecognised QT prolongation.

Document the monitoring location and assess pain on movement, ventilation and sedation before increasing rescue. Continue follow-up beyond discharge when the patient is likely to need short-acting opioids for more than a few days.

**Sources:** [BJA Education opioid-tolerant patients](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw049) · [NZ opioid substitution treatment guidance 2025](https://www.health.govt.nz/publications/new-zealand-practice-guidelines-for-opioid-substitution-treatment-2025) · [BJA Education substance use disorder in pregnancy 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.07.006)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises methadone as OUD treatment, not an analgesic, and continues baseline
- Verifies dose with prescriber/pharmacy and informs program
- Checks QTc, electrolytes and comorbidities (liver disease, hepatitis, OSA)
- Explains pharmacology: long half-life but short analgesic duration; split dosing
- Plans a formulation-specific specialist substitute if oral dosing is unavailable
- Selects procedure-specific multimodal and regional options
- Titrates rescue and distinguishes maintenance changes from pain treatment
- Monitoring and discharge plan with naloxone

items.title: 7. Injecting heroin user for emergency amputation
items.q: A patient who injects heroin requires emergency forearm amputation for gangrene. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Preop

Involve surgery early for urgent source control. Assess sepsis, perfusion and relevant organ dysfunction. Establish the last injected opioid and other substances, the usual prescription or maintenance programme, past withdrawal and overdose, and baseline pain. Use nonjudgmental language and verify opioid agonist therapy with the prescriber rather than repeating an uncertain dose. Distinguish intoxication and respiratory depression from withdrawal. Assess renal and hepatic function, electrolytes, glucose and blood count. Obtain cultures and antimicrobials as appropriate without delaying emergency care. Consider endocarditis when there is persistent bacteraemia, a murmur or embolic findings. Assess access, blood-borne virus history and standard precautions. Arrange skilled ultrasound-guided access if needed. Document limb neurology and negotiate analgesic and functional goals.

## Intraop

Choose a technique suitable for the patient's sepsis, haemodynamics, aspiration risk and surgery. Use appropriate monitoring and vascular access with resuscitation and direct vasopressor support when indicated. Consider a brachial plexus technique if it offers benefit, consent and cooperation permit and there is a safe needle path, acceptable bleeding risk and an agreed surveillance plan. Avoid traversing infected tissue. Use simple analgesics as appropriate and specialist adjuncts selectively. Treat surgical pain with titrated rescue when needed, while accounting for established tolerance and other sedatives. A verified maintenance dose prevents withdrawal but provides incomplete surgical analgesia. An opioid requirement cannot be inferred safely from the reported dose of an unregulated product.

## Postop

Determine the monitored destination by sepsis severity, baseline opioid use and rescue needs. Assess pain with movement, sedation, ventilation and withdrawal. Continue verified methadone or buprenorphine if already prescribed, with specialist adjustment for interruptions or safety concerns. Consult addiction medicine about inpatient treatment if opioid use disorder is untreated, timing induction to avoid precipitated withdrawal. Treat stump and phantom symptoms according to phenotype and support early rehabilitation. A catheter may reduce acute opioid exposure, with uncertain effect on long-term phantom pain. Plan wound, infection and pain follow-up. Give a coordinated discharge prescription, short-acting rescue taper if needed, overdose-prevention education and naloxone access where available. Arrange continuity with the addiction service and primary care.

If the patient declines treatment, clarify the reasons, address withdrawal and pain, and reassess clinical decision-making capacity as needed.

**Sources:** [BJA Education opioid-tolerant patients](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaed/mkw049) · [NZ opioid substitution treatment guidance 2025](https://www.health.govt.nz/publications/new-zealand-practice-guidelines-for-opioid-substitution-treatment-2025)

## Self-marking checklist

- Prioritises sepsis and source control
- Checks recent use, maintenance drugs and capacity
- Plans access, monitoring and blood-borne infection assessment
- Individualises regional and systemic analgesia
- Prevents withdrawal and monitors sedation and ventilation
- Coordinates addiction treatment, rehabilitation and discharge

items.title: 8. Recurrent hypoventilation after naloxone in a methadone patient
items.q: A hospital patient on methadone maintenance develops recurrent hypoventilation after initial naloxone reversal. Outline ongoing management and overdose prevention.
items.a:
## Recognition

Suspect overdose in any patient receiving opioids who is **sedated, bradypnoeic or hypoxic**. Risk factors include older age, renal or hepatic impairment, sleep apnoea, high dose, opioid-naive patients, co-sedatives (gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines, alcohol), PCA by proxy, patch heating and dosing errors.
- **Classic triad:** reduced conscious level, respiratory depression (rate below 8 to 10, shallow, snoring), and **pinpoint pupils**; also hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hyporeflexia.
- **Sedation precedes respiratory depression**, so use a sedation score (Australian sedation scale) with respiratory rate and oxygen saturation (BJA).
- Differentials: hypoxia, hypercarbia, sepsis, stroke, hypoglycaemia, other drugs, serotonin syndrome or other toxidromes (BJA table: opioid toxicity has miosis, hypothermia and hyporeflexia, unlike serotonin syndrome).

## Management

- **1.** **Call for help and stop** all opioids and infusions (PCA, patches removed, epidural opioid).
- **2.** **ABC:** open the airway, give oxygen, bag-mask ventilation if inadequate breathing; this is the priority, as naloxone is secondary.
- **3.** **Naloxone** if respiratory depression or a reduced conscious level: titrate 100 to 200 micrograms IV (or 0.4 mg IM) every 2 to 3 minutes to restore breathing, **not full consciousness**, to avoid abrupt withdrawal, pain, sympathetic surge and pulmonary oedema; the effect lasts 30 to 90 minutes, shorter than most opioids, so use a **naloxone infusion** (two-thirds of the effective dose per hour) or repeat doses.
- **4.** Opioids with prolonged effect, including methadone, transdermal preparations and buprenorphine, can outlast naloxone. High-affinity buprenorphine can be difficult to reverse. Escalate promptly and seek toxicology or critical care advice for repeated doses or infusion. Effective ventilation remains essential.
- **5.** For recurrent or long-acting toxicity use monitored care with a longer observation period guided by agent, formulation, clinical response, time since last rescue and local toxicology advice. Check renal failure, interacting drugs and administration errors.
- **6.** Consider ICU for recurrent depression or a long-acting drug.

## Naloxone in harm reduction

- Offer take-home naloxone and teach recognition, emergency calling and rescue breathing to patients at increased risk and their supporters. Confirm available formulations and access through local pharmacy, addiction or harm-reduction services.
- Offer it at hospital discharge for patients on high-dose opioids, substitution therapy, or with a past overdose; also consider for patients leaving prison and for those with loss of tolerance after withdrawal.
- Combine with safe prescribing (lowest dose, shortest duration, tapers, avoid co-sedatives) and addiction treatment.

After reversal, verify the methadone dose and last administration, check whether duplicate dosing or another sedative contributed, and review the ECG and electrolytes. Do not give the next maintenance dose until the team has reassessed toxicity and agreed a safe plan with the prescriber.

**Sources:** [BJA Education opioid-induced respiratory depression](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.12.007) · [ANZCOR suspected opioid overdose guidance](https://www.anzcor.org/home/first-aid/guideline-9-5-2-first-aid-management-of-opioid-overdose) · [FPM ANZCA PS01(PM) chronic non-cancer pain, 2025](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getattachment/7d7d2619-6736-4d8e-876e-6f9b2b45c435/PS01%28PM%29-Statement-regarding-the-use-of-opioid-analgesics-in-patients-with-chronic-non-cancer-pain)

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises overdose using sedation score, respiratory rate and pupils
- Identifies risk factors including dose, comorbidity and co-sedatives
- Prioritises airway, oxygen and ventilation
- Titrates naloxone to respiratory effort and uses an infusion
- Notes buprenorphine requires higher doses
- Post-reversal monitoring and cause
- Take-home naloxone and stewardship in harm reduction

items.title: 9. Depot buprenorphine (Buvidal) and elective knee replacement
items.q: A patient on monthly depot buprenorphine (Buvidal) requires elective total knee replacement. Outline the perioperative considerations, including analgesia.
items.a:
## Preop

Verify the formulation, dose, last and next injection and prescriber. Document other opioid or sedative exposure, previous perioperative pain experience and the patient's goals. Monthly depot buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial μ agonist with sustained release. Skipping one injection does not rapidly remove its effect and can destabilise treatment for opioid use disorder. Usually maintain scheduled treatment after discussion with the prescriber and acute pain service. Explain that maintenance treatment does not cover new surgical pain and full agonist rescue may still work. Plan the postoperative destination according to risk, including OSA, co-sedation and anticipated opioid needs.

## Intraop

Use a procedure-specific multimodal plan. Consider spinal or general anaesthesia, adductor canal block and periarticular infiltration, with coordination of cumulative local anaesthetic exposure. Assess whether posterior knee analgesia would add benefit. Use paracetamol, suitable NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor and dexamethasone when appropriate. A specialist may use ketamine for particular clinical indications. Avoid assuming all adjuncts are required. Ensure the block and other techniques support rather than hinder early physiotherapy. Use supplemental short-acting opioids when needed, titrated to response. A high-affinity full agonist may be appropriate in a monitored setting. Avoid a fixed dose escalation based solely on formulation.

## Postop

Continue the coordinated depot plan. Use non-opioids and regional measures with carefully titrated short-acting rescue as needed. Assess respiratory rate, sedation, oxygenation and ventilation, and increase observation according to dose and risk. Buprenorphine's partial agonism does not eliminate ventilatory depression in the presence of full agonists or sedatives. If clinically important depression occurs, prioritise airway and ventilation, stop excess dosing and follow the local naloxone and escalation protocol.

Monitor movement pain, quadriceps power, transfers and rehabilitation. Assess inadequate analgesia for surgical or block problems. Give a limited supply of immediate-release opioid only if necessary, with a written taper, named prescriber and early review. Communicate the next injection date, postoperative opioid exposure and rescue plan. Discuss overdose prevention, safe storage and local access to naloxone. The New Zealand opioid substitution guidance is particularly helpful for distinguishing depot formulations and maintaining continuity between inpatient and community care.

If pain remains difficult despite the published pathway, review the regional technique and examine before escalating sedating rescue.

**Sources:** [NZ opioid substitution treatment guidance 2025](https://www.health.govt.nz/publications/new-zealand-practice-guidelines-for-opioid-substitution-treatment-2025) · [Medsafe Buvidal Monthly product information](https://www.medsafe.govt.nz/DbSearch/ProductDetail?Product_id=21082) · [Multisociety perioperative buprenorphine recommendations](https://doi.org/10.1136/rapm-2021-103007) · [BJA Education total knee arthroplasty analgesia 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.004)

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies depot pharmacology and verifies dates
- Maintains continuity with prescriber
- Plans procedure-specific regional and non-opioid analgesia
- Titrates full agonist rescue and monitors ventilation
- Tracks functional recovery
- Plans discharge, taper and overdose prevention

items.title: 10. Regular cannabis and medicinal cannabinoids
items.q: Discuss the perioperative implications of regular cannabis use, including medicinal cannabinoids.
items.a:
## Preop

Ask nonjudgmentally about the product, THC and CBD content if known, route, frequency, amount, indication, last use and co-use of alcohol, nicotine, opioids or sedatives. Screen for intoxication, impaired capacity, withdrawal, cardiovascular or respiratory symptoms and hyperemesis. Recent smoked cannabis can raise heart rate and blood pressure and precipitate myocardial ischaemia in susceptible patients. Chronic smoking may be associated with airway inflammation. Vomiting, dehydration or impaired consciousness can alter the fasting and aspiration plan. Discuss prescribed cannabinoids with the usual clinician. Essential cannabidiol for epilepsy needs a specific continuation plan.

Postpone elective surgery when intoxication impairs capacity or safety. ASRA recommends delaying elective surgery for at least two hours after smoking cannabis because of acute myocardial risk. A two-hour interval does not establish fitness if symptomatic. Evidence is insufficient for applying the same interval to oral or other routes. Urgent surgery may proceed after assessment and resuscitation, with a documented capacity and airway plan.

## Intraop

Titrate anaesthetic drugs to observed clinical effect. Acute intoxication and regular exposure can have different effects, and no fixed dose multiplier is supported. Manage airway reactivity, haemodynamics and temperature according to symptoms, exposure and surgery. Review additive sedation and potential pharmacokinetic interactions with prescribed cannabinoids, including interactions between CBD and other sedating or antiseizure medicines. Choose suitable multimodal analgesia and local or regional techniques where indicated.

## Postop

Assess ventilation, alertness and dynamic pain before adding sedatives or opioids. Some regular users report higher postoperative pain or opioid use, but expected dose should be guided by clinical response. Treat nausea and vomiting and consider cannabinoid hyperemesis when recurrent symptoms fit. Assess withdrawal in heavy users with new anxiety, irritability, sleep disturbance, reduced appetite or autonomic symptoms after interruption. Seek specialist input for significant symptoms and screen for other causes of agitation. Discuss recovery, coordination of prescribed treatment, safe opioid use, driving and follow-up. Medicinal cannabinoids are not routine substitutes for standard acute postoperative analgesia. Ask what benefit the patient expects and discuss the strength and limits of pain evidence with them.

Check follow-up arrangements if recovery is delayed by respiratory symptoms, significant vomiting or withdrawal. Explain where the patient can seek help if symptoms worsen after discharge.

**Sources:** [ASRA perioperative cannabis guidance](https://doi.org/10.1136/rapm-2022-104013) · [BJA Education substance use disorder in pregnancy 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.07.006) · [ANZCA Blue Book editions](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Establishes product, route, timing and comorbidity
- Assesses intoxication, capacity and postponement
- Applies ASRA threshold to smoking with limitations
- Anticipates haemodynamic, airway and drug effects
- Individualises analgesia and monitoring
- Recognises withdrawal and hyperemesis

items.title: 11. Acute cocaine intoxication with chest pain
items.q: A 28-year-old with acute cocaine intoxication and chest pain needs urgent surgery. Outline the perioperative considerations and management.
items.a:
## Pharmacology

Cocaine blocks reuptake of noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin (so tachycardia, hypertension, vasoconstriction and hyperthermia), and blocks sodium channels (local anaesthetic effect, QRS widening, arrhythmias). Its half-life is short (about 1 hour), but metabolites persist and an alcohol co-ingestion creates cocaethylene, which is longer-acting and more cardiotoxic. MDMA releases serotonin, causing hyperthermia, hyponatraemia, serotonin toxicity and rhabdomyolysis.

## Preop

Obtain serial ECGs and troponin when appropriate and address alternative causes such as dissection. Clarify whether even a short period of resuscitation or cardiac assessment changes surgical risk. If surgery cannot wait, hand over unresolved ischaemia and resuscitation priorities to the theatre and postoperative teams.

- **Cardiac:** chest pain from coronary vasospasm, thrombosis or dissection: ECG, serial troponin, echocardiography.
- **Neuro:** agitation, seizures, stroke.
- **Metabolic:** temperature, sodium (MDMA), potassium, creatine kinase, renal function, acid-base.
- **Other:** pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum (smoked cocaine), co-ingestants, last use, aspiration risk.

**Initial treatment**
- **Benzodiazepines** first-line for agitation, hypertension and chest pain (AHA 2023 quoted in the BJA article); calcium channel blockers, nitrates and alpha-blockers (phentolamine) for severe hypertension or chest pain.
- In life-threatening cocaine toxicity with coronary vasospasm or hypertensive emergency, use titratable vasodilators and avoid beta blockers. Discuss refractory toxicity promptly with clinical toxicology or cardiology.
- Cooling for hyperthermia; correct hyponatraemia carefully (MDMA).

**Timing:** delay elective or semi-urgent surgery until the acute effects have resolved (hours to a day); for urgent surgery proceed with the risks understood.

## Intraop
- Arterial line, ECG, temperature; defibrillator available.
- Induction: titrated propofol and short-acting opioid; avoid **ketamine** and **ephedrine** (BJA); treat hypotension with phenylephrine or noradrenaline, and avoid indirect-acting agents.
- Volatile requirements may be higher with acute use; regional anaesthesia is an option if coagulation and cooperation allow.
- Avoid drugs that lower the arrhythmia threshold; treat wide-complex tachycardia with sodium bicarbonate.
- Avoid suxamethonium if rhabdomyolysis is likely.

## Postop
- Monitor in HDU for ischaemia and arrhythmia; psychiatric and addiction review; analgesia that is multimodal with regional options; opioid-tolerance is possible with polysubstance use.

## Practical points

If the patient needs urgent surgery, take a clear history of the time and amount of use and of any co-ingestants, because late hyperthermia or arrhythmia may follow after the first hours. Keep benzodiazepines available throughout, and avoid reversal drugs that cause a rebound in agitation or blood pressure.

**Sources:** [Perioperative psychostimulant review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10437106/) · [AHA 2025 resuscitation guidance, special circumstances](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation)

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes cocaine and MDMA pharmacology and complications
- Assesses cardiac, neurological and metabolic effects
- Benzodiazepines first-line; nitrates and calcium channel blockers; beta-blocker caution
- Considers timing of surgery
- Avoids ketamine and ephedrine; uses direct vasopressors
- Intraoperative monitoring and arrhythmia treatment
- Postoperative monitoring and referral

items.title: 12. Alcohol withdrawal and delirium after emergency surgery
items.q: A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence becomes agitated, tremulous and hallucinating on day 3 after emergency surgery. Outline your assessment and management.
items.a:
## Timeline

Alcohol withdrawal follows abrupt reduction of intake: minor symptoms at 6 to 24 hours (tremor, anxiety, sweating, nausea, tachycardia), seizures at 12 to 48 hours, **alcoholic hallucinosis** at 12 to 48 hours (visual hallucinations with a clear sensorium), and **delirium tremens** at 48 to 96 hours (disorientation, agitation, hallucinations, fever, autonomic instability), with mortality up to 5 to 15% if untreated. Day 3 after surgery fits.

## Assessment

- **Confirm the diagnosis and exclude alternatives:** the differential includes postoperative delirium from sepsis, hypoxia, pain, urinary retention, drugs (anticholinergics, opioids), electrolyte disturbance (sodium, magnesium), hypoglycaemia, Wernicke's encephalopathy, intracranial pathology, hepatic encephalopathy, and other withdrawal (benzodiazepines, baclofen) or toxidromes such as serotonin syndrome (BJA table: sedative-hypnotic withdrawal has autonomic dysfunction but no inducible clonus).
- Establish last intake, prior withdrawal, seizures and co-sedatives. Use CIWA-Ar only if the patient can reliably participate. In postoperative delirium, use objective signs and an ICU-appropriate monitoring scheme with specialist input.
- Examine for liver disease, cardiomyopathy, infection, and wound problems; check glucose, electrolytes (including magnesium and phosphate), liver tests, coagulation, blood gas, and consider imaging.

## Management

- **1.** **Supportive and safe environment:** quiet, well-lit room, observation, orientation, avoid restraint if possible; HDU for severe cases.
- **2.** Give benzodiazepines in a monitored setting with dosing guided by severity and local protocol. Use a suitable agent such as lorazepam in significant hepatic dysfunction. Phenobarbital may be added by experienced clinicians in an appropriate setting. Dexmedetomidine can help control autonomic symptoms in ICU, but does not replace seizure-protective treatment.
- **3.** Give prompt parenteral thiamine for patients at risk and a treatment regimen if Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected. Treat hypoglycaemia immediately. Monitor and replace relevant electrolytes and manage nutrition and refeeding risk.
- **4.** **Fluids, glucose and electrolytes**, and treat hyperthermia; correct sodium slowly.
- **5.** **Seizures:** benzodiazepine; phenytoin is not effective for withdrawal seizures.
- **6.** **Antipsychotics** (haloperidol) only as an adjunct for persistent hallucinations, since they lower the seizure threshold.
- **7.** Treat the underlying surgical complication or infection.
- **8.** **Analgesia:** regional if possible, paracetamol at reduced dose, avoid sedating opioids in excess.
- **9.** **Prevent recurrence:** nutritional support, addiction medicine and psychiatric review, brief intervention, and relapse prevention (acamprosate, naltrexone, disulfiram) before discharge.

Delirium tremens is a clinical diagnosis. Monitor airway, ventilation, haemodynamics and temperature when treatment requires repeated sedation. Treat concurrent infection or other triggers and document the last sedative dose at handover.

**Sources:** [Association of Anaesthetists alcohol consensus 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39780754/) · [ASAM guideline on alcohol withdrawal](https://www.asam.org/quality-care/clinical-guidelines/alcohol-withdrawal-management-guideline)

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes the timeline of withdrawal, hallucinosis, seizures and DTs
- Considers differential diagnoses of postoperative delirium including serotonin syndrome and Wernicke's
- Explains appropriate use and limitations of CIWA-Ar
- Benzodiazepines first-line with dosing and liver disease adjustment
- Gives prompt thiamine and immediate treatment for hypoglycaemia
- Seizure management; antipsychotics as adjunct only
- HDU care, analgesia and treat underlying cause
- Relapse prevention and referral

items.title: 13. Antidepressants, lithium and MAOIs perioperatively
items.q: Discuss the perioperative considerations for patients taking antidepressants, lithium or monoamine oxidase inhibitors.
items.a:
## Preop

Reconcile prescribed and non-prescribed medicines, indication, recent changes and previous withdrawal or relapse. Discuss unusual or high-risk combinations with psychiatry, pharmacy and the patient. Most SSRIs and SNRIs continue. Consider bleeding risk where stakes are high, sodium in susceptible patients, and QT or CYP effects of the specific drug. Tricyclics merit review for orthostasis, anticholinergic effects and conduction abnormalities. Get an ECG when risk warrants. An irreversible MAOI requires early planning of interaction-safe anaesthesia if continued or a supervised taper and adequate washout if stopped. A reversible MAOI has a different time course. Avoid unplanned cessation.

Establish the indication for lithium and check renal function, sodium, volume status and interacting medicines. Consider lithium level if toxicity or adherence is in question. Minor procedures with stable intake may permit continuation. For major surgery or substantial renal or fluid-shift risk plan a hold in advance according to local policy. UKCPA gives 24 hours for major surgery. Other protocols use longer intervals in selected patients. Urgent surgery may proceed with careful hydration, monitoring and communication.

## Intraop

Avoid pethidine and tramadol with serotonergic antidepressants, particularly MAOIs. IV methylene blue and linezolid can pose major interaction risk. Discuss alternatives and use a lower-risk opioid if clinically appropriate. Fentanyl and methadone have context-dependent serotonin risk. Use an MAOI-compatible technique. Avoid indirect sympathomimetics such as ephedrine and cautiously titrate a suitable directly acting vasopressor when needed. Tailor induction to cardiovascular effects and use ECG monitoring. Lithium can prolong neuromuscular blockade, so monitor quantitatively and confirm adequate recovery. Avoid dehydration and account for altered anaesthetic sensitivity.

## Postop

Monitor ventilation and alertness, haemodynamics and new neurological signs. Clonus, hyperreflexia and autonomic activation after a relevant exposure warrant assessment for serotonin toxicity. Consider other causes, including malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Resume antidepressants promptly when safe and document the plan if oral intake is delayed. Restart lithium when renal function, sodium and hydration are stable and the prescriber agrees. Avoid or review drugs that can raise lithium, such as NSAIDs, thiazides and renin–angiotensin inhibitors. Hand over interruption, restart, adverse effects and mental state review to the treating team.

**Sources:** [BJA Education perioperative serotonin syndrome](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.10.003) · [Medsafe opioid and serotonergic medicines](https://www.medsafe.govt.nz/profs/PUArticles/September2022/Opioids-and-serotonergic%20medicines-risk-of-serotonin-syndrome.html) · [UKCPA lithium perioperative handbook](https://periop-handbook.ukclinicalpharmacy.org/drug/lithium/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Reconciles medicines and psychiatric risks
- Plans safely for SSRIs, SNRIs and tricyclics
- Distinguishes MAOI interaction and cessation decisions
- Individualises lithium hold and restart
- Applies interaction-safe drugs and monitoring
- Plans recovery monitoring and handover

items.title: 14. Comparing the five toxidromes
items.q: Compare the clinical features and management of the sympathomimetic, opioid, anticholinergic, serotonergic and cholinergic toxidromes as they may present in the perioperative period.
items.a:
A toxidrome is a pattern of vital signs and examination findings (temperature, pulse, pressure, respiratory rate, pupils, skin, bowel sounds, tone and reflexes, mental state) that identifies a class of poison. In theatre the signs may be masked by anaesthesia, relaxants and drapes, so look for the pattern in vital signs and temperature.

| | **Sympathomimetic** | **Opioid** | **Anticholinergic** | **Serotonergic** | **Cholinergic** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mental state | Agitation, paranoia, seizures | Sedation, coma | Delirium, hallucinations | Agitation, delirium | Confusion, seizures, coma |
| Pupils | Dilated | **Pinpoint** | **Dilated** | Dilated | Pinpoint |
| Temperature | High | Low | High | **High (up to above 41°C)** | Normal |
| Heart rate, pressure | Tachycardia, hypertension | Bradycardia, hypotension | Tachycardia | Tachycardia, labile | **Bradycardia**, hypotension |
| Skin | **Sweating** | Normal | **Dry**, flushed | **Sweating** | Sweating, salivation |
| Bowel | Normal or increased | Decreased | **Decreased** | **Increased** (diarrhoea) | **Increased** (diarrhoea, cramps) |
| Tone, reflexes | Increased | **Decreased** | Normal | **Clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity** | Fasciculations, weakness |
| Respiration | Tachypnoea | **Depressed** | Normal or tachypnoea | Tachypnoea | Bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm |

## Management of each

- **Sympathomimetic** (cocaine, amphetamines, MDMA): benzodiazepines first-line; cooling; nitrates, calcium channel blockers or phentolamine for hypertension; avoid ketamine and ephedrine.
- **Opioid:** airway and ventilation; **titrated naloxone** (0.04 to 0.4 mg boluses) in respiratory depression, with an infusion for long-acting opioids; a higher dose is required for buprenorphine (2 to 3 mg then infusion).
- **Anticholinergic:** supportive care, benzodiazepines for agitation, cooling; **physostigmine** (1 to 2 mg slowly) for severe delirium without cardiac conduction defects or tricyclic overdose.
- **Serotonergic:** stop offending drugs. Reassess temperature and neuromuscular signs frequently. Give benzodiazepines, active cooling and supportive care. In severe hyperthermia with rigidity use early intubation, ventilation and non-depolarising paralysis. Cyproheptadine is an optional enteral adjunct with uncertain outcome benefit.
- **Cholinergic** (organophosphates, over-reversal): airway, oxygen and suction, **atropine** (titrated to dry the secretions) and pralidoxime for organophosphates.

## Distinguishing look-alikes

- **Malignant hyperthermia:** volatile or suxamethonium, rising ETCO2, rigidity, hyporeflexia, no clonus; treat with dantrolene.
- **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome:** antipsychotic, gradual onset over days, lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia.
- **Withdrawal states** (alcohol, baclofen, benzodiazepines): the baclofen withdrawal syndrome includes rebound spasticity, hyperthermia and hypotension (Blue Book).
- **Delirium:** no neuromuscular excitation.

Check bedside glucose and review the anaesthetic and drug charts. A mixed ingestion can obscure classic findings. Track ECG and temperature, use capnography when ventilatory depression is possible and seek toxicology advice for severe illness or diagnostic uncertainty.

**Sources:** [BJA Education perioperative serotonin syndrome](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.10.003) · [Chiew and Isbister, management of serotonin toxicity](https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16152) · [AHA 2025 resuscitation guidance, special circumstances](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines toxidromes and the difficulty identifying them under anaesthesia
- Compares pupils, temperature, skin, bowel sounds, tone, reflexes across five toxidromes
- Specific treatments for each toxidrome
- Details the serotonin syndrome management
- Differentiates MH, NMS, withdrawal and delirium
- Notes naloxone and physostigmine/atropine dosing and cautions

items.title: 15. Clozapine and elective hernia repair
items.q: A patient with schizophrenia treated with clozapine presents for elective inguinal hernia repair. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Preop

Assess psychiatric stability, decision-specific capacity, communication needs and supports. Confirm the clozapine dose, when it was last taken, and who prescribes and monitors it. Review sedation, hypersalivation and aspiration, constipation or ileus, orthostatic hypotension, seizures and evidence of cardiomyopathy or myocarditis when clinically suspected. Review blood count monitoring, ECG, electrolytes, metabolic risk, infection and smoking change. Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2 and cessation during admission may raise clozapine concentrations. Consider interactions with inhibitors such as ciprofloxacin or fluvoxamine. If toxicity is suspected, ask the clozapine team about a level and dose review.

Agree the plan with psychiatry and pharmacy. Avoid prolonged unplanned interruption. For elective surgery UKCPA advises holding clozapine for 12 hours to reduce sedation and hypotension. Check local policy and individual risk. For urgent surgery recent dosing may be unavoidable and should be communicated. If treatment is interrupted for more than 48 hours, seek specialist re-titration advice before restarting the regular dose.

## Intraop

Use a technique suitable for the hernia repair, aspiration risk and cooperation. Anticipate additive sedation with anaesthetics and opioids and hypotension from alpha blockade. Provide appropriate monitoring. Treat causes of hypotension, including hypovolaemia and anaesthetic depth, and titrate direct vasopressor support as indicated. In clozapine-related hypotension avoid adrenaline as a routine pressor because unopposed beta vasodilation can worsen hypotension. This is distinct from following the resuscitation algorithm in cardiac arrest. Escalate refractory shock promptly. Consider local infiltration and simple analgesics to reduce opioid and anticholinergic burden.

## Postop

Assess alertness, ventilation, swallowing, BP, bowels and mental state. Reduce avoidable co-sedatives and prescribe or continue a bowel regimen where indicated. Restart on the agreed schedule when haemodynamics and clinical condition permit. Never presume the usual dose can be given after a prolonged gap without checking. Review changes in smoking or medicines and monitor for toxicity or relapse. New fever, rigidity or altered mental state requires assessment for infection, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and other postoperative emergencies. Provide a handover specifying the last dose, restart decision, monitoring, bowel care and contact for the clozapine team.

If oral or enteral dosing will remain impractical, contact psychiatry early to avoid an inadvertent prolonged interruption and loss of tolerance.

**Sources:** [UKCPA clozapine perioperative handbook](https://periop-handbook.ukclinicalpharmacy.org/drug/clozapine/) · [BJA Education perioperative serotonin syndrome](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2019.10.003)

## Self-marking checklist

- Assesses capacity and psychiatric baseline
- Identifies aspiration, ileus, metabolic and cardiac risks
- Checks smoking, interactions and blood monitoring
- Discusses elective hold and specialist re-titration
- Plans haemodynamic rescue and avoids adrenaline as routine pressor
- Plans recovery monitoring and handover

items.title: 16. Acute low back pain with leg radiation
items.q: A 42-year-old presents with acute low back pain and leg radiation after lifting at work. Outline your assessment and initial management, and explain what would change your plan.
items.a:
## Assessment and triage

Establish onset, trauma, function, prior pain, previous surgery and leg symptoms. Ask about fever, cancer, immunosuppression, injecting drug use, prolonged steroids, history of fracture, anticoagulation, bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle change and progressive weakness. A new urinary retention pattern, saddle sensory change or bilateral/progressive neurological deficit raises concern for cauda equina compression and requires urgent spinal assessment and MRI. Consider infection, fracture, malignancy and non-spinal causes such as vascular or visceral pathology in the appropriate context. Check vital signs, gait, spine and relevant abdominal or vascular findings. Examine lower-limb power, sensation and reflexes and use a straight-leg raise when appropriate. Findings should localise a plausible root before labelling pain radicular.

## Initial management

Most acute mechanical episodes improve. Explain the findings and agree on a practical plan for gentle activity, pacing and return to work or usual roles. Discourage bed rest and provide written advice. Consider heat, simple exercise and access to physiotherapy based on severity and function. Imaging is unnecessary without suspicion of serious pathology or a result that would change management. Incidental abnormalities can lead to inappropriate treatment. In sciatica without significant deficit, assess symptoms and function over time and discuss expected recovery.

For non-specific low back pain, a short course of an oral NSAID is appropriate in selected patients after renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular and bleeding review. Use an appropriate low effective dose and consider gastroprotection. Paracetamol alone has limited evidence for non-specific low back pain. The OPAL trial found no benefit from a short opioid course versus placebo for acute non-specific low back or neck pain. Avoid routine opioid initiation. Gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines and oral corticosteroids are not routine treatments for sciatica. A trial for a different confirmed neuropathic condition is a separate decision.

## Reassessment

Check goals such as walking and sleep within an agreed time. Arrange urgent review for progressive weakness, bladder or bowel symptoms, fever or systemic illness. Severe persistent radicular pain or a new objective deficit may require specialist assessment, imaging and selected procedure-oriented care. Explore work, anxiety, poor sleep or fear of movement if recovery stalls. Document an activity plan and follow-up rather than repeatedly prescribing rescue medicines.

**Sources:** [NICE low back pain and sciatica NG59](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59/chapter/recommendations) · [OPAL acute spinal pain trial](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(23)00404-X)

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies cauda equina and other serious causes
- Localises or challenges radicular findings
- Explains when imaging changes management
- Prioritises activity and function
- Appraises NSAIDs and avoids routine opioids or gabapentinoids
- Gives follow-up and clear escalation

items.title: 17. Pharmacological management of chronic neuropathic pain
items.q: Outline the pharmacological management of a patient with chronic neuropathic pain, and discuss the evidence for the drugs you would use.
items.a:
## Establish the mechanism and treatment goals

Confirm a plausible lesion or disease of the somatosensory system. Document anatomical distribution, sensory signs, function, sleep and comorbidities. Treat reversible causes such as compression or poor diabetes control. Explain likely modest benefit and agree on a measurable goal and planned review. Established peripheral neuropathy is distinct from chronic primary pain, non-specific back pain and sciatica. The neuropathic drug evidence cannot be applied to all of these presentations.

## Initial drug selection

The 2025 NeuPSIG review supports tricyclic antidepressants, SNRIs and alpha-2-delta ligands as first-line classes. NICE suggests amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin for most neuropathic pain outside trigeminal neuralgia. In frailty or cardiac conduction disease avoid or use great caution with tricyclics because of orthostasis, arrhythmia and anticholinergic effects. Duloxetine can suit selected patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathy or mood symptoms. Check blood pressure, hepatic or renal impairment and other serotonergic medicines. Select a renal-adjusted gabapentinoid only when appropriate and explain dizziness, oedema, sedation, misuse potential and increased ventilatory risk with opioids. Start low and titrate. Carbamazepine is a separate first-line option for trigeminal neuralgia with disease-specific investigation and monitoring.

## Next steps and evidence

The updated evidence supports topical lidocaine or capsaicin as weaker, second-line options for selected localised peripheral pain. Discuss skin effects and how an 8% capsaicin patch requires trained application. A specialist may consider botulinum toxin, non-invasive stimulation or other treatments in refractory cases. The 2025 review assigned weak third-line support to opioids, while FPM advice makes prescribing for chronic non-cancer pain exceptional. Consider adverse effects and dependence. Avoid treating observational or short-term responder data as evidence of durable functional recovery. Head-to-head evidence is limited and average trial effects do not predict an individual response.

## Review and stop rules

Review adverse effects and progress before increasing doses. Reassess after an adequate trial at a tolerated dose. Continue when meaningful function or sleep improves. Taper ineffective treatment and document why it failed. Consider a different first-line class before indiscriminate combinations. Integrate physiotherapy, education, footwear or protection of affected skin and psychology as appropriate. Refer for disabling pain, diagnostic uncertainty, treatment intolerance or progressive neurological findings.

**Sources:** [NeuPSIG neuropathic pain meta-analysis, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40252663/) · [NICE neuropathic pain CG173](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg173/chapter/Recommendations) · [NICE chronic primary pain NG193](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng193/chapter/recommendations)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines neuropathic pain and sets realistic goals
- Identifies first-line drugs: tricyclics, SNRIs and gabapentinoids with doses
- Appraises the 2025 NeuPSIG evidence and separates short-term benefit from long-term outcomes
- Second and third line agents including topical agents and opioids
- Selects drugs by comorbidity and side effects
- Acknowledges limits of evidence
- Practical titration, review and referral

items.title: 18. Acute neuropathic pain and weakness after lower-limb surgery
items.q: A patient develops burning foot pain and new weakness after lower-limb surgery. Outline how you would diagnose an acute neuropathic component and decide when to seek specialist help.
items.a:
## Exclude limb or nerve injury requiring urgent action

Clarify the operation, position, tourniquet, dressings, local block, onset and trajectory. Ask about new weakness, unusual pain, numbness, fever and previous symptoms. Assess perfusion, swelling, wound, passive stretch pain where appropriate and dressings or cast pressure. Severe escalating pain or a new or progressive motor deficit requires timely surgical and anaesthetic review. Consider compartment syndrome, haematoma, direct surgical injury, ischaemia, compression, inflammation and expected or prolonged block. Arrange urgent imaging, pressure assessment or exploration if indicated. Do not wait for a pain-clinic visit or nerve-conduction study when a reversible cause is suspected.

## Confirm the pain mechanism

Map symptoms to a nerve, plexus or root distribution and compare with the opposite limb. Test light touch, pinprick and temperature as appropriate, screen for touch-evoked pain and test movement, power and reflexes. Burning, electric shocks, allodynia and sensory deficit support neuropathic pain in a plausible anatomical distribution. A history consistent with a lesion and plausible distribution supports possible neuropathic pain. Sensory signs in that distribution support probable neuropathic pain. A concordant confirmatory test or established lesion supports definite neuropathic pain. Nociceptive wound pain can coexist. Use serial findings and specialist-directed electrodiagnostics when appropriate. Consider CRPS only with suitable regional findings, Budapest criteria and exclusion of better explanations.

## Treat and refer

Treat the cause, including surgical decompression or correction of external pressure when indicated. Set goals for sleep, movement and protective footwear or mobilisation. Use appropriate simple analgesia for a nociceptive component. If neuropathic symptoms limit recovery, a monitored trial of an appropriate agent may be reasonable. Choose by comorbidities and risks such as renal impairment, sedation, anticholinergic effects or drug interactions. Influential neuropathic drug trials mainly concern established pain and do not justify starting every acute postoperative patient on a gabapentinoid. High opioid exposure or co-sedation warrants added caution. Selected topical treatment may be suitable for localised pain on intact skin.

Coordinate physical and occupational therapy to protect weak areas and promote graded function. Document baseline and evolving findings. Seek early specialist pain input for severe or refractory symptoms, suspected CRPS, diagnostic uncertainty or adverse drug effects. Progressive neurological deficits need surgical or neurological escalation as appropriate.

**Sources:** [NICE neuropathic pain CG173](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg173/chapter/Recommendations) · [NeuPSIG neuropathic pain meta-analysis, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40252663/) · [CRPS diagnosis and treatment guidelines, fifth edition](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9186375/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Rules out time-critical structural causes
- Maps pain and sensory signs to relevant anatomy
- Uses graded diagnostic certainty and serial examination
- Recognises possible mixed pain and CRPS mimics
- Selects mechanism-based treatment and monitoring
- Explains timing and destination of specialist referral

items.title: 19. Opioid prescribing patterns and patient beliefs across regions
items.q: Compare the patterns of opioid prescribing and harm in a low-consumption East Asian city with those in Australia, and discuss how patient beliefs about opioids should shape your perioperative practice.
items.a:
## Hong Kong: low use, rising harm

- The chapter describes relatively low consumption and several setting-specific measures of use. Compare the observation periods, metric and denominator rather than equating standardised daily doses, per-capita morphine equivalents and opioid orders after an operation.
- **Perioperative use is low**: after head and neck surgery, 0.4% of Hong Kong patients had an opioid order on day 6 against 86.8% of US patients, and tramadol orders were more frequent (13.4% against 0.9%).
- **Persistent use after surgery** was still 3.45% of 438,128 opioid-naive patients; discharge with an opioid raised the odds of persistent use (OR 2.30), emergency visits (1.28) and readmission (1.17).
- The chapter describes changes in the pattern of opioid-related deaths after wider opioid availability. Changes over time are descriptive and do not establish how much a particular drug or policy caused the observed trend.
- Opioids were the most abused substance in emergency departments (27.1%, 2004 to 2016). Opioid use disorder carried the highest self-harm risk, and 16.8% had a psychiatric disorder.
- **Policy gap**: the 2016 chronic pain guidelines are not mandatory and no framework addresses opioid hazards. The authors call for surveillance and patient education.

## Australia for contrast

Per capita use is far higher (494 mg morphine equivalent against Canada 967 and the US 700 in 2014), the defined daily dose rose from 4.6 to 17.4 per 1000 per day between 1990 and 2014, and about 1,045 opioid deaths occurred in 2016, mostly prescription related (Blue Book 2019). The shift was to strong, long-acting opioids.

## Cultural attitudes

In one Hong Kong cancer-pain survey respondents raised doubts about opioid effectiveness and concerns about addiction. Beliefs differ between individuals and settings. Ask what the patient understands by dependence, addiction and pain relief. Assess clinician and institutional prescribing barriers as well.

## Perioperative practice

- **1.** **Ask about beliefs and fears** and explain the benefits, risks and exit plan, without assuming attitudes from ethnicity.
- **2.** Treat pain adequately, with multimodal and regional analgesia.
- **3.** Practise **stewardship**: smallest quantity for the expected duration, avoid modified-release drugs, no repeat scripts, and consider naloxone for patients at elevated risk. Discuss safe storage and disposal (BJA 2023).
- **4.** Screen for risk of persistent use and follow up.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, Ho and Cheung on Hong Kong opioid harms](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [BJA Education opioid stewardship](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.007)

## Self-marking checklist

- Low-consumption pattern and perioperative use
- Persistent postoperative use and discharge opioid effect
- Rising harm after new opioid availability
- Comparison with Australian prescribing and deaths
- Patient beliefs: fear of addiction and undertreatment
- Individualised assessment rather than stereotyping
- Stewardship measures
- Policy and surveillance

items.title: 20. Chronic postsurgical pain versus persistent opioid use
items.q: An opioid-naïve patient has worsening functional pain and is still taking daily oxycodone six weeks after major surgery. Distinguish the risk of chronic postsurgical pain from persistent opioid use and outline your response.
items.a:
## Separate the two trajectories

At six weeks this patient has a concerning subacute pain trajectory. Chronic postsurgical pain develops or increases after surgery, lasts at least three months and follows an operative or related anatomic distribution after other causes are excluded. Persistent postoperative opioid use is an exposure outcome, commonly defined using continued use or prescription fills after an early postoperative period such as days 90–180, with differing definitions across studies. It can occur with a different pain generator or after the surgical pain resolves. Ongoing pain can likewise persist without continued opioid use.

## Investigate and treat the pain

Ask about recovery since discharge, location, neuropathic symptoms, fever, swelling, wound problems and functional change. Examine the surgical site and relevant nerves. Discuss promptly with the surgical team if there is worsening pain, a new deficit, concern for infection or mechanical failure. Explore anxiety, impaired sleep, fear of movement, work barriers and the original discharge instructions. Validate the experience and set one or two concrete goals such as walking, sleeping or tolerating physiotherapy. Choose non-opioid and non-drug treatments based on the identified mechanism and comorbidity. Escalate to specialist pain review if complex, with rehabilitation input.

## Review opioid exposure separately

Check prescribed versus actual use, dispensing, sedation, constipation and co-sedatives. Ask about benefit and previous attempts to reduce use. Review findings together and agree a supported reduction as recovery permits. With sustained daily use, withdrawal is possible. Match the pace to dose, duration and tolerance, with a named prescriber and review date. Limit additional supplies, avoid automatic repeats and counsel on storage, returns and overdose risk. Consider naloxone access according to local availability and risk, and assess for opioid use disorder if clinical criteria suggest it.

## Build the follow-up around function

Coordinate primary care, surgery, acute or transitional pain and physiotherapy rather than leaving each service to prescribe independently. Track movement pain, function and daily use separately. The 2025 Blue Book Hong Kong chapter illustrates an association between discharge opioid prescribing and subsequent use even in a relatively low-consumption setting. This is observational evidence and does not prove causation. A transitional service can support review and medication safety. Evidence that it prevents chronic postsurgical pain is still developing.

**Sources:** [ANZCA Blue Book 2025, Ho and Cheung on Hong Kong opioid harms](https://doi.org/10.60115/11055/1305) · [Anesthesiology 2025 transitional pain service scoping review](https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000005606) · [BJA 2026 regional anaesthesia and chronic postsurgical pain](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42425794/) · [Chronic postsurgical pain risk and mitigation review 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42479827/) · [BJA Education opioid stewardship](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.007)

## Self-marking checklist

- Separates pain and exposure definitions
- Recognises six weeks as subacute
- Excludes a surgical cause and assesses function
- Uses mechanism-directed care and rehabilitation
- Plans supported taper with one prescriber
- Interprets observational evidence and coordinates follow-up

items.title: 21. Spinal cord stimulator and elective knee arthroscopy
items.q: A patient with an implanted spinal cord stimulator presents for elective knee arthroscopy. Discuss the perioperative considerations.
items.a:
## Principles

A spinal cord stimulator (SCS) delivers electrical pulses through epidural leads connected to an implanted pulse generator, controlled by a patient programmer. Risks to the device come from electromagnetic interference (diathermy, MRI) and to the patient from stimulation changes, lead damage and infection. Always identify the **manufacturer and model**, and contact the implanting team or representative.

## Preop

- Establish the indication, lead position, implant date, programme, battery status, and whether it is a conventional, burst, high-frequency or closed-loop system (some have MRI conditions).
- Plan with the pain clinic to interrogate the device; most systems should be **turned off** (some closed-loop devices should be left in a defined mode) immediately before surgery.
- Review the chronic pain regimen and opioid tolerance, and continue baseline medicines.

## Intraop

- **Diathermy:** use **bipolar**; if monopolar is required, place the return pad so the current path is away from the generator and leads (for a knee, on the thigh or calf), use short bursts at the lowest effective power, and keep the cables away from the device.
- Check full-system MRI conditionality, lead status and manufacturer instructions. Therapeutic diathermy poses a distinct risk from electrosurgery. If urgent cardioversion is needed, prioritise resuscitation and check the device afterwards.
- Prefer general or suitable peripheral regional anaesthesia where feasible. Avoid routine neuraxial access because of risks to leads and infection. If essential, first review the lead trajectory with the pain team, choose a safe level and use appropriate image guidance. Thoracic epidural access near the leads is inappropriate.
- Position carefully to avoid lead damage and pressure on the generator pocket.

## Postop

- Interrogate the device and **restart** the stimulator at the previous settings; ask the manufacturer representative to check for malfunction.
- Multimodal analgesia with regional blocks, avoiding excess opioid in a chronic pain patient.
- Watch for infection and lead migration.

## Intrathecal pump (relevant extension)

The Blue Book notes baclofen withdrawal appears within 1 to 2 days of interruption (rebound spasticity, tachycardia, hyperthermia, seizures, rhabdomyolysis), and is an emergency; MRI magnets can stop the pump, and adverse events occur in 18 to 25% of patients, mostly from catheters. Continue the pump perioperatively and keep essential antispasticity drugs going.

**Sources:** [BJA Education spinal cord stimulators and anaesthesia](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.02.005) · [Practical perioperative spinal cord stimulation guide 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12605233/) · [2026 perioperative spinal cord stimulator case discussion](https://doi.org/10.1213/XAA.0000000000002303) · [ANZCA Blue Book editions](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29)

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies the device, its indication, programme and manufacturer
- Plans interrogation and switching off before surgery
- Diathermy: bipolar or return pad placement away from device
- Checks model-specific MRI and energy-device precautions
- Chooses anaesthetic technique with caution for neuraxial access
- Postoperative interrogation and restart
- Intrathecal pump: avoids baclofen withdrawal

items.title: 22. Neurolytic coeliac plexus block in pancreatic cancer
items.q: A patient with unresectable pancreatic cancer has severe upper abdominal and back pain despite systemic analgesia and has opioid toxicity. Evaluate the role of neurolytic coeliac plexus block.
items.a:
## Establish suitability

Clarify the pain pattern, imaging, tumour extent and analgesic response. Upper abdominal visceral pain with referral to the back may travel through the coeliac plexus. Abdominal wall pain, vertebral metastases, peritoneal disease, obstruction and other pain mechanisms may respond poorly to the block or require separate treatment. Check what toxicity means for the patient and assess prognosis, preferences, anticoagulants, platelet count, infection, haemodynamics and whether they can tolerate positioning or endoscopy. Involve oncology, palliative care and an experienced interventional pain service. Treat reversible causes and optimise systemic analgesia concurrently.

## Indication, effect and limits

NICE recommends considering an endoscopic ultrasound-guided or image-guided percutaneous neurolytic coeliac plexus block in pancreatic cancer when pain is uncontrolled, opioid adverse effects are unacceptable or opioid dose is escalating. Chemical neurolysis intentionally interrupts sensory and sympathetic transmission. A local anaesthetic block gives temporary analgesia and may sometimes help test a target. Neurolysis has the potential for longer relief with reduced opioid requirement in selected patients, but effect size and duration vary. Pain may recur as cancer progresses. Explain that the procedure is adjunctive and analgesia and other palliative treatments remain available.

## Procedure planning and consent

Select approach based on anatomy, imaging and local expertise. Review coagulation and antithrombotic timing with the procedural service. Check major vessels, tumour distortion and any route-specific contraindication. Discuss transient hypotension from sympathetic blockade, diarrhoea, local pain, failure, bleeding and infection. Explain the rare but serious consequences of vascular injection or injury, neural injury and paralysis. Consider treatment alternatives and goals, including continued medical management, radiotherapy or different anatomy-specific procedures through specialists. Confirm monitoring and recovery arrangements.

## Follow-up

Monitor blood pressure, pain, neurological status and procedure-related complications. Reassess pain with movement, sleep, nausea, alertness and actual opioid requirements. Reduce opioid doses cautiously if relief is substantial and sedation emerges, recognising dependence and the risk of withdrawal after abrupt reductions. Reassess any new pain mechanism instead of repeating a procedure by default. Establish who will review the response and ongoing medication, and provide a care plan with palliative and community teams.

If distress or anaemia is disproportionate after the procedure, assess for a complication rather than attributing it to expected sympathetic blockade.

**Sources:** [NICE pancreatic cancer NG85, neurolytic block](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/NG85/chapter/recommendations) · [ANZCA professional documents, including PS41 and PS45](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents)

## Self-marking checklist

- Links the intervention to the visceral pain phenotype
- States appropriate NICE indications
- Explains neurolysis and realistic benefit
- Reviews imaging, bleeding and infection risks
- Discusses common and serious adverse effects
- Plans monitoring, opioid adjustment and follow-up

items.title: 2026.2 Q12: CRPS arm and ORIF of the same limb
items.source: Past SAQ 2026.2 Q12 · pass rate not reported
items.q: A patient with complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) affecting their right arm is scheduled for an open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a radius fracture in that same limb. Outline the clinical features of CRPS. (30%) Discuss your perioperative pain management plan for this patient. (70%)
items.model:
