## Clinical features (30%)

CRPS causes continuing regional pain disproportionate to the inciting injury. Pain is not usually confined to one nerve territory. Type I has no identifiable major nerve lesion and type II has an identifiable lesion. The Budapest clinical criteria require continuing disproportionate pain, at least one reported symptom in three of four domains, at least one observed sign in two domains and no diagnosis that better explains the presentation.

- **Sensory:** hyperalgesia or allodynia.
- **Vasomotor:** temperature or skin colour asymmetry.
- **Sudomotor/oedema:** swelling, sweating change or asymmetry.
- **Motor/trophic:** reduced movement, weakness, tremor, dystonia or hair, nail and skin changes.

Warm and cold phenotypes may occur without a fixed stage sequence. Acute fracture itself can produce swelling and pain. Document baseline findings and look for vascular compromise, acute compartment syndrome, nerve injury or a tight cast.

## Preop

Establish urgency and what movement is safe with the fracture team. Do not defer necessary fixation simply because of CRPS. Ask about previous flare triggers and helpful treatments. Agree achievable analgesia and early hand therapy with the patient, surgeon and pain service. Document baseline pain map, motor and sensory function, perfusion and usual treatment. Continue established maintenance therapy as appropriate and make a specific rescue and monitoring plan if the patient already takes opioids.

## Intraop

Use regular simple analgesics where appropriate and choose regional or general anaesthesia according to surgical needs, the neurological examination and patient preference. A brachial plexus block or selected catheter can improve perioperative analgesia and enable later therapy, but evidence does not establish prevention of CRPS flare. Discuss catheter density, duration, breakthrough pain and the plan for reassessing function and perfusion with the ward and surgeon. Coordinate local anaesthetic exposure. Consider specialist ketamine selectively for refractory pain or substantial opioid tolerance. Avoid unnecessary compression and discuss tourniquet requirements with the surgeon.

## Postop

Assess movement pain, sedation, block regression and limb neurovascular status. Escalate a new deficit or unexpectedly severe pain promptly and exclude a surgical complication before attributing it to CRPS. Treat new nociceptive pain and provide titrated short-acting rescue as appropriate. Start graded hand therapy, desensitisation and range-of-motion exercises when fixation permits. Specialist teams may incorporate graded motor imagery or mirror therapy. Steroids, bisphosphonates and vitamin C are not routine perioperative flare prophylaxis. Plan oral treatment, opioid de-escalation, rehabilitation contact and early follow-up.

**Sources:** Official question paper verified. The examiner report was unavailable in the reviewed archive.
rubric: States all Budapest thresholds and excludes better explanations
Identifies four sign and symptom domains and CRPS types
Documents baseline function and plans fixation with pain service
Justifies regional or general strategy and qualifies prevention evidence
Monitors perfusion, motor function and evolving pain
Plans early hand therapy, discharge and follow-up

items.title: 2024.2 Q1: Methamphetamine-intoxicated patient for urgent surgery
items.q: Outline the perioperative management of a methamphetamine‑intoxicated 20‑year‑old who requires urgent surgery.
items.model:
## Preop

A positive urine screen can support a history, but it neither grades toxicity nor establishes incapacity. Assess capacity for this decision and follow the local emergency consent pathway if an urgent procedure is necessary and capacity is impaired.

- **Why the surgery is urgent, and whether it can wait.** Methamphetamine effects last 8 to 24 hours; if delay is safe and the delay would make anaesthesia safer, wait. If not (bleeding, ischaemia, sepsis), proceed with the risks understood.
- **Consent and capacity.** Intoxication, agitation, paranoia or psychosis may impair capacity. Assess it; if absent, apply the emergency exception (treatment in best interests, documented, with a second opinion) and involve family, and obtain consent when the patient recovers.
- **Behaviour:** the patient may be aggressive, hyperthermic and paranoid, which makes cannulation and monitoring difficult and endangers staff. A calm approach, security support and benzodiazepine sedation may be needed first.
- **Assessment:** what, when, how much and by what route; co-ingestants (alcohol, opioids, cannabis); last meal (delayed gastric emptying). Examine for hypertension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, hyperthermia (check temperature), pupils, agitation, chest pain, and signs of IV use, dental decay and weight loss. Investigations: ECG, troponin if symptomatic, electrolytes, creatine kinase, urea and creatinine, glucose, blood gas, and a urine toxicology screen if it will change management.

## Intraop

Pathophysiology: massive release of noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin, giving hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, vasospasm and ischaemia, hyperthermia, seizures and dehydration. With chronic use, catecholamine depletion produces cardiomyopathy and hypotension.
- **Monitoring:** arterial line for unstable patients, temperature, ECG with ST analysis; choose an aspiration mitigation and airway plan based on the actual fasting history, mental state and surgical context.
- Titrate anaesthesia to haemodynamics. Benzodiazepines can control agitation and an adrenergic surge. Consider titratable vasodilators for persistent severe hypertension, and treat pain, hypovolaemia and hyperthermia.
- **Avoid** ketamine, ephedrine and other indirect sympathomimetics (BJA); treat hypotension with phenylephrine or noradrenaline. Use caution with beta-blockers alone because of unopposed alpha stimulation (debated).
- Volatile anaesthetic requirement is increased acutely and reduced when chronically depleted. Watch for hyperthermia (MH look-alike), seizures and rhabdomyolysis; maintain fluids and warm/cool actively.

## Postop

- **Recovery:** monitor for recurrent haemodynamic instability, ischaemia, arrhythmia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, agitation or a stimulant crash. Assess other substances individually, including any opioid exposure.
- **Analgesia:** regional and multimodal, ketamine used cautiously, opioids as required.
- **Setting:** monitored recovery/HDU; psychiatry and addiction medicine review before discharge; harm-minimising advice.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Explain why surgery is urgent, behaviour and capacity, the physiological effects and structured preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative management.
rubric: Considers why surgery is urgent and whether it can safely wait
Addresses capacity and consent, including the emergency exception
Considers behaviour and safety of staff
Assesses intoxication, co-ingestants and organ effects with relevant investigations
Describes physiology (catecholamine excess, hyperthermia, arrhythmia) and how it shapes the anaesthetic
Avoids ketamine and ephedrine; uses phenylephrine/noradrenaline and benzodiazepines
Anticipates postoperative problems (pain, agitation, crash, withdrawal) and disposition

items.title: 2022.1 Q2: Chronic daily headache
items.q: Outline your management of a patient with chronic daily headache.
items.model:
## Assessment first

Chronic daily headache means headache on 15 or more days a month for over 3 months. Most are primary (chronic migraine, chronic tension-type headache, new daily persistent headache, hemicrania continua), or **medication-overuse headache**, whereas a new or changing pattern requires assessment for secondary disease.

**History**
- **Onset and course:** sudden or gradual, change in pattern, duration and frequency, diurnal pattern.
- **Character and associated features:** location, quality, severity, aura, nausea, photophobia, autonomic features (red eye, tearing), and effect on function and sleep.
- **Triggers and aggravators:** posture, cough, exertion, stress, hormones, caffeine, alcohol.
- **Drugs:** every analgesic, triptan and opioid, with days per month (simple analgesics on at least 15 days, or opioids, triptans and combination analgesics on at least 10 days per month for over three months, suggest medication overuse).
- **Psychosocial:** mood, anxiety, sleep, work and family.

**Red flags** (SNNOOP10 type): new headache after 50, thunderclap onset, progressive worsening, positional headache, fever, neck stiffness, papilloedema or focal neurology, cancer or immunosuppression, pregnancy, head trauma, visual change.

**Examination:** blood pressure, neurological examination including fundi, cervical spine, temporal artery, jaw and temporomandibular joint, sinuses.

**Investigations:** targeted. **Exclude intracranial pathology** (haemorrhage, tumour, trauma, raised ICP, venous thrombosis, hydrocephalus) with CT or MRI when red flags are present or the pattern is atypical; ESR/CRP where giant cell arteritis is suspected; avoid indiscriminate imaging when the picture is typical.

## Management

The examiners wanted recognition that **medication helps but will not cure, so a multidisciplinary approach** is required.

- **1.** **Explanation and goals:** reassure after exclusion of serious causes; set realistic aims (reduce frequency and disability); keep a headache diary.
- **2.** **Treat medication overuse:** withdraw the overused analgesic, triptan or opioid (supported withdrawal; headache often worsens for 1 to 2 weeks), and **avoid full mu agonists** which cause overuse and dependence.
- **3.** **Prevention:** tailor to diagnosis, comorbidity and reproductive risk. For migraine consider propranolol, amitriptyline or topiramate when appropriate. Observe pregnancy prevention requirements for topiramate. Specialist options include botulinum toxin or CGRP-targeted treatments, with eligibility and access checked locally.
- **4.** **Acute attacks:** paracetamol, NSAIDs, triptans (limited days a month), antiemetics.
- **5.** **Non-drug:** sleep hygiene, regular exercise, stress management, CBT and relaxation, physiotherapy for cervicogenic contribution, and treatment of mood disorders.
- **6.** **Interventions** from a headache or pain clinic: occipital nerve block, sphenopalatine ganglion block, neuromodulation for refractory cases.
- **7.** **Multidisciplinary referral:** neurology, pain medicine, psychology; GP follow-up.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Assess and exclude secondary pathology, then use cause-specific therapy and multidisciplinary care. Avoid reliance on full μ agonists.
rubric: Takes a structured headache history including onset, character, severity, frequency, triggers, function
Reviews all analgesic use and identifies medication overuse
Recognises red flags and excludes intracranial pathology with targeted imaging
Examines neurology, fundi, neck and temporal arteries
Explains that medication helps but is not a cure; sets realistic goals
Avoids full mu agonists; withdraws overused drugs
Prophylaxis, acute treatment, non-drug and interventional options
Multidisciplinary care and follow-up

items.title: 2021.2 Q15: Perioperative serotonin syndrome
items.q: Outline the clinical features, differential diagnoses, and management of serotonin syndrome in the perioperative period.
items.model:
## Clinical features

The syndrome is a **triad** of altered mental status, neuromuscular abnormality and autonomic hyperactivity, in a patient exposed to a serotonergic drug. Onset is typically sudden, within 24 to 48 hours of the trigger, and it resolves quickly once the drug is stopped.
- **Mental status:** agitation, confusion, delayed emergence, delirium.
- **Neuromuscular:** tremor, hyperreflexia, **inducible, ocular and spontaneous clonus** (Hunter criteria), myoclonus, rigidity (legs more than arms), nystagmus.
- **Autonomic:** hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypertension or labile pressure, diaphoresis, mydriasis, diarrhoea.
Severe cases develop temperature above 41°C, rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, renal failure and DIC. There is no confirmatory test; diagnosis uses the **Hunter criteria** (sensitivity 84%, specificity 97%), better than Sternbach (75%, 96%).

## Perioperative triggers

Consider SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs and interactions with IV methylene blue or linezolid. Pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan are high-risk opioid-related agents with serotonergic medicines. Fentanyl and methadone carry context-dependent risk, especially at higher doses. Review drug timing and combinations.

## Differential diagnosis

- **Malignant hyperthermia:** volatile or suxamethonium exposure, rigidity, hypercarbia, hyporeflexia, no clonus.
- **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome:** antipsychotic, gradual onset over days, lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia.
- **Anticholinergic toxicity:** dry skin, mydriasis, normal tone and reflexes.
- **Opioid toxicity:** miosis, hypothermia, respiratory depression, hyporeflexia.
- **Emergence delirium** and sedative-hypnotic withdrawal: no inducible clonus.
- Also sepsis, thyroid storm and stimulant intoxication.

## Management

- **1.** **Stop all serotonergic drugs** (including methylene blue, fentanyl and ondansetron) and check for interacting agents.
- **2.** **Supportive care in HDU/ICU:** oxygen, airway, IV fluids (aggressive if rhabdomyolysis), correct electrolytes, continuous monitoring.
- **3.** **Agitation and rigidity:** benzodiazepines (no evidence for one over another).
- **4.** **Autonomic instability:** hypotension with fluids and **direct** vasopressors (noradrenaline, phenylephrine, adrenaline), avoiding indirect agents (ephedrine, dopamine); hypertension and tachycardia with short-acting esmolol or GTN; avoid hydralazine (MAO inhibition) and propranolol.
- **5.** **Hyperthermia:** paracetamol is ineffective because it is muscle-driven; cooling and benzodiazepines. items.title: 2021.1 Q8: Slow-release morphine for chronic back pain
items.q: A patient takes a 60mg slow-release morphine tablet twice daily for chronic low back pain. They have been appropriately investigated and there is no surgically treatable pathology. In relation to this patient List the risks of long-term opioid therapy. (30%) Justify the appropriate treatment of chronic low back pain. (70%)
items.model:
## Risks of long-term opioid therapy (30%)

This patient takes 120 mg oral morphine daily. This level of exposure warrants review of dose-related harms, comorbidity, co-sedatives and access to overdose prevention. It does not provide an individual prediction of overdose.
- **Respiratory depression and overdose**, particularly with benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids or alcohol; the Blue Book notes 1045 Australian opioid deaths in 2016.
- **Tolerance, dependence and opioid use disorder;** opioids are rarely stopped (two-thirds of patients on over 120 mg continue for years).
- **Opioid-induced hyperalgesia** (diffuse, widespread, worsening pain).
- **Endocrine and immune:** hypogonadism, osteoporosis and fracture risk (doubling above 50 mg OMEDD), sleep-disordered breathing.
- **Gastrointestinal:** constipation, nausea, narcotic bowel.
- **Cognitive, mood and function**: sedation, falls, depression, driving, poor function and work outcomes.
- **Little evidence of long-term benefit** in chronic non-cancer pain.
- Diversion and perioperative complications.

## Justify treatment of the back pain (70%)

- **1.** **Reassess:** there is no surgically treatable pathology, so explain that opioids are neither safe nor effective and agree on **functional goals**, not pain scores.
- **2.** **Agree a supported reduction if harms outweigh benefit:** use a written individualised plan with the usual prescriber and early review. Remain flexible if withdrawal or function worsens. Assess for opioid use disorder and offer evidence-based addiction treatment if appropriate.
- **3.** **Rehabilitation as first-line:** supervised exercise and physiotherapy, graded activity, return to work, weight and sleep management.
- **4.** **Psychological therapy:** CBT, acceptance and commitment therapy, pain education, mindfulness; address depression, anxiety and catastrophising.
- **5.** **Medicines:** consider a short NSAID course only if suitable. Use a diagnosis-specific option for a separate neuropathic or mood condition. Avoid routine gabapentinoids, paracetamol monotherapy or adding another opioid for non-specific low back pain.
- **6.** **Interventions:** avoid routine injections or spinal cord stimulation for non-specific low back pain. Selected facet pain may warrant specialist assessment for medial branch blocks and possible denervation.
- **7.** **Multidisciplinary pain clinic** for complex cases; regular review with measurement of function.
- **8.** **Prevention of future harm:** limit new opioid prescriptions in hospital and at discharge (stewardship, BJA).

In the SPACE trial, opioid medication was no better than non-opioid medication for pain-related function at 12 months in chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis. This evidence informs long-term prescribing decisions and does not justify abrupt cessation for someone already taking morphine.

items.title: 2020.2 Q11: Perioperative implications of methamphetamine use
items.q: Discuss the perioperative implications for a patient known to use methamphetamine.
items.model:
## Pharmacology and acute versus chronic use

Methamphetamine releases and blocks reuptake of noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin. **Acute use** (effects 8 to 24 hours) causes sympathetic overactivity with increased MAC; **chronic use** depletes catecholamine stores, producing blunted responses, cardiomyopathy and hypotension at induction. These two patterns need different anaesthetics, so ask about timing, route, amount and last use.

## Effects relevant to anaesthesia

- **Cardiovascular:** hypertension, tachycardia, arrhythmias (including ventricular), coronary vasospasm and myocardial ischaemia or infarction, aortic dissection, stroke; chronic use: dilated cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension.
- **CNS:** agitation, paranoia, psychosis, seizures, intracranial haemorrhage; withdrawal depression and suicidality.
- **Respiratory:** pulmonary oedema, pulmonary hypertension, bronchospasm and chronic lung damage from smoked drug; aspiration risk.
- **Metabolic:** hyperthermia, dehydration, rhabdomyolysis, electrolyte disturbance, acute kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction.
- **Other:** dental decay and a difficult airway (jaw trauma, poor dentition), malnutrition, IV complications, co-ingestants, infection risk (HIV, hepatitis).

## Preop
- Ask about use, perform ECG (and echocardiography for cardiomyopathy), electrolytes, creatine kinase, and renal function; seek a toxicology screen if intoxication is suspected.
- For elective surgery, **postpone if recently intoxicated**; advise abstinence and involve addiction medicine. For urgent surgery, proceed with the risks understood.

## Intraop
- Monitoring: arterial line, ECG, temperature; caution with spinal and epidural anaesthesia in a hypovolaemic patient.
- Induction: titrated, anticipate both hypertensive surges (acute) and profound hypotension (chronic); use **benzodiazepines**, propofol, opioids; avoid ketamine and ephedrine. Treat hypotension with direct agents (phenylephrine, noradrenaline); treat hypertension with short-acting agents (esmolol with an alpha-blocker, GTN, nicardipine).
- Volatile requirement varies (increased acutely, reduced chronically); watch for hyperthermia (a malignant hyperthermia look-alike) and seizures.
- Airway: rapid sequence induction if full stomach; plan for difficult airway.

## Postop
- Analgesia: regional and multimodal; patients may be opioid-tolerant or hyperalgesic; opioids as needed.
- Monitor for arrhythmia, delirium, agitation, crash and withdrawal depression; psychiatric and addiction referral; harm-minimisation advice before discharge.

A positive urine test does not establish current impairment or mandate cancellation. Ask about timing, route and dose, co-ingestants and prescribed stimulants. Evaluate symptoms and end-organ disease, including cardiomyopathy or pulmonary hypertension where indicated. In severe toxicity postpone nonurgent surgery, treat hyperthermia and agitation and reconsider the plan after reassessment. After urgent surgery use a monitored setting according to organ injury and arrange nonjudgmental support for substance-related harm.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Distinguish acute and chronic use and link organ-system effects to perioperative decisions.

items.title: 2017.1 Q8: Fentanyl patch and total knee replacement
items.q: A 75-year-old lady scheduled for total knee replacement is currently using a fentanyl patch (75 µg/hour) for analgesia to manage her knee pain. Discuss how this influences your perioperative pain management.
items.model:
## What the patch means

A 75 microgram/hour patch represents substantial sustained opioid exposure. Estimate exposure using the local conversion reference. Prior use predicts tolerance and dependence, but does not diagnose hyperalgesia. Check functional benefit, sedation, frailty, sleep apnoea and other sedatives. Anticipate withdrawal if baseline treatment is interrupted and respiratory depression if rescue is layered without reassessment.

## Preop
- Assess pain, function, cognition, sleep apnoea, renal function and co-sedatives (gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines).
- Plan with the pain service; agree the aim: prevent withdrawal, provide effective analgesia, and plan **discharge and weaning**.
- **Leave the patch on** and continue the baseline dose (do not remove it, or withdrawal and a loss of analgesia follow; the effect persists 12 to 24 hours after removal). Note the patch site, avoid heat on it (warming devices and fever speed absorption), and check it is intact. If it must be removed, use another opioid to cover the baseline.

## Intraop
- Consider spinal anaesthesia and a motor-sparing adductor canal block or surgeon-delivered periarticular infiltration, often combined within a procedure-specific pathway. Coordinate total local anaesthetic exposure and mobilisation assessment.
- Avoid unnecessary high opioid exposure, including high-dose remifentanil (acute tolerance and hyperalgesia; Blue Book), use paracetamol, dexamethasone, **ketamine** (BJA: 1 to 3 days infusion), local infiltration, and consider tranexamic acid and standard knee protocols.

## Postop
- Maintain agreed baseline opioid coverage and add independently titrated short-acting rescue. For major pain consider acute pain service-managed PCA with tailored monitoring. Avoid using a fixed fraction of the patch equivalent as a default acute rescue dose.
- Regular paracetamol; NSAID if renal function allows; ketamine infusion; consider gabapentinoid only if pain remains poorly controlled (BJA) and with caution at her age.
- **Monitor** sedation score, respiratory rate and SpO2, and avoid other sedatives; naloxone available.
- If a patch is removed, document timing and anticipate residual fentanyl absorption. Specialist-guided substitution, close observation and a plan to avoid stacking are safer than direct conversion by a single ratio.
- **Discharge:** continue baseline patch, plan a taper with the GP, and avoid new additional strong opioids; physiotherapy and mobilisation.

Monitor the first mobilisation for quadriceps weakness, orthostasis and sedation. Check patch integrity and placement again during transfer, document the usual replacement date and discuss who will review rescue once the patient is home.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Recognise the high fentanyl dose, and explain what it changes about baseline therapy, new surgical pain and analgesic safety.

items.title: 2015.2 Q12: Chronic alcohol misuse and laparotomy
items.q: A 47 year old man presents to the emergency department with acute abdominal pain requiring a laparotomy. He is known to have chronic high intake of alcohol. Describe how chronic alcohol misuse will affect your perioperative management of this patient.
items.model:
## Preop

Coordinate early source control and resuscitation with surgery. Anticipate sepsis, aspiration risk and hypoglycaemia. Arrange critical care according to physiological reserve and anticipated postoperative support.

An emergency laparotomy cannot wait for optimisation, so the plan is to find out what matters in the time available.
- **Pattern of use:** amount, last drink, previous withdrawal, seizures, delirium tremens, and other drugs; screen with AUDIT. **Withdrawal** begins 6 to 24 hours after the last drink (tremor, anxiety, tachycardia, hypertension), seizures at 12 to 48 hours, delirium tremens at 48 to 96 hours; assess with a scale such as CIWA-Ar (BJA).
- **Intoxication versus withdrawal:** acute intoxication lowers anaesthetic requirement but increases aspiration risk (delayed gastric emptying), whereas chronic use increases requirements for anaesthetic agents (BJA).
- **Organ effects:** liver disease (coagulopathy, hypoalbuminaemia, encephalopathy, portal hypertension, varices, ascites, hepatorenal syndrome), cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation), hypertension, pancreatitis, gastritis and bleeding, peripheral neuropathy, Wernicke's encephalopathy, malnutrition, macrocytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, and immunosuppression.
- **Investigations:** full blood count, electrolytes (low potassium, magnesium, phosphate), glucose, liver function and **coagulation**, albumin, urea and creatinine, lipase, ECG, blood alcohol and group and hold.

## Intraop
- **Rapid sequence induction** (full stomach, ileus, intoxication); resuscitate with fluid, replace electrolytes and give **thiamine** (IV) promptly, without delaying emergency glucose; consider vitamin K for coagulopathy and platelets/FFP as indicated.
- Doses: expect higher requirements for induction agents when chronically using, but reduced and unpredictable when the liver is failing or the patient is hypotensive; titrate.
- Avoid hepatotoxic agents and drugs dependent on hepatic clearance; cisatracurium is a reasonable relaxant.

- Arterial line, invasive monitoring if unstable; beware hypotension from vasodilation, cardiomyopathy and hypovolaemia; use noradrenaline or vasopressin.
- Regional or neuraxial block is limited by coagulopathy; use wound catheters or TAP/rectus blocks if coagulation permits.
- Hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, and electrolyte shifts.

## Postop
- Use an appropriate monitored destination. Prescribe withdrawal prevention by history and local protocol. In active withdrawal use benzodiazepines, with a regimen suited to liver function. In delirium or inability to communicate use objective signs and an ICU-compatible scale instead of relying on CIWA-Ar.
- Assess hepatic reserve, nutrition, renal function and bleeding risk when choosing paracetamol and NSAIDs. Treat acute pain and titrate opioids to effect and ventilation. Make a separate plan for withdrawal.
- Pulmonary complications, wound infection, delirium, pancreatitis, and nutritional support. Offer brief intervention and addiction referral before discharge.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Explain the multisystem implications, bleeding, withdrawal and analgesia in the emergency laparotomy patient.

items.title: 2015.1 Q7: Long-term oxycodone and total hip replacement
items.q: An elderly patient is scheduled for total hip replacement and has been taking oxycodone 40mg twice daily in the last six months for severe hip pain. What issues do you anticipate with regard to her oxycodone use? (50%) How do these issues influence your postoperative management? (50%)
items.model:
## Issues anticipated (50%)

Oxycodone 40 mg twice daily is 80 mg a day, about **120 mg oral morphine equivalent daily** (oxycodone:morphine 1:1.5), after six months of use.
- **1.** **Tolerance:** baseline dosing may provide little additional analgesia for surgery. A larger short-acting dose may be needed, titrated to effect and ventilatory risk.
- **2.** **Withdrawal** if the drug is stopped or the patient cannot take it orally (immediate-release and slow-release combination likely).
- **3.** **Opioid-induced hyperalgesia:** diffuse, widespread pain that does not respond to dose increases (BJA, Blue Book on TLR4).
- **4.** **Overdose and sedation:** age, sustained opioid exposure, renal function, sleep apnoea and concurrent sedatives increase risk. Watch for ventilatory impairment, delirium, falls and delayed mobilisation.
- **5.** **Dependence and opioid use disorder:** physical dependence is expected after sustained dosing. Assess for an opioid use disorder by its clinical pattern, including impaired control and harm, without judging the patient’s credibility.
- **6.** **Persistent post-surgical opioid use** after discharge (BJA stewardship).
- **7.** **Hip surgery specifics:** surgery should relieve the pain, so the dose should fall afterwards.

## Influence on postoperative management (50%)

Agree the plan before surgery. Verify the actual formulation, dose, last dose and other sedatives. Preserve established baseline opioid exposure unless a safety concern requires adjustment. Arrange regional or local infiltration and non-opioid therapy suited to the hip operation and the patient’s renal, cardiovascular and bleeding risks. Involve the acute pain service for complex tolerance or difficult recovery.

Provide additional short-acting rescue for new surgical pain, with dosing titrated to observed effect, sedation and ventilation. If oral dosing is impossible, plan equivalent baseline cover with a monitored, specialist-guided alternative. Allow for incomplete cross-tolerance if the opioid changes. Check whether monitored PCA is suitable for cognition and ability to self-dose. Avoid stacking baseline, nurse rescue and PCA prescriptions. In refractory pain a specialist may consider ketamine. Avoid automatic addition of gabapentinoids or other sedatives in an older person.

Reassess alertness, ventilatory status, constipation, delirium, pain during movement and participation in physiotherapy. Investigate new disproportionate pain or functional deterioration rather than assuming tolerance. Recover on the verified baseline oral regimen when safe and taper additional rescue as surgical pain improves. With consent, ask the usual prescriber to review longer-term oxycodone need as chronic hip pain changes. Provide limited quantities, written instructions and a named follow-up, and consider overdose prevention by risk.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Address tolerance, physical dependence, possible addiction and harms, then apply them to the postoperative prescription and follow-up.

items.title: 2014.1 Q15: Persistent postsurgical pain: definition and prevention
items.q: Define persistent post surgical pain. Outline the interventions that are efficacious in reducing the transition of acute post surgical pain to persistent post surgical pain.
items.model:
## Definition and risk

Under the current IASP/ICD-11 definition, chronic postsurgical pain develops or increases after an operation, persists beyond healing for at least three months and is localised to the operative region, the territory of a nerve in that region or a referred dermatome. Exclude infection, malignancy, mechanical failure and unchanged continuation of a pre-existing pain disorder. Pain can be mixed nociceptive and neuropathic. The report used an older two-month definition.

Thoracotomy, breast or axillary surgery, major amputation and other operations with nerve injury are higher-risk examples. Pre-existing pain, poor function, sleep difficulties, distress and severe or poorly resolving postoperative pain prompt greater support. Predictors describe probability, and may reflect operation severity or other confounding. A high score in recovery by itself neither diagnoses a chronic disorder nor proves that a particular treatment will prevent one.

## Preop

Identify high-risk procedures and an adverse baseline pain trajectory. Ask about pain at the operative site and elsewhere, opioids, mood, sleep, fear of movement and expectations. Discuss expected recovery in practical terms and arrange targeted psychological or pain-service input for those already struggling with function. Maintain necessary baseline analgesia and discuss an individualised perioperative plan. Explain who to contact if movement or pain worsens after discharge.

## Intraop

Minimise tissue and nerve injury where surgical options allow. Use a procedure-specific multimodal regimen with appropriate non-opioids and regional or local analgesia. Regional evidence is strongest in selected procedures and differs by technique and time point. A 2026 network meta-analysis supports a potential preventive role for some extended regional approaches, with uncertainty across procedures. Balance any potential long-term benefit against immediate benefits, risk and monitoring needs. Avoid routine perioperative gabapentinoids for prevention. A ketamine infusion may have an acute role in selected opioid-tolerant patients, with uncertainty about reliable prevention of chronic pain.

## Postop

Assess pain on movement and its trajectory, neurological symptoms and function. Severe pain warrants review for complications, nerve injury or ineffective analgesia. Support appropriate mobilisation, sleep and function. Write an opioid taper or stop plan, with limited rescue and a named prescriber. Escalate pain that is poorly resolving over the first weeks or interferes with rehabilitation. A transitional pain service may coordinate medication, rehabilitation and psychological support, with limited comparative evidence for preventing chronic pain. Review persistent symptoms for infection, recurrence, unrelated pathology or an unchanged pre-existing pain disorder before diagnosing chronic postsurgical pain.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · The report expected a definition, exclusion of other causes and discussion of surgical, pharmacological, regional and psychological measures. Its historical duration criterion was two months.

items.title: 2012.1 Q1: Serotonin syndrome: risks, features, treatment
items.q: In regard to serotonin syndrome a. What are the risk factors? (20%) b. What are the clinical manifestations? (40%) c. What is the treatment for an acute episode of serotonin syndrome? (40%)
items.model:
## a. Risk factors (20%)

- **Drugs that raise serotonin:** SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and **MAO inhibitors** (including linezolid, moclobemide and **methylene blue**); **opioids** (tramadol, pethidine, fentanyl, oxycodone, methadone); ondansetron and granisetron; triptans; lithium; St John's wort; amphetamines, MDMA and cocaine; dextromethorphan; L-tryptophan.
- **Combinations**, rather than single drugs: an SSRI plus a serotonergic opioid or methylene blue (severe toxicity is not reported with single agents).
- **Pharmacokinetic:** CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 inhibition or polymorphism, a recent dose increase, overdose, and the long washout of fluoxetine (up to 7 days).
- **Setting:** about 13.7% of major-surgery patients receive an SSRI perioperatively, and cardiac surgery with high-dose fentanyl accounts for many cases.

## b. Clinical manifestations (40%)

The **triad** of mental state change, neuromuscular excitation and autonomic hyperactivity, usually developing suddenly within 24 to 48 hours.
- **Mental state:** agitation, confusion, anxiety, delirium, delayed emergence, coma in severe cases.
- **Neuromuscular:** tremor, hyperreflexia, **clonus (inducible, spontaneous or ocular)**, myoclonus, nystagmus, hypertonia (greatest in the lower limbs).
- **Autonomic:** hyperthermia, tachycardia, labile hypertension or hypotension, diaphoresis, mydriasis, diarrhoea and hyperactive bowel sounds, shivering.
- **Severe:** temperature above 41°C, rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, renal failure, DIC, seizures.
The Hunter criteria (sensitivity 84%, specificity 97%) are the preferred diagnostic tool. The differential (a diagnosis of exclusion) includes neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, anticholinergic toxicity and sepsis. Perioperatively the signs may be masked by anaesthesia, drapes and neuromuscular blockade, so unexplained hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating or delayed emergence should raise suspicion.

## c. Treatment of an acute episode (40%)

- **1.** **Admit** and **stop** all serotonergic agents and recognise and remove the trigger (for example methylene blue).
- **2.** **Supportive care**: airway, oxygen, IV fluids, monitoring in HDU/ICU, correct metabolic derangement, treat rhabdomyolysis with fluids.
- **3.** **Sedation with benzodiazepines** for agitation and muscle activity.
- **4.** **Cooling** for hyperthermia; paracetamol is not effective; for severe or rapidly rising hyperthermia with rigidity, intubate, ventilate and paralyse with a **non-depolarising** agent (avoid suxamethonium). Dantrolene is unproven.
- **5.** **Autonomic instability:** fluids and direct vasopressors for hypotension (noradrenaline, phenylephrine); short-acting esmolol or GTN for hypertension and tachycardia; avoid indirect agents (ephedrine, dopamine), hydralazine and long-acting beta-blockers.
- **6.** Enteral cyproheptadine may be considered with toxicology in selected cases. Outcome benefit remains uncertain and supportive treatment takes priority.
- **7.** Mild cases resolve within 24 hours of stopping the drug; observe severe cases for days.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Use the question weighting and connect symptoms, organ dysfunction and treatments.

items.title: 2011.2 Q10: Transdermal buprenorphine patch and knee arthroscopy
items.q: A 70-year-old patient wearing a transdermal buprenorphine slow release patch (Norspan®) (5μg/h) presents for knee arthroscopy. a. Describe the mechanism of action and pharmacokinetic profile of this patch. (50%) b. What are the implications for perioperative pain management? (50%)
items.model:
## a. Mechanism and pharmacokinetics (50%)

**Mechanism.** Buprenorphine is a **partial agonist at the mu receptor** (with very high affinity and slow dissociation), an **antagonist at kappa and delta** receptors, and an agonist at the ORL-1 (nociceptin) receptor. The partial agonism produces a **ceiling effect** for respiratory depression (not for analgesia at low doses) and lower abuse potential. Because of the high affinity, it can displace full agonists, which is the theoretical reason for antagonising effect (BJA).

**Norspan 5 micrograms/h** is a 7-day matrix patch (5, 10, 20 micrograms/h).
- **Absorption:** lipophilic, transdermal delivery through the skin matrix; bioavailability about 15%; steady state reached after the first patch, with first detectable levels at about 12 to 24 hours and **peak at about 3 days**, and a depot in skin means continued absorption for hours after removal.
- **Distribution:** highly protein bound (96%).
- **Metabolism:** hepatic (CYP3A4 N-dealkylation to norbuprenorphine, an active metabolite with weak activity, and glucuronidation); excretion mainly in faeces (biliary), with little renal dependence.
- **Elimination:** half-life about 26 hours after patch removal, so effects persist.
- Heat (fever, warming devices) increases absorption.

This is a low-dose analgesic patch. Dose equivalence is approximate and distinct from higher-dose sublingual or depot formulations for opioid use disorder.

## Preop

Confirm the indication, correct patch location, last change and other sedatives or opioids. Assess renal and respiratory risk and frailty. Continue this low-dose patch in usual circumstances to maintain baseline analgesia. Explain that its slow onset makes patch adjustment unsuitable for immediate surgical pain.

## Intraop

Avoid direct heat over the patch. Choose anaesthesia for the planned arthroscopy and use local infiltration, an appropriate peripheral technique or simple analgesia. Use short-acting full μ agonist rescue when needed. The low-dose patch generally does not prevent effective rescue. Titrate to clinical effect and ventilatory risk, especially in this older patient.

## Postop

Assess pain with activity, sedation and ventilation. Continue the regular patch schedule and avoid replacing it early to treat acute pain. Use paracetamol and NSAID if suitable, with limited immediate-release rescue only when needed, and communicate the taper and baseline regimen to the prescriber. Avoid unnecessary sedatives. For clinically important ventilatory depression, support the airway and breathing and use naloxone according to the local protocol, with ongoing monitoring for recurrence.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Address patch kinetics, adverse effects, older patients and how full μ agonist rescue can still be used.

items.title: 2009.1 Q14: Persistent pain after fracture on high-dose oxycodone
items.q: A previously healthy 28-year-old male has persistent pain 12 weeks after a compound fracture to his lower leg and is on slow release oxycodone 80mg twice daily and immediate-release oxycodone 20mg 4 hourly. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of switching his opioid to methadone in this situation and how this may be achieved safely.
items.model:
## Reassess before switching

Check actual oxycodone consumption, including whether every four-hour dose is taken, the reason for escalation, sedation, function and concurrent sedatives. Examine the limb and assess healing, infection, non-union, neuropathic injury, ischaemia and CRPS. Discuss tolerance, withdrawal between doses, opioid-induced hyperalgesia and opioid use disorder without assuming any one explains the symptoms. Agree functional goals and discuss rehabilitation, treatment of the underlying cause, opioid reduction or rotation. Rotation is neither mandatory nor a substitute for investigating persistent pain.

## Advantages and disadvantages

Methadone is an orally active full μ agonist without clinically important active metabolites. Rotation may improve tolerability or reduce reliance on frequent breakthrough doses in selected patients. Its NMDA and monoaminergic effects provide a theoretical rationale for selected mixed or neuropathic pain. These mechanisms do not establish clinical superiority for this patient. Analgesia may wear off before the drug is eliminated, and repeated doses can accumulate for days. Delayed respiratory depression, prolonged QT, interactions and incomplete cross-tolerance are major hazards. Consider the patient’s cardiac history, electrolytes, ECG, concurrent QT-prolonging or interacting medicines, sleep-disordered breathing, alcohol and benzodiazepine use. Methadone still carries dependence, constipation and overdose risks.

## Safe conversion

Refer to a pain or experienced opioid prescriber. Reconcile prescribed and actual dose and use a locally approved, methadone-specific nonlinear protocol. The ratio depends on the previous opioid exposure and a simple reciprocal conversion or standard rotation percentage is inappropriate. Choose a monitored setting according to dose, comorbidities and home support. A specialist may prescribe a low initial dose with a staged supervised replacement. Define how the old opioid is withdrawn and what limited short-acting rescue can be used without overlapping uncontrolled doses. Avoid frequent unsupervised increases. Review pain, mobility, sedation, respiratory status, rescue use and adverse effects frequently and after each change, especially as the methadone accumulates. Document whom to contact if oversedation occurs, review QT risk, consider access to naloxone and assign one clinician to oversee supply. Stop or revise the plan if there is no net functional benefit.

Use clear written instructions for the patient and family. Explain why the conversion needs days of observation despite early changes in pain, and which prescriber should authorise each adjustment.

items.title: 2008.2 Q11: Risk factors and mechanisms of chronic postsurgical pain
items.q: List the risk factors for the development of chronic pain following a surgical procedure. Outline possible mechanisms for the progression of acute to chronic pain.
items.model:
## Risk factors

Group risks by timing and ask what they mean for this patient. Preoperative risk includes persistent pain at the operative site or elsewhere, prior surgery, opioid exposure, severe distress, depression, anxiety, fear of movement, poor sleep and limited social support. Pain-related disability and expectations may help identify a need for structured rehabilitation. Associations with compensation or work disruption do not determine the credibility of pain or establish a single causal mechanism.

Intraoperative risks include an operation with substantial tissue trauma, a documented or possible nerve injury, prolonged dissection or repeated procedures. Examples include thoracotomy, breast or axillary surgery and amputation. After surgery, severe or poorly resolving dynamic pain, neuropathic features, painful complications, delayed rehabilitation and some subsequent cancer treatments are associated with persistent symptoms. Review alternative pathology and distinguish the pain trajectory from a single pain score.

## Mechanisms

At the surgical site, injury and inflammatory mediators sensitise peripheral nociceptors and reduce thresholds. Nerve injury can cause ectopic discharges in the injured nerve or dorsal root ganglion and produce symptoms linking electrically evoked, burning or stabbing pain to a relevant sensory territory. Persistent afferent input and disinhibition at the dorsal horn increase excitability, including NMDA-mediated responses and enhanced temporal summation. Previously non-painful input can become painful. Glial activation and neuroimmune signalling may contribute to the persistence of these changes.

Central pain modulation can shift towards facilitation or reduced descending inhibition. Changes in sensory processing can explain pain extending beyond the immediate injury site. Fear, poor sleep and avoidance can interact with biological sensitisation by increasing vigilance and reducing opportunities for confident movement. These factors do not imply that pain is imaginary. Several mechanisms may coexist, and a mechanism is not proved by pain intensity or a single symptom.

## Clinical connection

Chronic postsurgical pain develops or increases after surgery and lasts at least three months after alternative explanations have been assessed. Evaluate the mechanism when pain recovery deviates from expectation. A new objective deficit needs surgical assessment. Persistent sensory gain or loss in a plausible distribution warrants neuropathic evaluation. Document functional targets and arrange rehabilitation and follow-up rather than escalating opioids in isolation.

**Sources:** Examiner feedback · Weight risks and mechanisms evenly. The report highlighted pre-existing pain and distress, nerve injury procedures, severe postoperative pain and peripheral/central mechanisms.

Identifies nerve injury and higher-risk operations
Recognises postoperative pain trajectory and complications
Describes peripheral sensitisation and ectopic firing
Explains spinal central sensitisation and modulation
Links mechanisms and trajectory to assessment and follow-up
